Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between looping and depth-growing in LLMs, and do they share a common mechanism for improving reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies looping and depth-growing in LLMs, showing they share mechanistic signatures of iterative computation and can be composed to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Depth growing and looping are complementary methods for inducing iterative computation to improve reasoning, and their unification suggests a simple reasoning recipe.
papers.key_findings:
Looped and depth-grown models exhibit similar depth-wise computational signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and periodic patterns aligned with the block size.
Depth-grown models can be looped at inference time to improve reasoning performance without being trained to loop.
Looped and depth-grown models adapt better than baselines to in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning.
Depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using high-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures.
The 'grow first, loop later' strategy yields the strongest reasoning performance under matched data and inference FLOPs.
papers.limitation: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models may improve performance, but this is left for future work.
future_direction: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Looping, reusing a block of layers across depth, and depth growing, training shallow-to-deep models by duplicating middle layers, have both been linked to stronger reasoning, but their relationship remains unclear. We provide a mechanistic unification: looped and depth-grown models exhibit convergent depth-wise signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and recurring patterns aligned with the looped or grown block. These shared signatures support the view that their gains stem from a common form of iterative computation. Building on this connection, we show that the two techniques are adaptable and composable: applying inference-time looping to the middle blocks of a depth-grown model improves accuracy on some reasoning primitives by up to $2\times$, despite the model never being trained to loop. Both approaches also adapt better than the baseline when given more in-context examples or additional supervised fine-tuning data. Additionally, depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using higher-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures, which can be further boosted by adapting a middle block to loop. Overall, our results position depth growth and looping as complementary, practical methods for inducing and scaling iterative computation to improve reasoning.

papers.title: In Search of Grandmother Cells: Tracing Interpretable Neurons in Tabular Representations
papers.research_question: Do interpretable neurons (grandmother cells) exist in tabular foundation models, and can they be identified using simple information-theoretic measures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes two information-theoretic measures (surprisal and selectivity) to quantify neuronal saliency and selectivity for single concepts, and applies them to TabPFN, providing the first evidence that some neurons in tabular foundation models show moderate, statistically significant saliency and selectivity for high-level concepts.
papers.conclusion: The proposed information-theoretic testing framework provides a useful tool for mechanistic interpretability researchers and practitioners to analyze concept representations in foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Some neuron-concept pairs in TabPFN reach high surprisal (up to log(N)=7.74) and moderate selectivity (up to 0.73) values.
The proposed search procedure Pareto-dominates sparse probes based on SHAP values and optimal probing.
For two of the four prediction tasks (ICU transfer within 12h and hospitalization), the identified knee points (most salient and selective neuron-concept pairs) are statistically significant (p < 0.05).
Interpretable neurons can emerge naturally in tabular foundation models and can be uncovered, in some cases, with a simple search across neuron-concept pairs without complex interpretability techniques.
Neurons with significant saliency and selectivity were found across initial, middle, and final layers, suggesting concepts are not preferentially represented at certain layers.
papers.limitation:
The significance tests are asymptotic and assume i.i.d. mutual information and surprisal scores, which does not account for variations in empirical distributions (e.g., due to data scarcity) nor for structural dependencies in the network architecture or concept label space.
The surprisal and selectivity scores did not reach statistical significance in all tasks, which may reflect that some prediction targets depend on multiple interacting factors rather than single concepts.
The selectivity values remained at or below 0.73, meaning the method did not identify 'grandmother cells' that almost exclusively respond to single concepts.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are powerful yet often opaque in their decision-making. A topic of continued interest in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence is whether some neurons behave like grandmother cells, i.e., neurons that are inherently interpretable because they exclusively respond to single concepts. In this work, we propose two information-theoretic measures that quantify the neuronal saliency and selectivity for single concepts. We apply these metrics to the representations of TabPFN, a tabular foundation model, and perform a simple search across neuron-concept pairs to find the most salient and selective pair. Our analysis provides the first evidence that some neurons in such models show moderate, statistically significant saliency and selectivity for high-level concepts. These findings suggest that interpretable neurons can emerge naturally and that they can, in some cases, be identified without resorting to more complex interpretability techniques.

papers.title: Cross-Model Semantics in Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How do structural constraints affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures? To what extent are learned representations tied to specific architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes representational alignment across architectures and demonstrates that structural regularities induce more stable representational geometry, improving interoperability of learned features.
papers.conclusion: PGNN integrates structural priors to enhance learning efficiency and generalization, and structural constraints can improve representational transferability across models.
papers.key_findings:
PGNN exhibits faster convergence and slightly higher test accuracy compared to baseline MLP.
Ablation shows that removing structural projection in PGNN leads to lower performance, confirming its utility.
PGNN shows similar robustness to initialization noise as MLP, with slight advantages under mild noise.
Representational alignment metrics show that structured representations can be partially aligned across architectures.
The framework enables measurement of alignment using CKA, subspace overlap, and transfer accuracy.
papers.limitation: Extrapolation to more complex datasets like CIFAR-10 did not show a major advantage for PGNN.
future_direction: Adapting and scaling PGNN to broader domains and more complex data distributions.
papers.abstract: The internal representations learned by deep networks are often sensitive to architecture-specific choices, raising questions about the stability, alignment, and transferability of learned structure across models. In this paper, we investigate how structural constraints--such as linear shaping operators and corrective paths--affect the compatibility of internal representations across different architectures. Building on the insights from prior studies on structured transformations and convergence, we develop a framework for measuring and analyzing representational alignment across networks with distinct but related architectural priors. Through a combination of theoretical insights, empirical probes, and controlled transfer experiments, we demonstrate that structural regularities induce representational geometry that is more stable under architectural variation. This suggests that certain forms of inductive bias not only support generalization within a model, but also improve the interoperability of learned features across models. We conclude with a discussion on the implications of representational transferability for model distillation, modular learning, and the principled design of robust learning systems.

papers.title: Learning a Fourier Transform for Linear Relative Positional Encodings in Transformers
papers.research_question: How to efficiently incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs) into linear Transformers, enabling linear complexity for both sequential and geometric data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), a class of linear Transformers that efficiently incorporate relative positional encodings (RPEs) by learning their spectral representation, achieving linear complexity and applicability to sequential and geometric data.
papers.conclusion: FLTs provide an efficient and effective method for incorporating RPEs into linear attention Transformers, with theoretical approximation guarantees and strong empirical performance across text, image, and 3D molecular data.
papers.key_findings:
FLTs outperform other linear Transformers (e.g., Performer, CosFormer) on language modeling (WikiText-103) by achieving lower perplexity.
FLTs achieve higher accuracy than baselines on image classification tasks (ImageNet, Places365, Fashion-MNIST).
For 3D molecular property prediction (OC20 dataset), FLTs with RPEs provide better energy prediction accuracy (lower MAE, higher EwT) than Performers without RPEs.
FLTs maintain linear time and space complexity, being more memory-efficient than log-linear Performer baselines.
FLTs can learn local RPEs and exhibit both local and global attention patterns in language modeling.
papers.abstract: We propose a new class of linear Transformers called FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), which incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs). These include regular RPE techniques applied for sequential data, as well as novel RPEs operating on geometric data embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. FLTs construct the optimal RPE mechanism implicitly by learning its spectral representation. As opposed to other architectures combining efficient low-rank linear attention with RPEs, FLTs remain practical in terms of their memory usage and do not require additional assumptions about the structure of the RPE mask. Besides, FLTs allow for applying certain structural inductive bias techniques to specify masking strategies, e.g. they provide a way to learn the so-called local RPEs introduced in this paper and give accuracy gains as compared with several other linear Transformers for language modeling. We also thoroughly test FLTs on other data modalities and tasks, such as image classification, 3D molecular modeling, and learnable optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, for 3D molecular data, FLTs are the first Transformer architectures providing linear attention and incorporating RPE masking.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
papers.conclusion: Exploiting latent linearity in LLM representations provides a principled basis for effective and explainable molecular representation learning, improving accuracy, explainability, and efficiency in molecular property prediction.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-derived molecular representations exhibit latent linearity that can be expressed as a weighted combination of chemically meaningful functional group concepts.
MoleX outperforms existing GNN, LLM, and explainable machine learning baselines in predictive accuracy and explanation faithfulness on benchmark molecular property prediction tasks.
A residual calibration strategy corrects errors from the base linear predictor, further improving accuracy and explanation alignment with ground-truth substructures.
MoleX achieves significant computational efficiency, with CPU inference over 300x faster than LLMs and using 100,000 fewer parameters.
The linear predictor's performance scales with model size, training precision, and dataset size, but task-adapted training is crucial for converting capacity into performance gains.
papers.limitation: The linear predictor may underfit complex molecular patterns in some cases, as there is a trade-off between model complexity and performance.
future_direction: Examine the complexity–performance trade-off in LLM-based molecular representation learning to identify optimal balances between model complexity and downstream performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad utility across molecular domains, spanning drug discovery and materials design. Analyzing LLMs' latent representations is crucial for elucidating their underlying mechanisms, improving explainability, and ultimately advancing downstream performance. We propose MoleX, a simple yet effective framework that decomposes molecular embeddings within LLM representations into a concept-aligned space for explainable molecular representation learning. We further show that these high-dimensional embeddings admit a linear mapping onto chemically consistent concepts. Our analysis suggests that the uncovered linearity aligns with established chemical principles, indicating a mechanistically explainable latent structure in LLM representations for scientific applications. When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: Attention Sinks: A 'Catch, Tag, Release' Mechanism for Embeddings
papers.research_question: This paper investigates why attention sinks emerge in later tokens, whether they encode semantically meaningful information, how they differ between pretrained and reasoning models, and the impact of query-key normalization on attention sinks.
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism in LLMs, where attention sinks catch tokens, tag them with semantically meaningful information, and release the tags into the residual stream for later use. The mechanism is prevalent across model families, more pronounced in reasoning models, and persists despite query-key normalization.
papers.conclusion: This work uncovers and formalizes the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism mediated by attention sinks, showing that sinks implement a functional tagging system that propagates semantically meaningful information across tokens, offering a foundation for deeper mechanistic investigations.
papers.key_findings:
Attention sinks implement a 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, where sinks catch tokens, tag them with a common direction, and release the tags into the residual stream.
Tags encode semantically meaningful information, such as the truth value of statements, as shown by probing experiments.
Reasoning-distilled models exhibit the mechanism more strongly, with more attention sinks and higher variance explained by tags.
Attention sinks remain prevalent in models with query-key normalization, despite the normalization's intended effect.
The mechanism can emerge through training in a minimal theoretical model designed to solve a sequence averaging task.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical model does not prove the mechanism is necessary and may not reflect real-world complexity.
The threshold-based metric for identifying attention sinks may not capture all such tokens and lacks a principled method for setting the threshold.
The connection between the mechanism and reasoning is suggestive but not causally established.
future_direction: Deeper mechanistic investigations into token interactions and the role of implicit memory in transformers.
Establishing a causal link between the mechanism and reasoning.
Exploring practical applications such as steering activations for alignment and safety, and preserving the mechanism in model compression.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often concentrate their attention on a few specific tokens referred to as attention sinks. Common examples include the first token, a prompt-independent sink, and punctuation tokens, which are prompt-dependent. While the tokens causing the sinks often lack direct semantic meaning, the presence of the sinks is critical for model performance, particularly under model compression and KV-caching. Despite their ubiquity, the function, semantic role, and origin of attention sinks -- especially those beyond the first token -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation demonstrating that attention sinks: catch a sequence of tokens, tag them using a common direction in embedding space, and release them back into the residual stream, where tokens are later retrieved based on the tags they have acquired. Probing experiments reveal these tags carry semantically meaningful information, such as the truth of a statement. These findings extend to reasoning models, where the mechanism spans more heads and explains greater variance in embeddings, or recent models with query-key normalization, where sinks remain just as prevalent. To encourage future theoretical analysis, we introduce a minimal problem which can be solved through the 'catch, tag, release' mechanism, and where it emerges through training.

papers.title: The Representational Geometry of Number
papers.research_question: How do number representations in language models maintain a stable relational structure across different tasks, and how are task-specific subspaces related?
papers.core_contribution: Number representations in language models preserve a stable relational structure across tasks, with task-specific subspaces that are largely transformable via linear mappings, balancing shared structure and functional flexibility.
papers.conclusion: The representational geometry of numbers in LLMs reveals a shared relational structure that supports task flexibility through linear transformations, unifying previous theories and extending beyond number concepts.
papers.key_findings:
Number embeddings maintain a consistent sequential order across tasks, as visualized with t-SNE.
Distance, size, and ratio effects are preserved across tasks, indicating human-like magnitude encoding.
Low-level features like parity and magnitude are encoded in separable linear directions, with parity nearly orthogonal to magnitude.
Task-specific representations occupy distinct subspaces with low overlap but high canonical correlation, showing they are related by linear transformations.
The relational structure is shared across models and formats, as shown by low Procrustes disparity.
papers.abstract: A central question in cognitive science is whether conceptual representations converge onto a shared manifold to support generalization, or diverge into orthogonal subspaces to minimize task interference. While prior work has discovered evidence for both, a mechanistic account of how these properties coexist and transform across tasks remains elusive. We propose that representational sharing lies not in the concepts themselves, but in the geometric relations between them. Using number concepts as a testbed and language models as high-dimensional computational substrates, we show that number representations preserve a stable relational structure across tasks. Task-specific representations are embedded in distinct subspaces, with low-level features like magnitude and parity encoded along separable linear directions. Crucially, we find that these subspaces are largely transformable into one another via linear mappings, indicating that representations share relational structure despite being located in distinct subspaces. Together, these results provide a mechanistic lens of how language models balance the shared structure of number representation with functional flexibility. It suggests that understanding arises when task-specific transformations are applied to a shared underlying relational structure of conceptual representations.

papers.title: Discriminating image representations with principal distortions
papers.research_question: How can we quantify and compare the local geometry of different image representations, especially when global similarity measures are insufficient?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for comparing local geometries of image representations using a metric based on Fisher information matrices and optimizes 'principal distortions' to maximize variance across models.
papers.conclusion: Principal distortions provide an efficient method for comparing image representations and reveal differences in local geometries that are not captured by global similarity measures.
papers.key_findings:
The method differentiates early visual models (LN, LG, LGG, LGN) and suggests which are closer to human perception.
For deep neural networks, the method reveals architectural differences: AlexNet is more sensitive to distortions in textured regions, while ResNet50 is more sensitive to distortions in smooth regions.
Adversarial training changes local geometry more than stylized ImageNet training.
The method is efficient, requiring only two distortions to compare multiple models.
Principal distortions can be used for model interpretability and for designing psychophysics experiments.
papers.limitation:
The framework is based on local linear approximations, which may not hold for highly nonlinear models.
Assumption of additive Gaussian noise may not be realistic for neural systems.
The Fisher Information Matrix may be degenerate in some cases.
future_direction: Extending the method to synthesize more than two distortions (like additional principal components).
Comparing continuous families of models with a prior distribution.
Using Poisson noise to better capture neural responses.
papers.abstract: Image representations (artificial or biological) are often compared in terms of their global geometric structure; however, representations with similar global structure can have strikingly different local geometries. Here, we propose a framework for comparing a set of image representations in terms of their local geometries. We quantify the local geometry of a representation using the Fisher information matrix, a standard statistical tool for characterizing the sensitivity to local stimulus distortions, and use this as a substrate for a metric on the local geometry in the vicinity of a base image. This metric may then be used to optimally differentiate a set of models, by finding a pair of "principal distortions" that maximize the variance of the models under this metric. As an example, we use this framework to compare a set of simple models of the early visual system, identifying a novel set of image distortions that allow immediate comparison of the models by visual inspection. In a second example, we apply our method to a set of deep neural network models and reveal differences in the local geometry that arise due to architecture and training types. These examples demonstrate how our framework can be used to probe for informative differences in local sensitivities between complex models, and suggest how it could be used to compare model representations with human perception.

papers.title: The Logical Implication Steering Method for Conditional Interventions on Transformer Generation
papers.research_question: How to leverage concept vectors to build logical implication into pre-trained transformer models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments to induce generation behavior in response to concepts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS) method, which uses concept vectors to program logical implication into pre-trained transformer models for interpretable behavior steering.
papers.conclusion: LIMS unlocks new hand-engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
LIMS improves performance on hallucination detection, unanswerable question rejection, adversarial safety, and math reasoning tasks.
LIMS works effectively in low-data regimes (e.g., with 100 training examples).
LIMS outperforms 10-shot prompting and has advantages over DPO in interpretability and resource usage.
The method is interpretable, allowing decoupled analysis of sensing and steering components.
Mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) performs similarly to LIMS with easier deployment but slightly reduced interpretability.
papers.limitation: The mergeable LIMS (m-LIMS) variant reduces interpretability slightly compared to standard LIMS.
future_direction: Exploring LIMS across different models or modalities.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability in pre-trained transformer models has demonstrated substantial evidence supporting the ''linear representation hypothesis'', which is the idea that high level concepts are encoded as vectors in the space of activations of a model. Studies also show that model generation behavior can be steered toward a given concept by adding the concept's vector to the corresponding activations. We show how to leverage these properties to build a form of logical implication into models, enabling transparent and interpretable adjustments that induce a chosen generation behavior in response to the presence of any given concept. Our method, Logical Implication Model Steering (LIMS), unlocks new hand engineered reasoning capabilities by integrating neuro-symbolic logic into pre-trained transformer models.

papers.title: Representation Shattering in Transformers: A Synthetic Study with Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Why does knowledge editing (KE) degrade models' factual recall and reasoning abilities? The paper aims to develop a mechanistic understanding of how KE affects model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the phenomenon of representation shattering, where knowledge editing distorts the geometric structure of model representations, leading to degradation in factual recall and reasoning abilities.
papers.conclusion: Representation shattering, the distortion of geometric structures in model representations, is a key mechanism by which knowledge editing degrades model performance, highlighting the importance of preserving representational structures.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing degrades model accuracy on direct recall, logical inference, and compositional inference.
Transformers internalize the structure of the knowledge graph in their representations, forming geometric manifolds.
KE distorts these representations, shattering the geometric structure, which explains the degradation in model capabilities.
The degree of representation shattering increases with the distance between the original and edited fact on the manifold.
Representation shattering generalizes to pre-trained LLMs (e.g., Llama, Mamba) and other architectures.
papers.limitation: The use of simplified synthetic tasks and small models may not capture all dynamics of larger, more complex real-world models.
papers.abstract: Knowledge Editing (KE) algorithms alter models' weights to perform targeted updates to incorrect, outdated, or otherwise unwanted factual associations. However, recent work has shown that applying KE can adversely affect models' broader factual recall accuracy and diminish their reasoning abilities. Although these studies give insights into the potential harms of KE algorithms, e.g., performance evaluations on benchmarks, little is understood about why such destructive failures occur. Motivated by this, we define a novel synthetic task in which a Transformer is trained from scratch to internalize a "structured" knowledge graph. The structure enforces relationships between entities of the graph, such that editing a factual association has "trickling effects" on other entities (e.g., altering X's parent is Y to Z affects who X's siblings' parent is). Through evaluations of edited models on this task, we show that KE inadvertently affects representations of entities beyond the targeted one, distorting relevant structures that allow a model to infer unseen knowledge about an entity. We call this phenomenon representation shattering and demonstrate that it degrades models' factual recall and reasoning performance. We further corroborate our findings in naturalistic settings with pre-trained Llama and Mamba models as well. Overall, our work yields a precise mechanistic hypothesis to explain why KE has adverse effects on model abilities.

papers.title: Comparing Computational Pathology Foundation Models using Representational Similarity Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences in the representational structures of computational pathology foundation models, and how do training paradigms affect these representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the representational spaces of six computational pathology foundation models using representational similarity analysis, revealing differences in representational structures, slide- and disease-dependence, and intrinsic dimensionality, and showing that stain normalization reduces slide-dependence.
papers.conclusion: The analytical approach presented can be extended to other medical imaging domains, and gaining insight into the structure of learned representations can inform algorithmic refinement and support safe, effective deployment in clinical settings.
papers.key_findings:
UNI2 and Virchow2 have the most distinct representational structures, while Prov-GigaPath has the highest average similarity across models.
Having the same training paradigm (vision-only vs. vision-language) did not guarantee higher representational similarity.
All models show high slide-dependence but relatively low disease-dependence in their representations.
Stain normalization decreases slide-dependence for all models by a range of 5.5% (CONCH) to 20.5% (PLIP).
Vision-language models have relatively compact representations (lower intrinsic dimensionality) compared to the more distributed representations of vision-only models.
papers.limitation:
The study only used TCGA data, so the results may quantitatively differ in different datasets.
RSA has high CPU memory demand, scaling quadratically with the number of samples, which constrains sample size and requires high-memory computing nodes.
future_direction: Explicitly assess generalizability across different institutions, staining protocols, and scanner hardware, including how the studied representational metrics relate to downstream performance.
Systematically analyze how variations in training datasets and hyperparameters affect representational structure.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly developed in computational pathology (CPath) given their promise in facilitating many downstream tasks. While recent studies have evaluated task performance across models, less is known about the structure and variability of their learned representations. Here, we systematically analyze the representational spaces of six CPath foundation models using techniques popularized in computational neuroscience. The models analyzed span vision-language contrastive learning (CONCH, PLIP, KEEP) and self-distillation (UNI (v2), Virchow (v2), Prov-GigaPath) approaches. Through representational similarity analysis using H&E image patches from TCGA, we find that UNI2 and Virchow2 have the most distinct representational structures, whereas Prov-Gigapath has the highest average similarity across models. Having the same training paradigm (vision-only vs. vision-language) did not guarantee higher representational similarity. The representations of all models showed a high slide-dependence, but relatively low disease-dependence. Stain normalization decreased slide-dependence for all models by a range of 5.5% (CONCH) to 20.5% (PLIP). In terms of intrinsic dimensionality, vision-language models demonstrated relatively compact representations, compared to the more distributed representations of vision-only models. These findings highlight opportunities to improve robustness to slide-specific features, inform model ensembling strategies, and provide insights into how training paradigms shape model representations. Our framework is extendable across medical imaging domains, where probing the internal representations of foundation models can support their effective development and deployment.

papers.title: Editing Conceptual Knowledge for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs possess the capability to modify concepts (conceptual knowledge) and how to evaluate such modifications.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the task of conceptual knowledge editing for LLMs, constructs a benchmark dataset ConceptEdit, and establishes a suite of evaluation metrics including Instance Change and Concept Consistency.
papers.conclusion: Concept editing is a challenging task for LLMs, and existing editing methods have limitations in modifying conceptual knowledge without distorting related instances. This work provides a benchmark and metrics to inspire further research.
papers.key_findings:
Existing knowledge editing methods (FT, ROME, MEMIT, PROMPT) can achieve high reliability in modifying concept-level definitions in LLMs.
These methods perform poorly on concept-specific metrics like Instance Change and Concept Consistency, indicating they distort related instance knowledge.
There is a gap between reliability (token-level accuracy) and concept consistency (semantic similarity of generated definitions).
Concept editing is easier when the replacement definition comes from the same superclass (intra module) compared to a different superclass (inter module).
Causal tracing reveals that conceptual knowledge is stored differently from instance knowledge, with attention mechanisms in earlier layers playing a key role.
papers.limitation:
The experiments are limited to models up to 7B parameters; larger models may exhibit different behaviors.
The generalization of edited concepts to unseen instances or related concepts is not fully explored.
The mechanisms of how LLMs learn and represent concepts and concept hierarchies are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring concept editing in larger-scale language models.
Improving the generalization of edited concepts to related knowledge.
Studying the mechanisms of concept learning and representation in LLMs.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Analysis of Atomistic Representations Using Weighted Skip-Connections
papers.research_question: How do weighted skip-connections help in understanding the relative importance of interaction blocks in SchNet for property prediction, and how does this depend on chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sc-SchNet, a modified SchNet architecture with weighted skip-connections, enabling analysis of the relative importance of interaction blocks for property prediction, revealing dependencies on molecular structure and dataset.
papers.conclusion: sc-SchNet enables interpretable analysis of atomistic representations, showing that contribution weights vary with dataset and molecular structure, providing insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
sc-SchNet performs similarly to SchNet on energy and force prediction tasks.
During training on QM9, contribution weights shift from early layers to later layers as the model learns.
For MD17 trajectories, atom type embeddings have constant contribution due to fixed chemical composition.
Higher interaction blocks are more important for larger and more flexible molecules like salicylic acid and aspirin.
The relative weighting of interaction blocks depends on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules.
future_direction: Investigate if interaction coefficients encode information on locality of different molecular properties.
Explore relation to fundamental modes of molecular motion in the context of the MD17 molecules.
papers.abstract: In this work, we extend the SchNet architecture by using weighted skip connections to assemble the final representation. This enables us to study the relative importance of each interaction block for property prediction. We demonstrate on both the QM9 and MD17 dataset that their relative weighting depends strongly on the chemical composition and configurational degrees of freedom of the molecules which opens the path towards a more detailed understanding of machine learning models for molecules.

papers.title: Decoding Structure-Spectrum Relationships with Physically Organized Latent Spaces
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to construct an interpretable latent space that maps individual structure descriptors to spectral trends in XANES spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RankAAE, a semi-supervised method that constructs an interpretable latent space for spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships by disentangling contributions from multiple structural descriptors.
papers.conclusion: The RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers in interpreting complex scientific data, testing physical hypotheses, and revealing new patterns that extend scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
RankAAE produces a regularized latent space that ensures decoded spectra are physical, unlike standard autoencoders.
The method aligns individual latent dimensions with specific structure descriptors (e.g., oxidation state, coordination number) through a rank constraint.
RankAAE reveals new structure-spectrum relationships that are visually indiscernible in large datasets.
The method works consistently across eight transition metal oxide families (Ti to Cu).
RankAAE enables comparison of different sets of structure descriptors and assesses their importance in capturing spectral variations.
papers.abstract: A new semi-supervised machine learning method for the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships is developed and demonstrated using the specific example of interpreting X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra. This method constructs a one-to-one mapping between individual structure descriptors and spectral trends. Specifically, an adversarial autoencoder is augmented with a novel rank constraint (RankAAE). The RankAAE methodology produces a continuous and interpretable latent space, where each dimension can track an individual structure descriptor. As a part of this process, the model provides a robust and quantitative measure of the structure-spectrum relationship by decoupling intertwined spectral contributions from multiple structural characteristics. This makes it ideal for spectral interpretation and the discovery of new descriptors. The capability of this procedure is showcased by considering five local structure descriptors and a database of over fifty thousand simulated XANES spectra across eight first-row transition metal oxide families. The resulting structure-spectrum relationships not only reproduce known trends in the literature, but also reveal unintuitive ones that are visually indiscernible in large data sets. The results suggest that the RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers to interpret complex scientific data, test physical hypotheses, and reveal new patterns that extend scientific insight.

papers.title: Detection of Phase Transition via Convolutional Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can neural networks detect phase transitions in physical systems without prior knowledge of the order parameter or critical temperature?
papers.core_contribution: A convolutional neural network can detect the phase transition of the 2D Ising model without prior knowledge, and a novel order parameter derived from the network's weight matrix can identify the critical temperature.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks, particularly CNNs, can capture features of phase transitions and can be used to define order parameters that identify critical temperatures in physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrix of the trained CNN shows a domain-like structure with a boundary near the critical temperature.
An order parameter Wsum(β) defined from the weight matrix can be used to extract the critical temperature via fitting.
The extracted critical temperatures for different lattice sizes are consistent with the exact value to within 2-8% accuracy.
The CNN's convolutional filters resemble a real-space renormalization group transformation, capturing local magnetization.
A fully connected neural network also detects the phase transition but with less accuracy than the CNN.
future_direction: Applying the neural network design to other statistical models and non-trivial phases.
papers.abstract:
We design a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) which studies correlation
between discretized inverse temperature and spin configuration of 2D Ising
model and show that it can find a feature of the phase transition without
teaching any a priori information for it. We also define a new order parameter
via the CNN and show that it provides well approximated critical inverse
temperature. In addition, we compare the activation functions for convolution
layer and find that the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is important to detect the
phase transition of 2D Ising model.

papers.title: NeuroFaith: Evaluating LLM Self-Explanation Faithfulness via Internal Representation Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we measure the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations by aligning them with the model's internal reasoning processes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFaith, a framework that measures faithfulness of LLM self-explanations by extracting concepts from explanations and mechanistically testing their influence on predictions, and shows how to detect and improve faithfulness via linear probing and steering.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models tend to produce more faithful and correct self-explanations.
Models can arrive at correct answers through alternative reasoning pathways that bypass explicit bridge object computation (shortcut learning).
There is a gap between internal reasoning and expressed explanations, which decreases with model size.
NeuroFaith outperforms existing faithfulness measures (Counterfactual Intervention and Attribution Agreement) in several settings.
Faithfulness can be linearly detected in representation space and improved through steering.
papers.limitation: Human annotation for concept extraction is costly and may not scale, while LLM-as-a-Judge approaches offer scalability but may miss relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate plausible free text self-explanations to justify their answers. However, these natural language explanations may not accurately reflect the model's actual reasoning process, pinpointing a lack of faithfulness. Existing faithfulness evaluation methods rely primarily on behavioral tests or computational block analysis without examining the semantic content of internal neural representations. This paper proposes NeuroFaith, a flexible framework that measures the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanation by identifying key concepts within explanations and mechanistically testing whether these concepts actually influence the model's predictions. We show the versatility of NeuroFaith across 2-hop reasoning and classification tasks. Additionally, we develop a linear faithfulness probe based on NeuroFaith to detect unfaithful self-explanations from representation space and improve faithfulness through steering. NeuroFaith provides a principled approach to evaluating and enhancing the faithfulness of LLM free text self-explanations, addressing critical needs for trustworthy AI systems.

papers.title: On the Intrinsic Limits of Transformer Image Embeddings in Non-Solvable Spatial Reasoning
papers.research_question: Is the failure of Vision Transformers in spatial reasoning tasks due to insufficient data or an intrinsic complexity barrier of the architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a theoretical complexity boundary proving that constant-depth Vision Transformers cannot capture the algebraic structure of non-solvable spatial transformation groups (e.g., SO(3)), and empirically validates this with a novel benchmark showing structural collapse in ViT embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Spatial reasoning over non-solvable groups is computationally lower-bounded by NC1, making it impossible for constant-depth architectures like ViTs to faithfully capture these dynamics, necessitating a paradigm shift in architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Vision Transformers are theoretically bounded by the complexity class TC0 and cannot efficiently solve NC1-hard problems like the Word Problem for non-solvable groups.
Empirical evaluation using the Latent Space Algebra benchmark shows ViT representations suffer catastrophic structural collapse on non-solvable transformation sequences as compositional depth increases.
The failure is intrinsic to the constant-depth architecture and not merely due to insufficient data or optimization artifacts.
Even self-supervised models like DINOv2, trained to preserve geometry, cannot overcome this architectural limitation.
The phenomenon of 'Abelian Collapse' occurs where ViTs approximate the largest solvable quotient of a non-solvable group.
future_direction: Designing future architectures that reconcile the logical depth required for algebraic processing with the analog stability of neural training.
Developing hybrid architectures or explicit geometric modules to ensure logical robustness in safety-critical applications.
papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) excel in semantic recognition but exhibit systematic failures in spatial reasoning tasks such as mental rotation. While often attributed to data scale, we propose that this limitation arises from the intrinsic circuit complexity of the architecture. We formalize spatial understanding as learning a Group Homomorphism: mapping image sequences to a latent space that preserves the algebraic structure of the underlying transformation group. We demonstrate that for non-solvable groups (e.g., the 3D rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$), maintaining such a structure-preserving embedding is computationally lower-bounded by the Word Problem, which is $\mathsf{NC^1}$-complete. In contrast, we prove that constant-depth ViTs with polynomial precision are strictly bounded by $\mathsf{TC^0}$. Under the conjecture $\mathsf{TC^0} \subsetneq \mathsf{NC^1}$, we establish a complexity boundary: constant-depth ViTs fundamentally lack the logical depth to efficiently capture non-solvable spatial structures. We validate this complexity gap via latent-space probing, demonstrating that ViT representations suffer a structural collapse on non-solvable tasks as compositional depth increases.

papers.title: Understanding image representations by measuring their equivariance and\n equivalence
papers.research_question: How can we empirically establish the equivariance, invariance, and equivalence properties of image representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to empirically study equivariance, invariance, and equivalence of image representations, and applies them to reveal that shallow representations and early CNN layers transform predictably with image warps and are interchangeable, while deeper layers are more task-specific.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for learning equivariant and equivalence mappings are effective analytical tools for understanding image representations and have practical applications such as accelerating structured-output regression.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow representations (like HOG) and the first several layers of deep CNNs transform in an easily predictable manner with image warps.
Deeper CNN layers are less equivariant and more task-specific, but can still be partially transformed.
Different CNN architectures can be stitched together with linear transformations, showing equivalence in early layers.
The learned equivariant mappings can be used to accelerate structured-output regression, such as pose estimation.
Invariance to certain transformations (e.g., horizontal flips) is achieved in middle layers of CNNs, while invariance to unexpected transformations (e.g., vertical flips) is less common.
papers.abstract:
Despite the importance of image representations such as histograms of
oriented gradients and deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), our
theoretical understanding of them remains limited. Aiming at filling this gap,
we investigate three key mathematical properties of representations:
equivariance, invariance, and equivalence. Equivariance studies how
transformations of the input image are encoded by the representation,
invariance being a special case where a transformation has no effect.
Equivalence studies whether two representations, for example two different
parametrisations of a CNN, capture the same visual information or not. A number
of methods to establish these properties empirically are proposed, including
introducing transformation and stitching layers in CNNs. These methods are then
applied to popular representations to reveal insightful aspects of their
structure, including clarifying at which layers in a CNN certain geometric
invariances are achieved. While the focus of the paper is theoretical, direct
applications to structured-output regression are demonstrated too.

papers.title: Prometheus Mind: Retrofitting Memory to Frozen Language Models
papers.research_question: How can memory be retrofitted to a frozen pretrained language model without architectural changes or weight modification, and in a fully reversible manner?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that memory can be retrofitted to a frozen language model using 11 modular adapters (7% parameter overhead) that are fully reversible, by solving four key problems: extraction via Contrastive Direction Discovery, reliable stage-wise training, zero-training injection via Identity V (lm_head.weight), and fixing hidden state collapse via learned projections.
papers.conclusion: Memory can be retrofitted to frozen language models without architectural changes using modular, reversible adapters, and the principles of CDD, stage-wise training, Identity V, and hidden state projection provide a pathway for adding capabilities to frozen models.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Direction Discovery (CDD) can extract semantic directions (subject, verb, object, temporal) from transformer hidden states without labeled data by contrasting minimal pairs.
Stage-wise training of each adapter on simple proxy tasks succeeds where end-to-end joint optimization collapses.
Using the model's own lm_head.weight rows as value vectors (Identity V) for memory injection requires no training and generalizes to any token in the vocabulary, whereas learned value encoders fail to generalize.
Transformer hidden states collapse semantically distinct concepts (e.g., 'wife' vs 'brother' have 0.98+ cosine similarity), but a projection trained to match embed_tokens similarities can recover distinction (0.98→0.09).
The system achieves 94.4% retrieval accuracy on clean inputs with only 530MB (7%) of adapter parameters added to a frozen Qwen3-4B model.
papers.limitation:
All experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B); transfer to other model families is not validated.
No evaluation on standard memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo or BABILong.
Partially learned routing: while all decision boundaries are learned, the composition logic (control flow) remains in Python.
Testing limited to 88 entities; scaling behavior is unknown.
Injection layer sensitivity: the layer 35 (97% depth) injection point was empirically tuned; theoretical understanding is lacking.
Single-token injection: current implementation injects one token at a time; multi-token answers require extension.
future_direction: Validating the approach on other model families.
Evaluation on standard memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, BABILong).
Investigating the theoretical basis for Identity V and injection layer selection.
papers.abstract: Adding memory to pretrained language models typically requires architectural changes or weight modification. We present Prometheus Mind, which retrofits memory to a frozen Qwen3-4B using 11 modular adapters (530MB, 7% overhead) -- fully reversible by removing the adapters. Building this system required solving four problems: (1) Extraction -- we develop Contrastive Direction Discovery (CDD), which finds semantic directions via minimal pairs without labeled data. (2) Training -- end-to-end optimization collapses; stage-wise training of each adapter on simple proxy tasks succeeds. (3) Injection -- learned encoders fail to generalize; we find that lm_head-weight rows already provide the mapping we need, requiring no training. (4) Hidden state collapse -- transformers make ``wife'' and ``brother'' 0.98+ similar; we train projections to recover distinction (0.98 $\rightarrow$ 0.09). On PrometheusExtract-132 (132 cases), the system achieves 94.4% retrieval on clean inputs (n=54, 95% CI: [84.9%, 98.1%]), degrading to 19.4% on informal inputs with ellipsis, filler words, or implicit subjects (n=36). The primary bottleneck is relation classification (47.3% accuracy), responsible for most extraction errors.

papers.title: On the validation of crystallographic symmetry and the quality of structures
papers.abstract: In 2008, Zwart and colleagues observed that the fraction of the structures deposited in the PDB alleged to have "pseudosymmetry" or "special noncrystallographic symmetry" (NCS) was about 6%, and that this percentage was rising annually. A few years later, Poon and colleagues found that 2% of all the crystal structures in the PDB belonged to higher symmetry space groups than those assigned to them. Here, I report an analysis of the X-ray diffraction data deposited for this class of structures, which shows that most of the "pseudosymmetry" and "special NCS" that has been reported is in fact true crystallographic symmetry (CS). This distinction is important because the credibility of crystal structures depends heavily on quality control statistics such as Rfree that are unreliable when they are computed incorrectly, which they often are when CS is misidentified as "special NCS" or "pseudosymmetry". When mistakes of this kind are made, artificially low values of Rfree can give unjustified confidence in the accuracy of the reported structures.

papers.title: Exact direct-space asymmetric units for the 230 crystallographic space groups
papers.abstract: It is well known that the direct-space asymmetric unit definitions found in the International Tables for Crystallography, Volume A, are inexact at the borders. Face- and edge-specific sub-conditions have to be added to remove parts redundant under symmetry. This paper introduces a concise geometric notation for asymmetric unit conditions. The notation is the foundation for a reference table of exact direct-space asymmetric unit definitions for the 230 crystallographic space-group types. The change-of-basis transformation law for the conditions is derived, which allows the information from the reference table to be used for any space-group setting. We also show how the vertices of an asymmetric unit can easily be computed from the information in the reference table.

papers.title: Space groups and crystallographic symmetry: writing a multi-featured tutorial in a new style
papers.abstract: Knowledge of space groups and the implications of space group symmetry on the physical and chemical properties of solids are pivotal factors in all areas of crystalline solids. As Jerry Jasinski and I met to bring our ideas in teaching this subject to life, we both felt that 'early and often' - teaching the concepts with textual and visual reinforcement, is the key to providing a sound basis for students in this subject. The tutorial contains > 200 PowerPoint 'slides', in five modules, arranged by crystal class; a sixth module covers special topics. A 'credits' module gives the direct addresses of all embedded links. Space-group diagrams appear in Inter-national Tables format. The triclinic and monoclinic groups (2 + 13) are built from 'scratch', and are derived from the Hermann-Mauguin symbol. An additional section provides practice on many (but not all) of the ortho-rhom-bic groups in crystal class 222. Finally, a 'Special Topics' section on enanti-omorphous space groups features space groups P41 and P43. In the tutorial, lattice points build iteratively and inter-actively via keyclick, and the coordinates of points 'pop up' as the unit cell is filled. We trust that the elements of guidance, inquiry and occasional humor will make the learning process enjoyable.

papers.title: The centrosymmetric–noncentrosymmetric ambiguity: some more examples
papers.abstract: Four more examples are provided to emphasize the extreme difficulty in deciding, by diffraction methods, whether a crystal structure is centrosymmetric or only approximately so. In these examples, earlier workers described and refined structures in noncentrosymmetric space groups; refinements in the corresponding centrosymmetric space groups, based on the original data, lead to improved results. In one case, apparent violations of systematic absences seem to preclude the centrosymmetric description; however, other evidence – in particular, improved agreement for the very weak reflections (which are the most sensitive to the centrosymmetric non-centrosymmetric ambiguity) – suggest that the space-group violations might be spurious. In any event, the moral is clear: extreme caution is needed when attempting to derive a noncentrosymmetric description of a closely centrosymmetric structure.

papers.title: An introduction to data reduction: space-group determination, scaling and intensity statistics
papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of how to run the CCP4 programs for data reduction (SCALA, POINTLESS and CTRUNCATE) through the CCP4 graphical interface ccp4i and points out some issues that need to be considered, together with a few examples. It covers determination of the point-group symmetry of the diffraction data (the Laue group), which is required for the subsequent scaling step, examination of systematic absences, which in many cases will allow inference of the space group, putting multiple data sets on a common indexing system when there are alternatives, the scaling step itself, which produces a large set of data-quality indicators, estimation of |F| from intensity and finally examination of intensity statistics to detect crystal pathologies such as twinning. An appendix outlines the scoring schemes used by the program POINTLESS to assign probabilities to possible Laue and space groups.

papers.title: The space group of NaNbO<sub>3</sub>and (Na<sub>0.995</sub>K<sub>0.005</sub>)NbO<sub>3</sub>
papers.abstract: A method is described for the determination of possible space groups for pseudosymmetric structures, i.e. structures derived from an idealised structure of higher symmetry by small displacements of the atoms from special positions. Conventionally, systematic absences are used to infer the presence of symmetry operators; this method is difficult to apply in the case of a pseudosymmetrie structure where the space group absences occur among a set of systematically weak reflections. The new method uses systematic variations of intensity among these weak reflections to infer the sense and magnitude of the displacements of atoms from their idealised positions; symmetry operators are then introduced in a manner consistent with the displacements. The detailed application of the method to NaNbO a is described and the possible space groups are shown to be t:'bma or one of its subgroups Pb21a or P21212.

papers.title: Analyzing Symmetry in Group Theory: Applications in Crystallography
papers.abstract: Mathematics relies heavily on symmetry to study crystallography because this concept acts as an essential factor. The paper investigates group theory applications towards crystallographic symmetry investigations through examination of symmetry operations and crystallographic point groups and space groups studies. A theoretical model explains why crystal physical features including optical properties as well as elasticity and thermal conductivity derive from symmetry relationships. The research emphasizes how group theory enables progress in material science and crystallographic issue resolution.

papers.title: Application of Energy-Resolved Measurements to Laue Diffraction: Determination of Unit-Cell Parameters, Deconvolution of Harmonics and Assignment of Systematic Absences
papers.abstract: The use of energy-resolved area detection of Laue diffraction patterns for the determination of unit-cell parameters and systematic absences is demonstrated. Seven different crystals having previously known unit cells were re-examined using Laue diffraction methods. These crystals included four different crystal systems including cubic, orthorhombic, tetragonal and monoclinic cells. The crystals had cell sizes ranging from 179.4 to 4588.3 A(3). Comparison of known and re-determined cells showed good agreement (ratio of known to measured cells = 0.987 +/- 0.18). A single procedure was suitable for all unit-cell determinations. The accuracy of the method is presently limited by the quality of the available energy measurements. Some of the crystals represent space groups containing systematic absences normally obscured by harmonic overlap when using the Laue method. These include absences due to 2(1) screw axes (h, k or 1 = 2n + 1) and cell centering (h + k = 2n + 1). All systematic absences were identified using a combination of multiple linear regression with either stepwise elimination or stepwise inclusion and an F test for assignment of systematic absence. The methods are discussed in detail and simulations are used to evaluate critical tolerances for future systems.

papers.title: Fundamental motifs and parity within the crystallographic point groups
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes the Hasse diagram, or family tree, of the 3D crystal classes, also called geometric crystal classes. The 32 point-group classes are partitioned into seven crystal systems. In this paper, the structures of these systems are analyzed, leading to a new understanding of the relationships among and within them. The point groups, including their subgroups up to conjugacy, appear in six structural motifs in the Hasse diagram or family tree. Each motif has a parity - even or odd - that determines its structure. In three dimensions, the odd motifs are called monads, trigonals and cubics, and the even motifs are called dyads, tetragonals and hexagonals. Of the 32 classes of 3D point groups, 29 have a well defined parity, in that they appear in either an even or an odd motif. In contrast, the three monoclinic point groups are 'ambidextrous', in that they appear in two motifs, one of each parity. An analysis of the ten 2D point groups reveals an analogous structure, except for the presence of an ambidextrous crystal system. The striking structural uniformity of the motifs across the Hasse diagram confirms that they are essential building blocks of the crystallographic point groups.

papers.title: How many symmetry operations are needed to generate a space group?
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite interesting applications in chemistry, mineralogy and materials science, the rank d of a space group G has never been the main focus of crystallographic investigations before. As a rule, the conventional generating subset of a space group listed in Volume A of International Tables of Crystallography does not fit for correctly estimating d ( G ). The initial generating subset was modified and the code was developed and written in GAP environment to obtain reliable values of d ( G ) (ranging from 2 to 6) for all the 230 space-group types.

papers.title: Phase determination from new joint probability distribution; space groupP1
papers.abstract: A procedure for calculating phases in space group P1 is described.The new formulas constitute an improvement over earlier ones in that they make more effective use of the available data.In addition, two fundamental identities are presented which play an important role in the procedure.The derivation of the new formulas is based on the joint probability distributions of several normalized structure factors, obtained by fixing the crystal structure and allowing the indices to range uniformly but not independently over the vectors in reciprocal space.From these, the expected values of the products of powers of several structure factors are found.The expected values, together with a subsequent integrating process, lead to explicit formulas for the magnitudes of certain structure invariants in terms of the observed intensities alone.By means of the first fundamental identity, the initial values for the magnitudes of the structure invariants are improved, thus facilitating the problem of selecting one of the two enantiomorphous structures permitted by the given set of observed intensities.Once an enantiomorph has been chosen the second identity leads to refined values (both signs and magnitudes) of the invariants.Initial values of the individual phases are then readily obtainable, and a final least-squares adjustment procedure yields improved values for the phases.

papers.title: Spglib: a software library for crystal symmetry search
papers.abstract: A computer algorithm to search the symmetries of crystal structures, as implemented in the spglib code, is described. An iterative algorithm is employed to robustly identify space group types, tolerating a certain amount of distortion in the crystal structures. The source code is distributed under the 3-Clause BSD License, a permissive open-source software license. This paper focuses on the algorithm for identifying the space group symmetry of crystal structures.

papers.title: Centrosymmetric or noncentrosymmetric?
papers.abstract: In cases where diffraction data do not provide a clear choice between a centrosymmetric and a noncentrosymmetric space group, it is better to opt for the centrosymmetric description even though disorder may result. The disorder model implies that the crystal is a composite of two or more molecular structures that cannot be distinguished from one another. On the other hand, attempts to refine a single, ordered model in the noncentrosymmetric space group (which should lead to poor convergence because of near singularities) may lead to the erroneous conclusion that a unique structure has been found. Three examples of this latter situation are given.

papers.title: A Computer Program for Objective Point Symmetry Classifications of Pseudosymmetric Electron Diffraction Spot Patterns
papers.abstract: A Python program for calculating the metrics necessary to perform information-theory based symmetry classifications and quantifications of transmission electron diffraction spot patterns is introduced. It is the first of its kind, in that it implements objectivity into crystallographic symmetry classifications and quantifications of approximate zone axis patterns from crystals. The equations by which the program operates as well as the required inputs are given. The results of the program's analysis of an experimental transmission electron diffraction spot pattern from a crystal with a pseudo-hexagonal lattice metric and a rectangular-centered Bravias lattice is used as an example. The program will eventually be appended to allow analysis of the other hierarchical translational pseudo-symmetry and Bravais lattice type combinations. Crystallographic Rsym values of traditional classifications into projected point symmetry groups are provided alongside information-theoretic results of the new program's analysis for comparison purposes.

papers.title: Crystallography: Symmetry groups and group representations
