This confirms the hypothesis that the symmetries of network primitives can carry unintended inductive biases, leading to task-independent artefactual structures in representations. The discrete symmetry of contemporary forms is shown to be a strong predictor for the production of symmetry-organised discrete representations emerging from otherwise continuous distributions -- a quantisation effect. This motivates further reassessment of functional forms in common usage due to such unintended consequences. Moreover, this supports a general causal model for a mode in which discrete representations may form, and could constitute a prerequisite for downstream interpretability phenomena, including grandmother neurons, discrete coding schemes, general linear features and a type of Superposition. Hence, this tool and proposed mechanism for the influence of functional form on representations may provide insights into interpretability research. Finally, preliminary results indicate that quantisation of representations correlates with a measurable increase in reconstruction error, reinforcing previous conjectures that this collapse can be detrimental.

papers.title: Physical Symmetries Embedded in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can physical constraints (such as symmetries and conservation laws) be embedded into neural network architectures to guarantee that predictions obey known physics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network architecture (hub layer) that embeds physical constraints (symmetries and conservation laws) exactly into the network structure, guaranteeing that predictions satisfy the underlying physics without the need for explicit regularization terms.
papers.conclusion: Embedding physical constraints into neural networks via hub layers improves predictive power, training efficiency, and robustness, and is crucial for reliable predictions in data-scarce regimes.
papers.key_findings:
A hub layer can enforce even/odd symmetry in regression tasks, outperforming standard MLPs in preserving symmetry while fitting noisy data.
For energy-conserving regression, a hub layer that corrects the MLP prediction using Hamiltonian dynamics ensures energy conservation and closed phase-space trajectories.
An unsupervised symplectic neural network, designed by embedding Hamilton's equations, conserves energy when solving differential equations and converges faster than a standard MLP.
future_direction: Embed other important symmetries into neural networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are a central technique in machine learning. Recent years have seen a wave of interest in applying neural networks to physical systems for which the governing dynamics are known and expressed through differential equations. Two fundamental challenges facing the development of neural networks in physics applications is their lack of interpretability and their physics-agnostic design. The focus of the present work is to embed physical constraints into the structure of the neural network to address the second fundamental challenge. By constraining tunable parameters (such as weights and biases) and adding special layers to the network, the desired constraints are guaranteed to be satisfied without the need for explicit regularization terms. This is demonstrated on upervised and unsupervised networks for two basic symmetries: even/odd symmetry of a function and energy conservation. In the supervised case, the network with embedded constraints is shown to perform well on regression problems while simultaneously obeying the desired constraints whereas a traditional network fits the data but violates the underlying constraints. Finally, a new unsupervised neural network is proposed that guarantees energy conservation through an embedded symplectic structure. The symplectic neural network is used to solve a system of energy-conserving differential equations and out-performs an unsupervised, non-symplectic neural network.

papers.title: Quantum-chemical insights from interpretable atomistic neural networks
papers.research_question: How can atomistic neural networks be made interpretable to provide insights into chemical properties and underlying quantum-chemical regularities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that atomistic neural networks, through their inherent atom-wise contributions and learned embeddings, provide interpretable insights that align with chemical knowledge, enabling validation and new research avenues in quantum chemistry.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability is crucial for validating and trusting machine learning models in quantum chemistry, and the presented techniques, which yield explanations grounded in physics and chemistry, open up new venues for data-driven research in chemistry, physics, and materials science.
papers.key_findings:
Atomistic neural networks yield consistent atom-wise partitionings of energy and partial charges, which serve as local explanations.
The atom-wise energy contributions can be used to rank the stability of aromatic rings, agreeing with chemical concepts like mesomeric and inductive effects.
Local chemical potentials, derived by probing the model with a virtual atom, provide spatially resolved visualizations that reflect chemical intuition such as bond saturation and aromaticity.
Electrostatic potentials computed from latent partial charges approximate the molecular charge distribution and show excellent agreement with basic chemical reasoning.
Element embeddings learned by SchNet from crystal structures recover a structure resembling the periodic table, indicating the model infers chemical similarities from data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to measure chemical similarity of local structures.
papers.abstract: With the rise of deep neural networks for quantum chemistry applications, there is a pressing need for architectures that, beyond delivering accurate predictions of chemical properties, are readily interpretable by researchers. Here, we describe interpretation techniques for atomistic neural networks on the example of Behler-Parrinello networks as well as the end-to-end model SchNet. Both models obtain predictions of chemical properties by aggregating atom-wise contributions. These latent variables can serve as local explanations of a prediction and are obtained during training without additional cost. Due to their correspondence to well-known chemical concepts such as atomic energies and partial charges, these atom-wise explanations enable insights not only about the model but more importantly about the underlying quantum-chemical regularities. We generalize from atomistic explanations to 3d space, thus obtaining spatially resolved visualizations which further improve interpretability. Finally, we analyze learned embeddings of chemical elements that exhibit a partial ordering that resembles the order of the periodic table. As the examined neural networks show excellent agreement with chemical knowledge, the presented techniques open up new venues for data-driven research in chemistry, physics and materials science.

papers.title: Beyond the Permutation Symmetry of Transformers: The Role of Rotation for Model Fusion
papers.research_question: How can rotation symmetry in transformers be leveraged to improve model fusion via parameter matching?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces rotation symmetry for transformers, a continuous generalization of permutation symmetry, and proposes a theoretically optimal parameter matching algorithm that improves model fusion by reducing the distance between end models.
papers.conclusion: Rotation symmetry is a valuable extension of parameter space symmetry for transformers, and the proposed parameter matching algorithm effectively enhances model fusion, demonstrating the potential of symmetry for improving deep learning applications.
papers.key_findings:
Rotation symmetry extends the equivalence set of transformers to a continuous space, enabling more flexible and effective parameter matching than discrete permutation symmetry.
The proposed parameter matching algorithm, based on rotation symmetry, significantly reduces the Euclidean distance between end models and improves the performance of various model fusion techniques.
Matching self-attention layers (using rotation symmetry) contributes more to fusion performance in some merging methods (e.g., Fisher, RegMean), while FFN matching (using permutation symmetry) is more beneficial for others (e.g., OTFusion).
Integrating rescaling symmetry with rotation symmetry further refines parameter alignment and leads to additional performance gains.
Matching a subset of layers (particularly the head layers) can achieve most of the performance improvement, offering a trade-off between efficiency and utility.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical optimality guarantee for the parameter matching algorithm is for the two-model case and does not naturally extend to optimal multi-model matching, which remains an open challenge.
The symmetry set considered (rotation, permutation, rescaling) may not be the complete symmetry group of transformers; other structural symmetries may exist.
The sequential optimization of rotation and then rescaling does not guarantee global optimality for the joint optimization over rotation and rescaling parameters.
future_direction: Extending the parameter matching framework to the optimal multi-model setting.
Exploring a richer set of structural symmetries in transformers beyond rotation, permutation, and rescaling.
Developing a joint optimization framework for rotation and rescaling symmetries to achieve global optimality.
papers.abstract: Symmetry in the parameter space of deep neural networks (DNNs) has proven beneficial for various deep learning applications. A well-known example is the permutation symmetry in Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), where permuting the rows of weight matrices in one layer and applying the inverse permutation to adjacent layers yields a functionally equivalent model. While permutation symmetry fully characterizes the equivalence set for MLPs, its discrete nature limits its utility for transformers. In this paper, we introduce rotation symmetry, a novel form of parameter space symmetry for transformers that generalizes permutation symmetry by rotating parameter matrices in self-attention layers. Unlike permutation symmetry, rotation symmetry operates in a continuous domain, thereby significantly expanding the equivalence set for transformers. Based on this property, we propose a theoretically optimal parameter matching algorithm as a plug-and-play module to enhance model fusion. We evaluate our approach using pre-trained transformers across diverse natural language and vision tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our rotation symmetry-based matching algorithm substantially improves model fusion, highlighting the potential of parameter space symmetry to facilitate model fusion. Our code is available on https://github.com/zhengzaiyi/RotationSymmetry.

papers.title: Learning Layer-wise Equivariances Automatically using Gradients
papers.research_question: How can the type and amount of layer-wise equivariance symmetries be automatically learned from training data, as opposed to being hard-coded?
papers.core_contribution: A method to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances from data using differentiable Laplace approximations and improved parameterizations of relaxed equivariance, balancing data fit and model complexity.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method allows artificial neural networks to automatically adapt symmetry structure from training data, reducing reliance on trial-and-error in architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
The method can learn convolutional structure in early layers from data, achieving equivalent or improved performance compared to architectures with hard-coded symmetry.
The method can automatically select the most relevant symmetry group from a set of multiple groups, with learned symmetries correlating with data augmentations.
Layers learn to become convolutional, except sometimes at the end of the network where spatial dimensions become 1x1, aligning with common practice.
papers.limitation: The method requires a list of symmetry groups and associated group representations to be considered as candidates.
future_direction: Extending the method to other architecture search problems, such as learning network depth or filter sizes from training data.
papers.abstract: Convolutions encode equivariance symmetries into neural networks leading to better generalisation performance. However, symmetries provide fixed hard constraints on the functions a network can represent, need to be specified in advance, and can not be adapted. Our goal is to allow flexible symmetry constraints that can automatically be learned from data using gradients. Learning symmetry and associated weight connectivity structures from scratch is difficult for two reasons. First, it requires efficient and flexible parameterisations of layer-wise equivariances. Secondly, symmetries act as constraints and are therefore not encouraged by training losses measuring data fit. To overcome these challenges, we improve parameterisations of soft equivariance and learn the amount of equivariance in layers by optimising the marginal likelihood, estimated using differentiable Laplace approximations. The objective balances data fit and model complexity enabling layer-wise symmetry discovery in deep networks. We demonstrate the ability to automatically learn layer-wise equivariances on image classification tasks, achieving equivalent or improved performance over baselines with hard-coded symmetry.

papers.title: Why does Deep Learning work? - A perspective from Group Theory
papers.research_question: Why does unsupervised deep learning work, and how does it capture representations of increasing complexity?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a group-theoretic framework for unsupervised deep learning, showing that layer-wise pretraining corresponds to finding features with minimal orbits, which explains why simple features are learned first and how higher-order representations emerge in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a group-theoretic framework for unsupervised deep learning, connecting layer-wise pretraining to the orbit-stabilizer principle and explaining the emergence of simple features and higher-order representations.
papers.key_findings:
The learning process in autoencoders can be viewed as searching for stabilizers of input features.
There is an inverse relationship between stabilizer size and orbit size: simpler features have larger stabilizers and smaller orbits, making them more likely to be learned first.
The action of a neural network can be approximated by a shadow group (homeomorphism group) and locally by linear transformations (GL(S)).
The sigmoid function enables the construction of moduli spaces, allowing deeper layers to learn increasingly complex representations.
The orbit-stabilizer principle explains the emergence of Gabor-like filters in the first layer of image learning networks.
papers.limitation: The theory is limited to unsupervised learning and cannot be readily extended to supervised learning because the orbit-stabilizer principle relies on input reconstruction.
future_direction: Extending the theory to supervised learning to unify representation learning under a single theory.
papers.abstract: Why does Deep Learning work? What representations does it capture? How do higher-order representations emerge? We study these questions from the perspective of group theory, thereby opening a new approach towards a theory of Deep learning. One factor behind the recent resurgence of the subject is a key algorithmic step called pre-training: first search for a good generative model for the input samples, and repeat the process one layer at a time. We show deeper implications of this simple principle, by establishing a connection with the interplay of orbits and stabilizers of group actions. Although the neural networks themselves may not form groups, we show the existence of {\em shadow} groups whose elements serve as close approximations. Over the shadow groups, the pre-training step, originally introduced as a mechanism to better initialize a network, becomes equivalent to a search for features with minimal orbits. Intuitively, these features are in a way the {\em simplest}. Which explains why a deep learning network learns simple features first. Next, we show how the same principle, when repeated in the deeper layers, can capture higher order representations, and why representation complexity increases as the layers get deeper.

papers.title: Representation Theory of $UT_3(\mathbb{F}_3)$ and its Applications to Equivariant Decomposition in Neural Architectures
papers.research_question: How can the irreducible representations of the group UT3(F3) be explicitly constructed and used to decompose equivariant feature spaces and filters in group-equivariant convolutional neural networks (G-CNNs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides explicit matrix forms for all irreducible representations of UT3(F3) and proves decomposition theorems for equivariant feature spaces and filters, establishing a foundation for designing G-CNN architectures that respect the algebraic structure of the group.
papers.conclusion: The representation theory of UT3(F3) provides a rigorous foundation for designing symmetry-preserving neural network layers with structured decompositions, and this approach can be generalized to other groups such as larger upper-triangular groups.
papers.key_findings:
Explicit matrix forms for all irreducible complex representations of UT3(F3) are given.
Theorem 3.1: Equivariant feature spaces decompose into direct sums of isotypic components corresponding to irreducible representations.
Theorem 3.2: Equivariant filters decompose into block-diagonal form, acting only within matching irreducible subrepresentations.
Theorem 3.4: G-equivariant convolution preserves chains of invariant subspaces, ensuring hierarchical consistency.
A novel architecture combining a G-CNN based on these irreducible representations with a Transformer decoder is proposed for handwritten mathematical expression recognition.
future_direction: Generalize the framework to larger upper-triangular groups UT_n(F_q) for n > 3 and arbitrary finite fields.
Extend to other classes of finite nilpotent or solvable groups, such as Heisenberg groups over F_q.
Examine practical trade-offs in filter count and computational cost, and gains in equivariance and data efficiency on larger symmetry groups.
papers.abstract: In this paper we prove theorems characterizing the decomposition of equivariant feature spaces, filters and a structural preservation theorem for invariant subspace chains in group equivariant convolutional neural networks(G-CNN). Furthermore, we give explicit matrix forms for irreducible representations of $UT_3(\F_3)$-the unitriangular matrix groups over the field with three elements. These results provide a foundation for designing new G-CNN architectures via representations of $UT_3(\F_3)$ that respect deep algebraic structure, with potential applications in symbolic visual learning.

papers.title: Human-Like Geometric Abstraction in Large Pre-trained Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do large pre-trained neural network models demonstrate human-like abstract geometric processing, specifically sensitivity to geometric complexity, regularity, and parts/relations?
papers.core_contribution: Large pre-trained neural networks (DINOv2, CLIP) show human-like biases in geometric abstraction tasks, challenging the hypothesis that symbolic structure is necessary for such capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Large pre-trained neural networks can reproduce key behavioral phenomena associated with abstract geometric reasoning without explicit symbolic machinery, though gaps remain in parts-and-relations understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings from large models (CLIP, DINOv2) contain information about geometric complexity (Minimum Description Length) and can predict human choice times as well as symbolic models.
CLIP and DINOv2 exhibit a human-like bias towards geometric regularity in an oddball task, while ResNet-50 does not.
DINOv2 and CLIP outperform ResNet-50 on a geometric parts-and-relations task (Geoclidean) but still fall short of human performance.
DINOv2 generally outperforms CLIP in reproducing human behavior, suggesting joint vision-language training may not be necessary for geometric abstraction.
Larger models trained on more data (DINOv2, CLIP) show more human-like geometric processing than a smaller model (ResNet-50) trained on ImageNet.
papers.limitation:
Static embeddings from pre-trained models may not be expressive enough to encode relational features, explaining their lower accuracy on the Geoclidean task compared to humans.
The factors contributing to human-like processing (architecture, scale, training objective) are not disentangled.
future_direction: Search for more appropriate metrics derived from embedding spaces to predict human encoding times.
Explore serialization methods like chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought to enhance performance on geometric reasoning tasks.
Disentangle the importance of architecture, model size, training data scale, and training objective in achieving human-like visual geometric processing.
papers.abstract: Humans possess a remarkable capacity to recognize and manipulate abstract structure, which is especially apparent in the domain of geometry. Recent research in cognitive science suggests neural networks do not share this capacity, concluding that human geometric abilities come from discrete symbolic structure in human mental representations. However, progress in artificial intelligence (AI) suggests that neural networks begin to demonstrate more human-like reasoning after scaling up standard architectures in both model size and amount of training data. In this study, we revisit empirical results in cognitive science on geometric visual processing and identify three key biases in geometric visual processing: a sensitivity towards complexity, regularity, and the perception of parts and relations. We test tasks from the literature that probe these biases in humans and find that large pre-trained neural network models used in AI demonstrate more human-like abstract geometric processing.

papers.title: Manifolds and Modules: How Function Develops in a Neural Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are the representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a neural foundation model (FNN) using decoding/encoding manifolds and trajectories, finding that different processing stages (encoder, recurrent, readout) exhibit distinct representational structures. The recurrent module enriches temporal representations, while the readout achieves biological fidelity through numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Neural foundation models may be more similar in internal operation to other foundation models than to their biological counterparts. Future architectures incorporating recurrence after a light-weight retinal-like encoder and constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity could bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.key_findings:
The feedforward encoder module lacks biologically plausible stimulus-dependent temporal patterns and mainly reports input features with varying intensity.
The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities by 'pushing apart' representations of different temporal stimulus patterns, enabling better stimulus separability.
The readout module accounts for biological variability by relying on a large number of self-similar feature maps, differing from known biological counterparts in V1.
The output layer achieves a continuous representation by linearly combining the readout features to associate spike trains with input movies.
The model's internal dynamics (quantified by tubularity metrics) are less complex and entangled than those observed in biological retina and V1 data.
papers.limitation:
The analysis utilized a single foundation model, due to the limited availability of other video-based foundation models of neural activity over time.
The work used a restricted set of stimuli to ensure comparability to biological results.
future_direction: Future architectures incorporating recurrence directly after a more light-weight retinal-like encoder.
Constraining feature dimensionality to match biological cell type diversity to yield models that bridge the gap between computational performance and biological plausibility.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns; while the readout module achieves biological fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, we present this work as a study of the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns.

papers.title: Symmetry in language statistics shapes the geometry of model representations
papers.research_question: Why do geometric structures (circles, loops, manifolds) arise in the internal representations of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that translation symmetry in pairwise co-occurrence statistics of natural language explains the emergence of geometric structures (e.g., circles, manifolds) in the internal representations of language models.
papers.conclusion: Representational manifolds have a universal origin: symmetry in the statistics of natural data.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical observation of representation manifolds (circles, loops) and linear coordinate decoding in shallow word embedding models like word2vec.
Evidence that words embodying a continuous latent concept have pairwise co-occurrence statistics that exhibit translation symmetry.
Analytical expressions that predict the representational geometry directly from these translation symmetric statistics.
Validation that the predicted representational structure is present and stable in both word embedding models and deep transformer-based models.
Theoretical and empirical demonstration that representation manifolds are robust to significant perturbations in co-occurrence statistics, explained by collective effects involving many words.
papers.abstract: Although learned representations underlie neural networks' success, their fundamental properties remain poorly understood. A striking example is the emergence of simple geometric structures in LLM representations: for example, calendar months organize into a circle, years form a smooth one-dimensional manifold, and cities' latitudes and longitudes can be decoded by a linear probe. We show that the statistics of language exhibit a translation symmetry -- e.g., the co-occurrence probability of two months depends only on the time interval between them -- and we prove that the latter governs the aforementioned geometric structures in high-dimensional word embedding models. Moreover, we find that these structures persist even when the co-occurrence statistics are strongly perturbed (for example, by removing all sentences in which two months appear together) and at moderate embedding dimension. We show that this robustness naturally emerges if the co-occurrence statistics are collectively controlled by an underlying continuous latent variable. We empirically validate this theoretical framework in word embedding models, text embedding models, and large language models.

papers.title: Discovering symmetry invariants and conserved quantities by interpreting siamese neural networks
papers.research_question: Can Siamese Neural Networks learn symmetry invariants and conserved quantities in physical systems, and can they be interpreted to reveal these quantities without prior knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces interpretable Siamese Neural Networks to theoretical physics and shows they can learn and reveal symmetry invariants and conserved quantities without prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: SNNs are a useful tool in theoretical physics and can be interpreted to reveal physical invariants, challenging the black box nature of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
SNNs learn the spacetime interval in special relativity.
SNNs learn angular momentum and energy in central potential motion.
SNNs learn the two electromagnetic invariants (E·B and |E|^2-|B|^2).
The bottleneck layer of the SNN can be interpreted via polynomial regression to approximate the invariants.
The SNN fails to learn when the invariant is fixed, indicating it relies on that invariant.
future_direction: Upgrade polynomial regression to symbolic regression.
Combine interpretable SNNs with mathematical reasoning tools (solvers or theorem provers).
Apply to quantum error correction or particle tracking at the LHC.
papers.abstract: The authors train a Siamese neural network to decide whether two different descriptions describe the same physical object. The neural network learns to identify the objects by calculating the underlying invariants and conserved quantities.

papers.title: Black Boxes and Looking Glasses: Multilevel Symmetries, Reflection Planes, and Convex Optimization in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: Is there a fundamental difference in the nature of functions learned by deep networks, as opposed to shallow networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that training deep narrow networks with absolute value activation is equivalent to convex Lasso problems, revealing that deep networks learn multilevel symmetries via reflections of training data.
papers.conclusion: The paper proves an equivalence between neural networks and Lasso problems with novel geometric features, and suggests that multi-level symmetries may hold for standard ReLU networks as future work.
papers.key_findings:
Training deep neural networks with absolute value activation can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems.
Deep networks favor symmetric structures, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries (symmetries within symmetries).
The Lasso features represent distances to reflection hyperplanes that are spanned by training data and orthogonal to optimal weight vectors.
For 3-layer networks, explicit Lasso dictionaries are given and the optimal first-layer weight is orthogonal to a subset of augmented training data.
Neural networks trained using LLM embeddings learn reflection features similar to those predicted by the Lasso model.
papers.limitation: The choice of absolute value activation and ℓ1 regularization is needed for analytic tractability, which may limit direct applicability to standard ReLU networks.
future_direction: Extensions to ReLU networks.
Analysis of Lasso solution sets and stationary points for higher dimensional data.
Investigation of reflection features in wider ReLU architectures with higher-dimensional data.
papers.abstract: We show that training deep neural networks (DNNs) with absolute value activation and arbitrary input dimension can be formulated as equivalent convex Lasso problems with novel features expressed using geometric algebra. This formulation reveals geometric structures encoding symmetry in neural networks. Using the equivalent Lasso form of DNNs, we formally prove a fundamental distinction between deep and shallow networks: deep networks inherently favor symmetric structures in their fitted functions, with greater depth enabling multilevel symmetries, i.e., symmetries within symmetries. Moreover, Lasso features represent distances to hyperplanes that are reflected across training points. These reflection hyperplanes are spanned by training data and are orthogonal to optimal weight vectors. Numerical experiments support theory and demonstrate theoretically predicted features when training networks using embeddings generated by Large Language Models.

papers.title: Learning Group Structure and Disentangled Representations of Dynamical Environments
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations of dynamical environments by learning the structure of the symmetry group that generates the environment's evolution, without prior knowledge of the symmetry group?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework, built on group representation theory, for learning disentangled representations of dynamical environments by mapping observations to a latent space and transformations to orthogonal matrices, with an entanglement regularizer to encourage interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of learning physics-based disentangled representations as defined by Higgins et al. (2018), providing a principled and scalable step for representation learning in dynamical environments.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully learns the toroidal structure of a grid world with periodic boundary conditions.
It disentangles spatial rotations and color changes in a 3D teapot environment without supervision.
It can learn continuous Lie groups (SO(3)) from continuous transformations.
Disentangled representations, enforced by the regularization, lead to more accurate long-horizon predictions compared to entangled representations.
papers.limitation:
The parameterization involves O(n^2) rotation matrices, which could become a computational bottleneck for larger models with many generative factors.
The method is at a proof-of-principle stage on model datasets, and its societal impact (e.g., fairness and bias in interpretability) requires further consideration.
future_direction: Extending the method to learn representations of more complex real-world environments, which may require more expressive groups than SO(n) or different parameterizations.
papers.abstract: Learning disentangled representations is a key step towards effectively discovering and modelling the underlying structure of environments. In the natural sciences, physics has found great success by describing the universe in terms of symmetry preserving transformations. Inspired by this formalism, we propose a framework, built upon the theory of group representation, for learning representations of a dynamical environment structured around the transformations that generate its evolution. Experimentally, we learn the structure of explicitly symmetric environments without supervision from observational data generated by sequential interactions. We further introduce an intuitive disentanglement regularisation to ensure the interpretability of the learnt representations. We show that our method enables accurate long-horizon predictions, and demonstrate a correlation between the quality of predictions and disentanglement in the latent space.

papers.title: Equivariant neural networks and piecewise linear representation theory
papers.research_question: How can representation theory be used to decompose equivariant neural networks into simple representations and study the piecewise linear maps arising from activation functions, to provide a tool for interpretation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies representation theory to equivariant neural networks, showing that decomposing layers into simple representations leads to a filtration and interaction graphs that generalize Fourier series, providing a tool for interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The decomposition of equivariant neural networks into simple representations provides a useful tool for interpreting these networks, and piecewise linear representation theory is a rich and interesting area for further study.
papers.key_findings:
Decomposing equivariant neural networks into simple representations is meaningful and leads to the study of piecewise linear maps between these representations.
Equivariant neural networks must be built from permutation representations (Theorem 2E.7).
The existence of equivariant piecewise linear maps is controlled by normal subgroups, similar to Galois theory (Theorem 2H.3).
In equivariant neural networks, there is a flow of information from low to high frequency, but not conversely, leading to a filtration.
The interaction graphs for cyclic groups are computed, showing how simple representations interact under piecewise linear maps like ReLU and absolute value.
future_direction: Extending the theory to other groups such as dihedral and symmetric groups.
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks are neural networks with symmetry. Motivated by the theory of group representations, we decompose the layers of an equivariant neural network into simple representations. The nonlinear activation functions lead to interesting nonlinear equivariant maps between simple representations. For example, the rectified linear unit (ReLU) gives rise to piecewise linear maps. We show that these considerations lead to a filtration of equivariant neural networks, generalizing Fourier series. This observation might provide a useful tool for interpreting equivariant neural networks.

papers.title: Correlator convolutional neural networks as an interpretable architecture for image-like quantum matter data
papers.research_question: How can we design an interpretable neural network architecture for analyzing image-like quantum matter data to distinguish between candidate theories for the doped Fermi-Hubbard model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops Correlator Convolutional Neural Networks (CCNNs), an interpretable architecture for image-like quantum matter data, and applies it to distinguish between geometric string theory and π-flux theory for the doped Fermi-Hubbard model, finding that fourth-order spin-charge correlators are key distinguishing features.
papers.conclusion: CCNNs provide an interpretable method for analyzing quantum matter data, enabling automated discovery of relevant multi-site correlators and offering new physical insights.
papers.key_findings:
The CCNN architecture produces features directly interpretable as physical correlation functions.
When distinguishing geometric string theory and π-flux theory, fourth-order spin-charge correlators are the most important features.
The learned filters reveal specific four-site correlators that correspond to physical motifs, such as the wake of a propagating hole in geometric string theory.
The CCNN achieves performance comparable to traditional CNNs while being interpretable.
Regularization path analysis effectively identifies the most relevant features for classification.
papers.limitation:
The method considers only short-range multi-point correlation functions and does not include long-range two-point correlations needed for identifying spontaneous symmetry breaking.
Experimental uncertainties on doping level without spin-resolution led the CCNN to focus on doping level rather than meaningful hypothesis testing.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a broader collection of candidate theories.
Apply to snapshots generated using finite-T tensor network methods and spin-resolved experimental data.
Extend the method to include longer range correlations by expanding filter size or using dilated convolutions.
papers.abstract: Image-like data from quantum systems promises to offer greater insight into the physics of correlated quantum matter. However, the traditional framework of condensed matter physics lacks principled approaches for analyzing such data. Machine learning models are a powerful theoretical tool for analyzing image-like data including many-body snapshots from quantum simulators. Recently, they have successfully distinguished between simulated snapshots that are indistinguishable from one and two point correlation functions. Thus far, the complexity of these models has inhibited new physical insights from such approaches. Here, we develop a set of nonlinearities for use in a neural network architecture that discovers features in the data which are directly interpretable in terms of physical observables. Applied to simulated snapshots produced by two candidate theories approximating the doped Fermi-Hubbard model, we uncover that the key distinguishing features are fourth-order spin-charge correlators. Our approach lends itself well to the construction of simple, versatile, end-to-end interpretable architectures, thus paving the way for new physical insights from machine learning studies of experimental and numerical data.

papers.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the universality hypothesis: whether different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks, by studying how small neural networks learn to implement group composition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the group composition via representations (GCR) algorithm and shows that neural networks consistently learn this algorithm when trained on group composition tasks, providing evidence for weak universality (underlying principles exist) but against strong universality (specific circuits vary).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that while there is an underlying algorithm (GCR) that networks learn for group composition, the specific features and circuits are arbitrary, supporting weak universality but not strong universality.
papers.key_findings:
Networks learn the GCR algorithm for group composition, which uses representation theory to compute compositions.
The specific representations (circuits) learned vary across different runs and hyperparameters, indicating that while the algorithm is universal, the implementation is not.
The order in which representations are learned is arbitrary and not consistent across runs.
The network's logits can be approximated as a sum of characters from a sparse set of representations.
Ablations confirm that the identified components are causally important for the task.
papers.limitation: The algorithm does not perfectly explain all logits due to limitations of the architecture (e.g., ReLU activations imperfectly implement matrix multiplication).
future_direction: Extending to other group theoretic tasks such as conjugacy, group actions, and automata.
Studying semigroups (which lack representation theory).
Investigating inductive biases of networks more broadly.
papers.abstract: Universality is a key hypothesis in mechanistic interpretability -- that different models learn similar features and circuits when trained on similar tasks. In this work, we study the universality hypothesis by examining how small neural networks learn to implement group composition. We present a novel algorithm by which neural networks may implement composition for any finite group via mathematical representation theory. We then show that networks consistently learn this algorithm by reverse engineering model logits and weights, and confirm our understanding using ablations. By studying networks of differing architectures trained on various groups, we find mixed evidence for universality: using our algorithm, we can completely characterize the family of circuits and features that networks learn on this task, but for a given network the precise circuits learned -- as well as the order they develop -- are arbitrary.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Loss Landscape Geometry and the Learning of Symmetries: Or, What Influence Functions Reveal About Robust Generalization
papers.research_question: Do neural emulators of PDE solution operators internalize physical symmetries, and how can we diagnose this through learning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an influence-based diagnostic that measures gradient coherence across symmetry orbits to determine whether neural PDE emulators have internalized physical symmetries, linking it to generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed influence-based diagnostic reveals that gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is essential for robust generalization, providing a tool to assess whether models truly learn physics or just fit data.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient coherence across symmetry orbits is necessary for models to generalize over symmetry transformations.
Models can achieve low test error without learning symmetries, indicated by weak gradient coherence.
UNets and ViTs exhibit different patterns of gradient coherence: UNets show more uniform coupling, while ViTs concentrate influence on a subset of symmetry transformations.
Symmetry breaking in forward passes corresponds to suppressed cross-influence in the loss landscape.
The diagnostic can be used to evaluate symmetry learning and guide data augmentation.
papers.limitation:
Certain physically relevant symmetries (Galilean boosts, scaling) are not studied.
Empirical analysis is limited to UNet and ViT architectures.
Diagnostics characterize symmetry learning relative to the training distribution; when symmetry transformations are poorly represented in data, influence-based measures reflect this bias.
future_direction: Extending the influence-based analysis to probe the response under small Galilean boosts.
Development of approximate or relaxed symmetry mechanisms that retain structure to guide generalization while preserving optimization flexibility.
papers.abstract: We study how neural emulators of partial differential equation solution operators internalize physical symmetries by introducing an influence-based diagnostic that measures the propagation of parameter updates between symmetry-related states, defined as the metric-weighted overlap of loss gradients evaluated along group orbits. This quantity probes the local geometry of the learned loss landscape and goes beyond forward-pass equivariance tests by directly assessing whether learning dynamics couple physically equivalent configurations. Applying our diagnostic to autoregressive fluid flow emulators, we show that orbit-wise gradient coherence provides the mechanism for learning to generalize over symmetry transformations and indicates when training selects a symmetry compatible basin. The result is a novel technique for evaluating if surrogate models have internalized symmetry properties of the known solution operator.

papers.title: Dynamic neuron approach to deep neural networks: Decoupling neurons for renormalization group analysis
papers.research_question: How can we reformulate the cost function of deep neural networks to reveal translational symmetry and enable the application of renormalization group transformations and analysis of critical phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the dynamic neuron approach (DNA), which reformulates the cost function of deep neural networks by treating neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, revealing translational symmetry and enabling the application of renormalization group transformations to analyze critical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The dynamic neuron approach provides a new framework for analyzing deep neural networks using statistical physics, revealing translational symmetry and enabling renormalization group transformations and critical phenomena analysis.
papers.key_findings:
The dynamic neuron approach (DNA) reformulates the DNN cost function by introducing neurons as dynamic degrees of freedom, simplifying interactions and revealing approximate translational symmetry.
Using DNA, the renormalization group transformation can be applied to DNNs, leading to a renormalized system with reduced depth and new constraints.
In a simplified DNN example with one neuron per layer, the RG transformation yields fixed points and scaling laws, indicating potential critical phenomena.
Monte Carlo simulations show that the correlation functions of the DNA system closely resemble those of the original DNN, validating DNA as a theoretical approximation.
The DNA Hamiltonian, under certain assumptions, resembles a spin glass model, connecting DNN training to statistical physics models.
papers.limitation:
The simple example with assumptions (one neuron per layer, single data point, Heaviside activation, discrete weights) may oversimplify and differ from actual DNNs.
The DNA introduces a large number of dynamic neurons (LMN), making it computationally infeasible for practical applications.
future_direction: Develop theoretical tools for inference to study neural scaling laws.
Develop optimization methods to make DNA practically feasible.
papers.abstract: Deep neural network architectures often consist of repetitive structural elements. We introduce an approach that reveals these patterns and can be broadly applied to the study of deep learning. Similarly to how a power strip helps untangle and organize complex cable connections, this approach treats neurons as additional degrees of freedom in interactions, simplifying the structure and enhancing the intuitive understanding of interactions within deep neural networks. Furthermore, it reveals the translational symmetry of deep neural networks, which simplifies the application of the renormalization group transformation, a method that effectively analyzes the scaling behavior of the system. By utilizing translational symmetry and renormalization group transformations, we can analyze critical phenomena. This approach may open new avenues for studying deep neural networks using statistical physics.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Toward Manifest Relationality in Transformers via Symmetry Reduction
papers.research_question: How can internal redundancies in transformers due to continuous symmetries be eliminated by reformulating representations and optimization in terms of invariant relational quantities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a conceptual framework for symmetry reduction in transformers, reformulating representations, attention mechanisms, and optimization dynamics in terms of invariant relational quantities to eliminate redundant degrees of freedom by construction.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a framework for relational, symmetry-reduced transformers and suggests future work on scalable implementations and empirical evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers contain substantial internal redundancy due to continuous symmetries in model space and head space.
Symmetry reduction via relational invariants (e.g., Gram matrices) can eliminate these redundancies by reformulating attention in terms of invariant quantities.
Optimization can be performed on reduced parameter spaces using invariant composites (e.g., G_QK = W_Q^T W_K) to avoid motion along symmetry orbits.
The framework provides a principled geometric approach to reduce parameter redundancy and analyze optimization dynamics.
The proposed relational formulation may lead to more interpretable and efficient transformer architectures.
papers.limitation:
The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically evaluated.
Practical transformers include symmetry-breaking components (e.g., LayerNorm, biases) that reduce the symmetry, making the full symmetry only approximate.
The relational formulation may require O(n^2) interactions and increased memory, which could be computationally costly.
future_direction: Developing scalable implementations of invariant relational attention.
Designing optimizers that operate directly on reduced parameter spaces.
Empirical evaluation of the proposed framework on practical tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformer models contain substantial internal redundancy arising from coordinate-dependent representations and continuous symmetries, in model space and in head space, respectively. While recent approaches address this by explicitly breaking symmetry, we propose a complementary framework based on symmetry reduction. We reformulate representations, attention mechanisms, and optimization dynamics in terms of invariant relational quantities, eliminating redundant degrees of freedom by construction. This perspective yields architectures that operate directly on relational structures, providing a principled geometric framework for reducing parameter redundancy and analyzing optimization.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Data-driven emergence of convolutional structure in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can fully-connected neural networks learn convolutional structure directly from translation-invariant data, and what conditions drive the emergence of localized, space-tiling receptive fields?
papers.core_contribution: Fully-connected neural networks can learn convolutional structure (localized, space-tiling receptive fields) directly from translation-invariant data with non-Gaussian higher-order statistics, and this emergence is driven by higher-order correlations.
papers.conclusion: Higher-order statistics in translation-invariant data drive the emergence of convolutional structure in fully-connected neural networks, providing a new perspective on the development of low-level feature detectors.
papers.key_findings:
Fully-connected networks develop localized receptive fields when trained on non-Gaussian translation-invariant data, but not on Gaussian data with the same covariance.
The localized receptive fields tile the input space and resemble filters learned by convolutional networks trained on the same task.
The emergence of receptive fields is linked to tensor decomposition of higher-order input correlations, specifically the fourth-order cumulant.
Existing Gaussian theories of learning break down when receptive fields form, indicating the importance of non-Gaussian statistics.
The network learns higher-order statistics sequentially, with receptive field formation coinciding with a decrease in the excess kurtosis of pre-activations.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic data model and a simple two-layer network, limiting generalizability to more complex architectures and real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper architectures and recurrent networks.
Generalizing to other symmetry groups and understanding the conditions for learning invariances.
Studying the minimal amount of data necessary to detect such invariances.
papers.abstract: Exploiting data invariances is crucial for efficient learning in both artificial and biological neural circuits. Understanding how neural networks can discover appropriate representations capable of harnessing the underlying symmetries of their inputs is thus crucial in machine learning and neuroscience. Convolutional neural networks, for example, were designed to exploit translation symmetry and their capabilities triggered the first wave of deep learning successes. However, learning convolutions directly from translation-invariant data with a fully-connected network has so far proven elusive. Here, we show how initially fully-connected neural networks solving a discrimination task can learn a convolutional structure directly from their inputs, resulting in localised, space-tiling receptive fields. These receptive fields match the filters of a convolutional network trained on the same task. By carefully designing data models for the visual scene, we show that the emergence of this pattern is triggered by the non-Gaussian, higher-order local structure of the inputs, which has long been recognised as the hallmark of natural images. We provide an analytical and numerical characterisation of the pattern-formation mechanism responsible for this phenomenon in a simple model and find an unexpected link between receptive field formation and tensor decomposition of higher-order input correlations. These results provide a new perspective on the development of low-level feature detectors in various sensory modalities, and pave the way for studying the impact of higher-order statistics on learning in neural networks.

papers.title: “Amide − amine + alcohol = carboxylic acid.” chemical reactions as linear algebraic analogies in graph neural networks
papers.research_question: Do graph neural network (GNN) atom-embeddings exhibit linear algebraic analogies similar to word embeddings in NLP, and how do these analogies relate to chemical reactions and properties?
papers.core_contribution: Atom-embeddings in pretrained graph neural networks exhibit linear algebraic analogies that correspond to chemical reactions, revealing a highly structured latent space that mirrors chemical syntax.
papers.conclusion: The latent space of GNNs in chemistry is highly structured and organized according to chemical syntax, with linear analogies providing a global explanatory framework for chemical transformations and properties.
papers.key_findings:
Atom-embeddings in a pretrained GNN (SchNet) show arithmetic properties allowing linear analogies that represent valid chemical reaction formulas, similar to word analogies in NLP.
Reaction vectors (differences between reactant and product embeddings) are approximately constant for a given reaction type and are colinear for similar reactions (e.g., oxidations).
The linear analogies can be explained by a perturbational replicate model based on neighborhood chemical composition, linking the embedding structure to chemical principles.
The structured embedding space facilitates transfer learning and reveals linear relations in chemical properties like NMR chemical shifts and atomization energies.
The organization of the embedding space has two levels: substructure composition and changes to substructure, with similar changes aligning in direction.
papers.limitation:
The QM9 dataset only includes equilibrium geometries, so the reaction datasets only account for initial and product states, not mechanistic transitions.
Geometry optimization using force fields may introduce non-equilibrium geometries from the perspective of the DFT-trained model.
The replicate model is an approximation and ignores the exact layout of the graph.
future_direction: Mapping out the trajectories of reactions in the latent space to study transition states.
Studying how the global explanatory framework reduces to local explanations on a case-by-case basis.
Improving the replicate model by incorporating the exact graph layout and using the same geometry optimization as the GNN model.
papers.abstract: In deep learning methods, especially in the context of chemistry, there is an increasing urgency to uncover the hidden learning mechanisms often dubbed as "black box." In this work, we show that graph models built on computational chemical data behave similar to natural language processing (NLP) models built on text data. Crucially, we show that atom-embeddings, a.k.a atom-parsed graph neural activation patterns, exhibit arithmetic properties that represent valid reaction formulas. This is very similar to how word-embeddings can be combined to make word analogies, thus preserving the semantic meaning behind the words, as in the famous example "King" - "Man" + "Woman" = "Queen." For instance, we show how the reaction from an alcohol to a carbonyl is represented by a constant vector in the embedding space, implicitly representing "-H<sub>2</sub>." This vector is independent from the particular carbonyl reactant and alcohol product and represents a consistent chemical transformation. Other directions in the embedding space are synonymous with distinct chemical changes (ex. the tautomerization direction). In contrast to natural language processing, we can explain the observed chemical analogies using algebraic manipulations on the local chemical composition that surrounds each atom-embedding. Furthermore, the observations find applications in transfer learning, for instance in the formal structure and prediction of atomistic properties, such as <sup>1</sup>H-NMR and <sup>13</sup>C-NMR. This work is in line with the recent push for interpretable explanations to graph neural network modeling of chemistry and uncovers a latent model of chemistry that is highly structured, consistent, and analogous to chemical syntax.

papers.title: Learning symmetries in datasets
papers.research_question: How symmetries present in datasets affect the structure of the latent space learned by Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).
papers.core_contribution: When symmetries or approximate symmetries are present, the VAE self-organizes its latent space, effectively compressing the data along a reduced number of latent variables, capturing the intrinsic dimensionality determined by the symmetry constraints.
papers.conclusion: Deep generative models not only learn to represent the data distribution but can also internalize fundamental structural properties, offering new possibilities for data-driven discovery in physics and beyond.
papers.key_findings:
VAEs self-organize their latent space to align with symmetry directions in the data.
A relevance measure (std(⟨zj⟩)/mean(σj)) identifies the intrinsic dimensionality of the data.
For a 2D dataset with O(2) symmetry (circle), the VAE uses one dominant latent dimension to encode the angular position.
For electron-positron collision data, the VAE reduces six input dimensions to three latent dimensions, reflecting momentum conservation constraints.
For proton-proton collision data, a similar reduction to three latent dimensions is observed, consistent with kinematic constraints.
papers.limitation:
No general mathematical proof guarantees this behavior for arbitrary datasets and standard VAE architectures.
The method is somewhat sensitive to model architecture and dataset characteristics.
future_direction: Extending this approach to more complex datasets.
Exploring different generative model architectures.
Incorporating explicit regularization for symmetry properties.
papers.abstract: We investigate how symmetries present in datasets affect the structure of the latent space learned by Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). By training VAEs on data originating from simple mechanical systems and particle collisions, we analyze the organization of the latent space through a relevance measure that identifies the most meaningful latent directions. We show that when symmetries or approximate symmetries are present, the VAE self-organizes its latent space, effectively compressing the data along a reduced number of latent variables. This behavior captures the intrinsic dimensionality determined by the symmetry constraints and reveals hidden relations among the features. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of a simple toy model, demonstrating how, under idealized conditions, the latent space aligns with the symmetry directions of the data manifold. We illustrate these findings with examples ranging from two-dimensional datasets with $O(2)$ symmetry to realistic datasets from electron-positron and proton-proton collisions. Our results highlight the potential of unsupervised generative models to expose underlying structures in data and offer a novel approach to symmetry discovery without explicit supervision.

papers.title: Integrating geometries of ReLU feedforward neural networks
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to analyze the geometric properties (polyhedral decomposition) of ReLU feedforward neural networks and uses this to study network behavior, including adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a toolbox for analyzing the polyhedral decomposition of ReLU feedforward neural networks and uses it to study geometric properties, including Hamming distance, bisection method, and Chebyshev centers, providing insights into network behavior and adversarial examples.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a toolbox and methodologies for analyzing the geometries of ReLU neural networks, offering insights into their structure, behavior, and response to adversarial inputs, and serves as a foundation for future analysis on larger datasets and more complex architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Hamming distance between binary vectors can reveal distinct geometric properties between normal and adversarial data points.
The number of polyhedra (linear regions) increases with network depth and width, correlating with model expressivity.
The Chebyshev center and radius of polyhedra differ between training/test data and adversarial examples, indicating different geometric regions.
The bisection method can identify sample points along a Euclidean path where adjacent points have a Hamming distance of 1, revealing network connectivity.
The toolbox enables visualization and analysis of the polyhedral decomposition, aiding in understanding decision boundaries and network geometry.
future_direction: Extend the application of the toolbox and methodologies to conduct comprehensive geometric analyses on much larger real-world datasets together with much more intricate neural network architectures.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the integration of multiple geometries present within a ReLU-based neural network. A ReLU neural network determines a piecewise affine linear continuous map, M, from an input space ℝm to an output space ℝn. The piecewise behavior corresponds to a polyhedral decomposition of ℝm. Each polyhedron in the decomposition can be labeled with a binary vector (whose length equals the number of ReLU nodes in the network) and with an affine linear function (which agrees with M when restricted to points in the polyhedron). We develop a toolbox that calculates the binary vector for a polyhedra containing a given data point with respect to a given ReLU FFNN. We utilize this binary vector to derive bounding facets for the corresponding polyhedron, extraction of "active" bits within the binary vector, enumeration of neighboring binary vectors, and visualization of the polyhedral decomposition (Python code is available at https://github.com/cglrtrgy/GoL_Toolbox). Polyhedra in the polyhedral decomposition of ℝm are neighbors if they share a facet. Binary vectors for neighboring polyhedra differ in exactly 1 bit. Using the toolbox, we analyze the Hamming distance between the binary vectors for polyhedra containing points from adversarial/nonadversarial datasets revealing distinct geometric properties.
