A bisection method is employed to identify sample points with a Hamming distance of 1 along the shortest Euclidean distance path, facilitating the analysis of local geometric interplay between Euclidean geometry and the polyhedral decomposition along the path. Additionally, we study the distribution of Chebyshev centers and related radii across different polyhedra, shedding light on the polyhedral shape, size, clustering, and aiding in the understanding of decision boundaries.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Emergence of Lie Symmetries in Functional Architectures Learned by CNNs
papers.research_question: How do symmetries (rotational and orientation-specific) spontaneously emerge in the early layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) during learning on natural images, and how do they parallel the functional architecture of the biological visual system?
papers.core_contribution: A biologically inspired CNN architecture with an LGN pre-filtering layer and lateral connections, when trained on natural images, spontaneously develops rotational symmetry in the LGN layer and orientation-specific connectivity in the first convolutional layer, mirroring symmetries found in the early visual pathway.
papers.conclusion: Approximate group invariances (rotational and orientation-specific) arise spontaneously in the early layers of the proposed biologically inspired CNN during learning on natural images, establishing a parallel with the functional architecture and plasticity of the early visual pathway.
papers.key_findings:
The pre-filtering layer ℓ0 evolves a radially symmetric filter well approximated by a Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), similar to LGN receptive profiles.
The first convolutional layer ℓ1 filters are Gabor-like and sharply tuned for orientation, with no radially symmetric filters present due to the ℓ0 pre-filtering.
The learned lateral connectivity kernel K1 shows a 'Mexican hat'-like profile for short-range connections, sharpening orientation tuning.
The connectivity kernel, when re-parameterized in position-orientation space, induces association fields that link neurons with collinear or co-circular tuning, resembling psychophysical association fields and edge co-occurrence statistics from natural images.
These geometric properties arise spontaneously during training, driven by the statistics of natural images and the convolutional structure of the network.
papers.limitation: The learned lateral connectivity kernel is localized (spatially limited) and may not capture long-range interactions as effectively as other models.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include the learning of feature maps and investigating phenomena like radial bias.
Considering larger natural images and examining wider horizontal connectivity obtained via multiple diffusion steps (self-convolution of K1).
Extending the model by comparing the properties of deeper network layers to the processing in higher cortices of the visual system.
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the spontaneous development of symmetries in the early layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) during learning on natural images. Our architecture is built in such a way to mimic some properties of the early stages of biological visual systems. In particular, it contains a pre-filtering step ℓ<sup>0</sup> defined in analogy with the Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN). Moreover, the first convolutional layer is equipped with lateral connections defined as a propagation driven by a learned connectivity kernel, in analogy with the horizontal connectivity of the primary visual cortex (V1). We first show that the ℓ<sup>0</sup> filter evolves during the training to reach a radially symmetric pattern well approximated by a Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), which is a well-known model of the receptive profiles of LGN cells. In line with previous works on CNNs, the learned convolutional filters in the first layer can be approximated by Gabor functions, in agreement with well-established models for the receptive profiles of V1 simple cells. Here, we focus on the geometric properties of the learned lateral connectivity kernel of this layer, showing the emergence of orientation selectivity w.r.t. the tuning of the learned filters. We also examine the short-range connectivity and association fields induced by this connectivity kernel, and show qualitative and quantitative comparisons with known group-based models of V1 horizontal connections. These geometric properties arise spontaneously during the training of the CNN architecture, analogously to the emergence of symmetries in visual systems thanks to brain plasticity driven by external stimuli.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of internal representations in multilayer neural networks with binary weights
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the weight space structure of multilayer neural networks with binary weights, focusing on the distribution of volumes associated with internal representations of learning examples. It also analyzes the learning behavior and symmetry breaking transition in such networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies the internal representation volumes approach to multilayer neural networks with binary weights, deriving the distribution of volumes and analyzing learning behavior and symmetry breaking transitions, with numerical validation.
papers.conclusion: The internal representation volumes approach is confirmed by numerical simulations for binary weight networks, revealing differences from continuous weight networks in where symmetry breaking occurs.
papers.key_findings:
The distribution of internal representation volumes for the binary parity machine can be computed analytically, revealing a freezing transition at α=0.41.
The number of implementable internal representations NR and the number of domains contributing to the Gardner volume ND are derived as functions of the loading parameter α.
The analytical predictions show remarkable agreement with numerical simulations on finite systems.
Multilayer networks with binary weights exhibit symmetry breaking inside representation volumes, unlike continuous weights where it occurs between volumes.
The method provides a detailed geometrical interpretation of the learning transition and the freezing phenomena.
future_direction: Study of the distribution of metastable states arising from a gradient learning process.
papers.abstract: We study the weight space structure of the parity machine with binary weights by deriving the distribution of volumes associated to the internal representations of the learning examples. The learning behavior and the symmetry breaking transition are analyzed and the results are found to be in very good agreement with the extended numerical simulations. \textcopyright{} 1996 The American Physical Society.

papers.title: Learning unfolded networks with a cyclic group structure
papers.research_question: How can domain knowledge, specifically rotational equivariance, be explicitly encoded into neural network architectures to improve interpretability and reduce the number of trainable parameters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an equivariant unrolled network architecture that explicitly encodes rotational equivariance via a cyclic group structure, leading to interpretable models with sparse activations and a significant reduction in trainable parameters while maintaining competitive performance.
papers.conclusion: Equivariant unrolled networks with a cyclic group structure successfully incorporate domain knowledge (rotational equivariance) into the architecture, reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offer an interpretable model through sparse activations and structured filters.
papers.key_findings:
Equivariant unrolled networks (R90-CNN, R60-CNN) achieve comparable or better classification performance than a baseline unrolled network on MNIST, rotated MNIST, and CIFAR-10, despite having a fraction of the trainable parameters.
The learned filters in the equivariant models exhibit a topographic structure by construction, as they are generated as rotations of a few basis filters, unlike the baseline which must learn all orientations from data.
The R90-CNN model, with elementary rotations, generalizes better to rotated data (rotated MNIST) than the baseline, demonstrating the benefit of built-in equivariance.
The R60-CNN model, with 60-degree rotations, shows slightly improved performance on CIFAR-10 compared to the baseline and R90-CNN, indicating the effectiveness of the cyclic group structure.
The proposed architecture reduces the number of trainable parameters significantly (e.g., R60-CNN uses 17.89K parameters vs. 56.29K for the baseline on CIFAR-10).
papers.limitation: R90-CNN displays reduced performance on the rotated MNIST dataset, which the authors speculate is due to interpolation artifacts.
future_direction: Learning the generator g of the cyclic group from data, rather than pre-defining it, is identified as an exciting avenue for future work.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks lack straightforward ways to incorporate domain knowledge and are notoriously considered black boxes. Prior works attempted to inject domain knowledge into architectures implicitly through data augmentation. Building on recent advances on equivariant neural networks, we propose networks that explicitly encode domain knowledge, specifically equivariance with respect to rotations. By using unfolded architectures, a rich framework that originated from sparse coding and has theoretical guarantees, we present interpretable networks with sparse activations. The equivariant unfolded networks compete favorably with baselines, with only a fraction of their parameters, as showcased on (rotated) MNIST and CIFAR-10.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Representation Potentials of Foundation Models for Multimodal Alignment: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes evidence for the representation potentials of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within and across modalities, and analyzes the key factors driving this potential.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes substantial evidence for the representation potential of foundation models, demonstrating their capacity for alignment within individual modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to neuroscience. It analyzes the key factors that foster representation potentials and discusses open questions.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment.
Scale, architectural inductive biases, training objectives, and task and instruction diversity are key factors that foster representation potentials for alignment.
Evidence for alignment is found within vision, language, and speech modalities, across multimodal combinations, and in relation to representations observed in neuroscience.
papers.limitation:
Differences across modalities constrain the extent to which their representations can perfectly align, as certain information may be unique to a given sensory channel.
There is an ongoing debate regarding the effectiveness and interpretability of alignment metrics, and the absence of a universally accepted standard complicates cross-study comparisons.
Training data biases and sociotechnical context shape representation spaces and constrain the universality of alignment claims.
future_direction: Pursue a deeper theoretical grounding of representation potentials.
Develop more robust evaluation frameworks for alignment.
papers.abstract: Foundation models learn highly transferable representations through large-scale pretraining on diverse data. An increasing body of research indicates that these representations exhibit a remarkable degree of similarity across architectures and modalities. In this survey, we investigate the representation potentials of foundation models, defined as the latent capacity of their learned representations to capture task-specific information within a single modality while also providing a transferable basis for alignment and unification across modalities. We begin by reviewing representative foundation models and the key metrics that make alignment measurable. We then synthesize empirical evidence of representation potentials from studies in vision, language, speech, multimodality, and neuroscience. The evidence suggests that foundation models often exhibit structural regularities and semantic consistencies in their representation spaces, positioning them as strong candidates for cross-modal transfer and alignment. We further analyze the key factors that foster representation potentials, discuss open questions, and highlight potential challenges.

papers.title: Versor: A Geometric Sequence Architecture
papers.research_question: Can using Conformal Geometric Algebra (CGA) in place of traditional linear operations lead to better generalization, performance, and interpretability in sequence modeling? Specifically, can embedding states in the Cl4,1 manifold and evolving them via geometric transformations (rotors) natively represent SE(3)-equivariant relationships without explicit structural encoding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Versor, a novel sequence architecture based on Conformal Geometric Algebra (Cl4,1) that replaces traditional linear operations with geometric transformations (rotors), achieving superior scale generalization, interpretability, and parameter efficiency compared to Transformers and other baselines on tasks like chaotic dynamics and topological reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Versor provides a powerful geometric alternative to traditional sequence models, embedding symmetry priors via Conformal Geometric Algebra to achieve improved generalization, interpretability, and efficiency across a range of tasks from physics simulation to multimodal benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Versor achieves strong scale generalization, e.g., 0.993 MCC on topological connectivity vs. 0.070 for Vision Transformers.
It uses orders-of-magnitude fewer parameters (200x vs. Transformers) while maintaining or improving performance.
Its Geometric Product Attention (GPA) decomposes into interpretable scalar (proximity) and bivector (orientational) components.
The Recursive Rotor Accumulator (RRA) enables O(L) linear temporal complexity for efficient long-sequence modeling.
Custom Clifford kernels achieve over 100x speedup via bit-masked contraction and Matrix Isomorphism optimizations.
papers.limitation:
The 32-dimensional multivector representation may be wasteful for simple tasks, leading to a 'curse of dimensionality'.
Formal guarantees for the architecture's behavior at foundation-model scale are lacking.
Numerical drift can occur, though addressed by the Lie algebra path and manifold normalization.
Energy drift in dynamical systems, addressed by a Hamiltonian extension.
Potential metric bias when the learned metric deviates from the true physical metric, addressed by a Riemannian path.
Optimization on Lie manifolds is non-trivial and requires specialized techniques.
future_direction: Addressing the 'curse of dimensionality' in the multivector representation.
Establishing formal guarantees for the architecture's scaling behavior to foundation-model scales.
Further exploration of the Lie algebra, Hamiltonian, and Riemannian paths to address numerical drift, energy conservation, and metric bias.
papers.abstract: A novel sequence architecture design is introduced, Versor, which uses Conformal Geometric Algebra (CGA) in place of the traditional fundamental non-linear operations to achieve structural generalization and significant performance improvements on a variety of tasks, while offering improved interpretability and efficiency. By embedding states in the $Cl_{4,1}$ manifold and evolving them via geometric transformations (rotors), Versor natively represents $SE(3)$-equivariant relationships without requiring explicit structural encoding. Versor is validated on chaotic N-body dynamics, topological reasoning, and standard multimodal benchmarks (CIFAR-10, WikiText-103), consistently outperforming Transformers, Graph Networks, and geometric baselines (GATr, EGNN). Key results include: orders of magnitude fewer parameters ($200\times$ vs. Transformers); interpretable attention decomposing into proximity and orientational components; zero-shot scale generalization (99.3% MCC on topology vs. 50.4% for ViT); and $O(L)$ linear complexity via the novel Recursive Rotor Accumulator. In out-of-distribution tests, Versor maintains stable predictions while Transformers fail catastrophically. Custom Clifford kernels achieve up to $78\times$ speedup, providing a scalable foundation for geometrically-aware scientific modeling.

papers.title: Probing the 3D Awareness of Visual Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do visual foundation models represent the 3D structure of scenes and objects, and are their representations consistent across views?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the 3D awareness of visual foundation models by probing their representations for single-view surface reconstruction and multiview consistency, revealing that while some models encode surface properties, they lack 3D consistency across large viewpoint changes.
papers.conclusion: Visual foundation models exhibit varying degrees of 3D awareness, with self-supervised models performing best on single-view tasks, but all models lack robust multiview consistency, indicating limited true 3D understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised models like DINOv2 learn representations that encode depth and surface normals well, while vision-language models like CLIP perform poorly.
Models struggle with multiview consistency, especially for large viewpoint changes, despite performing well on small viewpoint changes.
Correspondence estimation is often semantic in nature rather than geometric, leading to confusion between semantically related parts.
Performance on single-view depth and surface normal tasks is strongly correlated, but multiview consistency is not strongly correlated with single-view performance.
The training objective significantly impacts 3D awareness, with self-supervised and generative models outperforming classification and language-supervised models.
papers.limitation:
Comparisons are limited to publicly available checkpoints, which confounds the effects of training objectives with differences in datasets and training recipes.
The analysis focuses on only two specific aspects of 3D awareness (single-view surface reconstruction and multiview consistency), which are not comprehensive.
The experimental methodology focuses on probing methods and does not evaluate fine-tuning or prompting-based adaptations.
future_direction: Conduct more controlled experiments by training the same backbone architecture with different objectives on the same dataset.
Develop more comprehensive benchmarks for 3D understanding that include additional capabilities like full 3D shape reconstruction and physical property estimation.
Explore prompting-based methods to analyze the 3D awareness of models that support in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large-scale pretraining have yielded visual foundation models with strong capabilities. Not only can recent models generalize to arbitrary images for their training task, their intermediate representations are useful for other visual tasks such as detection and segmentation. Given that such models can classify, delineate, and localize objects in 2D, we ask whether they also represent their 3D structure? In this work, we analyze the 3D awareness of visual foundation models. We posit that 3D awareness implies that representations (1) encode the 3D structure of the scene and (2) consistently represent the surface across views. We conduct a series of experiments using task-specific probes and zero-shot inference procedures on frozen features. Our experiments reveal several limitations of the current models. Our code and analysis can be found at https://github.com/mbanani/probe3d.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Representation Mechanics: Invariant-Governed Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection achieve generalization by learning and preserving invariants, as evidenced by early phase transitions (the Platonic Spike)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Representation Mechanics, showing that neural networks with set-valued operations and learned selection can achieve generalization by learning invariants, as evidenced by the Platonic Spike (early phase transition where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that invariant-preserving inductive bias is sufficient for rule learning and that constructing reliable AI requires respecting the mechanics of representation (treating embeddings as physical objects with inertia, boundaries, and elasticity).
papers.key_findings:
Set-valued weights with learned selection lead to early phase transitions (Platonic Spike) where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
Classical activations (e.g., GELU, ELU, ReLU) interfere with basin preservation and cause overfitting or boundary erosion.
Basin preservation via path freezing can prevent catastrophic forgetting by maintaining separatrix integrity.
The Surgical Clutch mechanism allows for invariant maintenance under continual learning by dynamically routing gradients.
The architecture achieves high accuracy on synthetic logic and language tasks without relying on n-gram statistics.
papers.limitation: The current work uses explicit rule contexts, which may not be available in all domains, and the architecture has not yet been tested at scale.
future_direction: Testing the architecture at scale
Exploring amplification strategies (more branches, hierarchical scoring, contrastive loss)
Extending to domains without explicit rule contexts
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> We present Representation Mechanics, a theoretical and empirical framework characterizing learning in invariant-governed domains. We demonstrate that neural networks with set-valued operations (discrete potentials {-W, 0, +W}) and learned selection exhibit sharp phase transitions to generalization without pretraining. The Platonic Spike (Early Phase Transition)—where validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy in early epochs—signals the discovery of structural invariants before instance memorization. We validate these findings on controlled synthetic tasks (spiral classification, closed-world logic, declarative language) to isolate geometric mechanics from natural language statistical confounds. We contrast this Form-First paradigm with diffusion-dominated learning and define the conditions (Basin Preservation and Friction Set tracking) required to maintain these invariants under continual learning pressure. Our results suggest that restricting representational freedom via discrete potentials is not a limitation but a necessary inductive bias for rule-consistent generalization.

papers.title: A Group Theoretic Perspective on Unsupervised Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can unsupervised deep learning, specifically autoencoder pre-training, be explained from a group theory perspective using the orbit-stabilizer principle?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a group-theoretic framework for understanding unsupervised deep learning, explaining how autoencoders learn simpler features first due to the inverse relationship between orbit and stabilizer sizes.
papers.conclusion: The group-theoretic perspective provides a theoretical explanation for why neural networks learn hierarchical representations, with each layer discovering locally simple features.
papers.key_findings:
An autoencoder learning a feature is equivalent to searching for a transformation that stabilizes that feature.
Simpler features have larger stabilizers (and smaller orbits), making them more likely to be found early in training, aligning with empirical observations.
This orbit-stabilizer principle can be extended to multiple layers, with each layer learning 'edge-like features' relative to the previous layer's representation space.
papers.abstract: Why does Deep Learning work? What representations does it capture? How do higher-order representations emerge? We study these questions from the perspective of group theory, thereby opening a new approach towards a theory of Deep learning. One factor behind the recent resurgence of the subject is a key algorithmic step called {\em pretraining}: first search for a good generative model for the input samples, and repeat the process one layer at a time. We show deeper implications of this simple principle, by establishing a connection with the interplay of orbits and stabilizers of group actions. Although the neural networks themselves may not form groups, we show the existence of {\em shadow} groups whose elements serve as close approximations. Over the shadow groups, the pre-training step, originally introduced as a mechanism to better initialize a network, becomes equivalent to a search for features with minimal orbits. Intuitively, these features are in a way the {\em simplest}. Which explains why a deep learning network learns simple features first. Next, we show how the same principle, when repeated in the deeper layers, can capture higher order representations, and why representation complexity increases as the layers get deeper.

papers.title: Standard Attention as a Small-Angle Limit of Riemannian Geometric Algebra Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the geometric interpretation of standard Transformer attention? The paper shows that standard attention arises as a degenerate limit of a curved geometric operator family on the rotor manifold Spin(3).
papers.core_contribution: Standard Transformer attention is a small-angle limit of a curved geometric operator family on the rotor manifold Spin(3), and depth in Transformers accumulates curvature through Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff commutators.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can be analyzed as approximate rotor flows with curvature emerging from depth, suggesting a mathematical program for studying representation geometry, stability, and symmetry directly in the operator calculus of Spin(3).
papers.key_findings:
Standard attention is a flat limit of a Riemannian operator family on Spin(3), realized in the Clifford algebra Cl(3,0).
The geometric softmax (GSM) attention reduces to classical dot-product attention in the small-angle regime.
Depth in Transformers accumulates curvature through BCH commutators, providing a geometric interpretation of deep composition.
The Euclidean limit is controlled by the small-angle parameter and depth, with error bounds scaling as O(ε²) per head and O(Lε²) with depth L.
future_direction: Connecting curvature scales to spectral gaps and mixing times of the diffusion operator.
Studying the stability of the Euclidean limit under perturbations of the metric.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Transformers implicitly assume a flat representational geome- try: similarity is Euclidean, composition is linear, and attention is a softmax of dot products. We show that these operations arise as a degenerate limit of a curved geometric operator family on the rotor manifold Spin(3), realized in the Clifford algebra Cl(3, 0). In the small-angle regime, geometric soft- max reduces to classical dot-product attention; yet, at depth, many small-angle steps accumulate curvature through Baker– Campbell–Hausdorff commutators, providing a precise sense in which standard Transformers approximate rotor dynamics. The paper focuses on this mathematical discovery and its struc- tural implications for interpretability; performance studies are a separate empirical program.

papers.title: Noether: The More Things Change, the More Stay the Same
papers.research_question: How do symmetries in neural networks interact with learning algorithms, and what conserved quantities arise from these symmetries during optimization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that symmetries in neural networks lead to conserved quantities during optimization, which constrain the optimization path and help understand dynamics like balance conditions and boundedness.
papers.conclusion: Symmetry is an important tool for understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.
papers.key_findings:
For ReLU networks, gradient descent leads to balance equations between consecutive layers.
For linear networks, symmetries lead to balancedness conditions on weight matrices.
Data augmentation introduces symmetries that constrain the optimization path.
Conserved quantities are derived for various activation functions (ReLU, linear, Swish) and optimization algorithms (gradient flow, Newtonian dynamics, Nesterov).
future_direction: Determine if conservation laws for Swish can explain its empirical advantage over ReLU.
Derive bounds for Nesterov's accelerated gradient flow similar to Newtonian dynamics.
papers.abstract: Symmetries have proven to be important ingredients in the analysis of neural networks. So far their use has mostly been implicit or seemingly coincidental. We undertake a systematic study of the role that symmetry plays. In particular, we clarify how symmetry interacts with the learning algorithm. The key ingredient in our study is played by Noether's celebrated theorem which, informally speaking, states that symmetry leads to conserved quantities (e.g., conservation of energy or conservation of momentum). In the realm of neural networks under gradient descent, model symmetries imply restrictions on the gradient path. E.g., we show that symmetry of activation functions leads to boundedness of weight matrices, for the specific case of linear activations it leads to balance equations of consecutive layers, data augmentation leads to gradient paths that have "momentum"-type restrictions, and time symmetry leads to a version of the Neural Tangent Kernel. Symmetry alone does not specify the optimization path, but the more symmetries are contained in the model the more restrictions are imposed on the path. Since symmetry also implies over-parametrization, this in effect implies that some part of this over-parametrization is cancelled out by the existence of the conserved quantities. Symmetry can therefore be thought of as one further important tool in understanding the performance of neural networks under gradient descent.

papers.title: Learning Invariances in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we automatically discover the appropriate symmetries (invariances and equivariances) in neural networks from training data alone?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Augerino, a method to learn invariances and equivariances in neural networks by learning a distribution over augmentations from training data alone.
papers.conclusion: Augerino is a framework that can learn symmetries from training data alone and improve generalization across various tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Augerino can learn the correct set and extent of invariances from training data alone, including full invariance (rotMNIST), soft invariance (Mario & Iggy), and no invariance (Olivetti faces).
Augerino improves test accuracy on CIFAR-10 compared to fixed augmentations and is competitive with Fast AutoAugment.
Augerino improves molecular property prediction on QM9, competitive with hand-chosen augmentations.
Augerino can learn equivariances for semantic segmentation on rotCamVid.
Augerino solutions are flatter in the loss landscape, which explains better generalization.
papers.abstract: Invariances to translations have imbued convolutional neural networks with powerful generalization properties. However, we often do not know a priori what invariances are present in the data, or to what extent a model should be invariant to a given symmetry group. We show how to \emph{learn} invariances and equivariances by parameterizing a distribution over augmentations and optimizing the training loss simultaneously with respect to the network parameters and augmentation parameters. With this simple procedure we can recover the correct set and extent of invariances on image classification, regression, segmentation, and molecular property prediction from a large space of augmentations, on training data alone.

papers.title: Attentive Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks
papers.research_question: How can attention be incorporated into group equivariant convolutional networks to learn meaningful relationships among symmetries and improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces attentive group convolutions, a generalization of group convolutions that uses attention to accentuate meaningful symmetry combinations, leading to improved performance and interpretability through equivariant attention maps.
papers.conclusion: Attentive group convolutions are an effective drop-in replacement for group convolutions, improving performance and providing interpretable equivariant attention maps.
papers.key_findings:
Attentive group convolutions consistently outperform conventional group convolutions on rot-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and PCam datasets.
The learned attention maps are equivariant and provide interpretability by highlighting relevant parts of the input.
Channel and spatial attention components can be factorized and computed efficiently.
Exact equivariance requires careful handling of stride and input size in convolutional layers.
papers.limitation:
High memory requirements for attentive group convolutions on datasets like CIFAR-10
Approximate equivariance in some network architectures due to stride and input size mismatches
papers.abstract: Although group convolutional networks are able to learn powerful representations based on symmetry patterns, they lack explicit means to learn meaningful relationships among them (e.g., relative positions and poses). In this paper, we present attentive group equivariant convolutions, a generalization of the group convolution, in which attention is applied during the course of convolution to accentuate meaningful symmetry combinations and suppress non-plausible, misleading ones. We indicate that prior work on visual attention can be described as special cases of our proposed framework and show empirically that our attentive group equivariant convolutional networks consistently outperform conventional group convolutional networks on benchmark image datasets. Simultaneously, we provide interpretability to the learned concepts through the visualization of equivariant attention maps.

papers.title: The Spotlight Resonance Method: Resolving the Alignment of Embedded Activations
papers.research_question: What causes the observed tendency of neural network representations to align with neurons (or a privileged basis)? The paper investigates whether this alignment is due to functional form choices, such as activation functions, that break symmetry and induce a privileged basis.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Spotlight-Resonance Method (SRM), a versatile visualization tool for determining the axis alignment of embedded activations in deep learning models. It demonstrates that representations tend to align with a 'privileged basis' induced by functional form choices like activation functions, not due to any innate property of the standard neuron basis.
papers.conclusion: The Spotlight-Resonance Method is a simple, interpretable, and versatile tool for establishing representational alignment in deep learning models. It shows that alignment is caused by functional form choices (like activation functions) that induce a privileged basis, explaining prior observations.
papers.key_findings:
The Spotlight-Resonance Method (SRM) can detect whether embedded activations cluster around vectors of a privileged basis.
Representations in trained models tend to align (or anti-align) with the privileged basis vectors induced by the activation function.
The observed alignment with the standard basis in prior works is a consequence of elementwise activation functions privileging that basis, not a fundamental phenomenon.
The method can identify 'grandmother neurons' (neurons responding to specific human-interpretable concepts) in various networks.
The privileged basis is the fundamental quantity for representational alignment, not the standard basis.
future_direction: Expanding analysis on the functional form hierarchy of basis privileging.
More thoroughly investigating local coding through meaningful subsets of the dataset.
Exploring isotropic deep learning (including isotropic activation functions).
papers.abstract: Understanding how deep learning models represent data is currently difficult due to the limited number of methodologies available. This paper demonstrates a versatile and novel visualisation tool for determining the axis alignment of embedded data at any layer in any deep learning model. In particular, it evaluates the distribution around planes defined by the network's privileged basis vectors. This method provides both an atomistic and a holistic, intuitive metric for interpreting the distribution of activations across all planes. It ensures that both positive and negative signals contribute, treating the activation vector as a whole. Depending on the application, several variations of this technique are presented, with a resolution scale hyperparameter to probe different angular scales. Using this method, multiple examples are provided that demonstrate embedded representations tend to be axis-aligned with the privileged basis. This is not necessarily the standard basis, and it is found that activation functions directly result in privileged bases. Hence, it provides a direct causal link between functional form symmetry breaking and representational alignment, explaining why representations have a tendency to align with the neuron basis. Therefore, using this method, we begin to answer the fundamental question of what causes the observed tendency of representations to align with neurons. Finally, examples of so-called grandmother neurons are found in a variety of networks.

papers.title: Composing Linear Layers from Irreducibles
papers.research_question: Can we identify/synthesize linear transformations from a minimal set of geometric primitives?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to represent linear layers using compositions of bivectors (geometric primitives) via rotors, requiring O(log d) parameters, and shows it matches baseline performance when replacing projections in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide an algebraic perspective on how geometric primitives can compose into higher-level functions within deep models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear layers can be expressed as compositions of bivectors using rotors, requiring O(log2 d) parameters versus O(d2) for dense matrices.
A differentiable invariant decomposition algorithm enables closed-form computation of rotors from bivectors.
Empirically, rotor-based layers match the performance of low-rank and block-Hadamard approximations when replacing key, query, and value projections in LLMs across various datasets.
The method provides an algebraic perspective on compositional structure in deep models.
papers.limitation: The approach is not a drop-in replacement yet, as practical benefits require additional system-level integration.
papers.abstract: Contemporary large models often exhibit behaviors suggesting the presence of low-level primitives that compose into modules with richer functionality, but these fundamental building blocks remain poorly understood. We investigate this compositional structure in linear layers by asking: can we identify/synthesize linear transformations from a minimal set of geometric primitives? Using Clifford algebra, we show that linear layers can be expressed as compositions of bivectors -- geometric objects encoding oriented planes -- and introduce a differentiable algorithm that decomposes them into products of rotors. This construction uses only O(log^2 d) parameters, versus O(d^2) required by dense matrices. Applied to the key, query, and value projections in LLM attention layers, our rotor-based layers match the performance of strong baselines such as block-Hadamard and low-rank approximations. Our findings provide an algebraic perspective on how these geometric primitives can compose into higher-level functions within deep models.

papers.title: Deep sequence models tend to memorize geometrically; it is unclear why
papers.research_question: Why do deep sequence models learn geometric memory, a form of storage that encodes global relationships between entities, instead of associative memory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies geometric memory, a form of storage where models synthesize embeddings encoding global relationships between entities, and shows it arises from a spectral bias in training.
papers.conclusion: The geometric view of memory provides a new perspective on how deep sequence models store knowledge, with implications for reasoning, creativity, and model design.
papers.key_findings:
Deep sequence models learn geometric memory, encoding global relationships between entities, enabling implicit reasoning tasks like path-finding.
Geometric memory emerges even when it is more complex than associative memory and without explicit global supervision.
The emergence of geometric memory cannot be attributed to typical pressures from supervision, architecture, or optimization.
In Node2Vec, geometric memory arises from a spectral bias that naturally occurs when minimizing cross-entropy loss.
Transformers have less geometric memory than Node2Vec, indicating headroom for improvement.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to symbolic tasks and may not directly translate to natural language.
The analysis of Node2Vec is preliminary and may not fully explain geometric memory in Transformers.
future_direction: Study competition between associative and geometric memory under gradient descent.
Investigate aspects of data and optimization that favor geometric memory.
Extend geometric memory analysis to natural language tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep sequence models are said to store atomic facts predominantly in the form of associative memory: a brute-force lookup of co-occurring entities. We identify a dramatically different form of storage of atomic facts that we term as geometric memory. Here, the model has synthesized embeddings encoding novel global relationships between all entities, including ones that do not co-occur in training. Such storage is powerful: for instance, we show how it transforms a hard reasoning task involving an $\ell$-fold composition into an easy-to-learn $1$-step navigation task. From this phenomenon, we extract fundamental aspects of neural embedding geometries that are hard to explain. We argue that the rise of such a geometry, as against a lookup of local associations, cannot be straightforwardly attributed to typical supervisory, architectural, or optimizational pressures. Counterintuitively, a geometry is learned even when it is more complex than the brute-force lookup. Then, by analyzing a connection to Node2Vec, we demonstrate how the geometry stems from a spectral bias that -- in contrast to prevailing theories -- indeed arises naturally despite the lack of various pressures. This analysis also points out to practitioners a visible headroom to make Transformer memory more strongly geometric. We hope the geometric view of parametric memory encourages revisiting the default intuitions that guide researchers in areas like knowledge acquisition, capacity, discovery, and unlearning.

papers.title: Occupancies vs Embeddings: Internal representations of Ab Initio and Graph Probabilistic Models*
papers.research_question: To what degree does the end-to-end data-driven approach (graph neural networks) coalesce with traditional ab initio predictions of molecular behavior? Does the model contain internal characteristics of the wave function or electron density from DFT?
papers.core_contribution: This study compares atomwise representations from graph neural networks (GNNs) and ab initio density functional theory (DFT), revealing that GNN embeddings offer higher resolution and can accurately predict DFT-derived atomic occupancy values, whereas the reverse mapping is significantly less accurate.
papers.conclusion: GNN embeddings serve as a richer, more informative molecular representation than DFT-derived atomic occupancies, demonstrating the power of end-to-end statistical models to encapsulate and extend traditional quantum chemical information, though further exploration is needed regarding their robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.key_findings:
Both GNN embedding vectors and DFT-derived atomic occupancy vectors can separate and label chemical environments, but embeddings provide much higher resolution and lower classification error.
Embedding vectors can predict atomic occupancy values with high accuracy (MAE 2.5e-3, R2 0.996), but the reverse mapping from occupancies to embeddings is an order of magnitude less accurate (MAE 0.235, R2 0.379).
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals qualitative similarities in the eigenvalue spectra between the two representations, but the embedding space captures more nuanced information.
The embedding representation contains more information than the occupancy representation, enabling precise mapping to occupancies but not vice versa within the same model chemistry.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) shows embeddings achieve near-perfect functional group classification, while occupancy vectors show higher error, especially for similar chemical environments.
papers.limitation: Interatomic information was omitted due to the need to respect rotational equivariance for the embeddings, and the use of Mulliken population analysis might hamper a faithful analysis of the information content in the occupancies.
future_direction: Further studies to tighten conclusions about the relationship between embeddings and electron density.
Exploration of GNN embeddings' robustness beyond equilibrium structures.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Chemical modeling has traditionally been separated into two fairly non-overlapping frameworks: the exact framework of \textit{ab initio} models and the data-driven framework of statistical models. However, recent advances in machine learning approaches have intercepted the exact \textit{ab initio} frameworks by using an \textit{end-to-end} probabilistic model of the Schr\"odinger equation in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation---from raw nuclear configurations to quantum observables such as the energy. While probabilistic modelling offers promising advancements to speed up computational predictions, the internal representation and its connection to the underlying quantum data---the wave function or electron density---which they implicitly rely on for training, remains relatively poorly understood. This study seeks to make a first comparison of the internal representation from a probabilistic end-to-end models with those from pure \textit{ab initio} frameworks such as density functional theory. We do this by comparing the internal atomwise representation of graph models, also called embeddings, to their most natural \textit{ab initio} counterpart, electron occupancy values. Our findings show that the embedding representations can be employed to transfer learn atomic occupancy values whereas the reverse mapping appears to be less accurate. We discuss the assumption that the probabilistic model could infer the existence of an underlying electron density underpinning the computational \textit{ab-initio} data.

papers.title: Lorentz Group Equivariant Neural Network for Particle Physics
papers.research_question: How to design a neural network architecture that is fully equivariant to the Lorentz group for particle physics applications, and whether such an architecture can achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters and improved interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Lorentz group equivariant neural network architecture for particle physics that achieves competitive performance on top tagging with drastically fewer parameters and improved physical interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The Lorentz-equivariant architecture is a successful early step in building physics-informed machine learning algorithms based on group theory, demonstrating the need for symmetry- and geometry-based approaches in scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
The LGN architecture is fully equivariant to the Lorentz group, using tensor products and Clebsch-Gordan decompositions.
On a top tagging classification task, LGN achieves competitive performance with only 4.5k parameters, far fewer than leading approaches like ParticleNet (498k parameters).
The network's weights are Lorentz-invariant, making them more interpretable as physical quantities.
The architecture demonstrates the benefits of symmetry-based approaches for physics-informed machine learning.
The equivariant design leads to simpler models with fewer learnable parameters.
papers.limitation:
The equivariant architecture takes more time to develop and its evaluation is more computationally intensive.
The performance does not match the state of the art, though it uses far fewer parameters.
future_direction: Once developed for a specific symmetry group, the architecture is broadly applicable to many problems with the same symmetry.
Optimizing the tensor product operation with a custom CUDA kernel to improve computational efficiency.
papers.abstract: We present a neural network architecture that is fully equivariant with respect to transformations under the Lorentz group, a fundamental symmetry of space and time in physics. The architecture is based on the theory of the finite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group and the equivariant nonlinearity involves the tensor product. For classification tasks in particle physics, we demonstrate that such an equivariant architecture leads to drastically simpler models that have relatively few learnable parameters and are much more physically interpretable than leading approaches that use CNNs and point cloud approaches. The competitive performance of the network is demonstrated on a public classification dataset [27] for tagging top quark decays given energy-momenta of jet constituents produced in proton-proton collisions.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: The Locality and Symmetry of Positional Encodings
papers.research_question: What are the core properties of positional encodings in bidirectional masked language models, and how do they correlate with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies locality and symmetry as fundamental properties of positional encodings in bidirectional masked language models, demonstrates their correlation with downstream task performance, and reveals a weakness of symmetry via new word-swap probing tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that locality and symmetry are two key properties of positional encodings, with locality aiding local composition and symmetry having a flaw in handling semantic role swaps, and hopes these findings inspire better design of positional encodings.
papers.key_findings:
Positional encodings in BERT-style models exhibit locality and symmetry properties, which are learned during pre-training.
Higher locality and symmetry in positional encodings lead to better inductive bias and improved performance on downstream natural language understanding tasks.
Locality helps positional encodings capture short-distance syntactic dependencies, while contextual weights handle long-distance dependencies.
Symmetry, while beneficial for many tasks, causes models to be insensitive to semantic role swaps, as shown by new probing tasks (Constituency Shuffling and Semantic Role Shuffling).
Initializing positional encodings with suitable locality and symmetry properties improves model performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on bidirectional masked language models, not decoder-only models like GPT.
Analysis limited to English language; different languages have different word order properties.
Handcrafted positional encodings replicate limitations of current positional encodings and do not fully address the symmetry flaw.
future_direction: Study decoder-only language models (GPT-style) for positional encoding properties.
Extend analysis to other languages and include natural language generation tasks.
Develop architectures that address the symmetry flaw in positional encodings.
papers.abstract: Positional Encodings (PEs) are used to inject word-order information into transformer-based language models. While they can significantly enhance the quality of sentence representations, their specific contribution to language models is not fully understood, especially given recent findings that various positional encodings are insensitive to word order. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of positional encodings in \textbf{Bidirectional Masked Language Models} (BERT-style) , which complements existing work in three aspects: (1) We uncover the core function of PEs by identifying two common properties, Locality and Symmetry; (2) We show that the two properties are closely correlated with the performances of downstream tasks; (3) We quantify the weakness of current PEs by introducing two new probing tasks, on which current PEs perform poorly. We believe that these results are the basis for developing better PEs for transformer-based language models. The code is available at \faGithub~ \url{https://github.com/tigerchen52/locality\_symmetry}

papers.title: Transformers trained on proteins can learn to attend to Euclidean distance
papers.research_question: How can standard Transformers learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models for 3D data, such as proteins?
papers.core_contribution: Standard Transformers can learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models when given linear embeddings of coordinates, without requiring architectural modifications.
papers.conclusion: Standard Transformers are capable of structural reasoning by learning SE(3)-invariant distance filters, providing a basis for using them as hybrid structure-language models for proteins and other 3D tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn to approximate a 3D Gaussian attention filter of relative distance when given linear embeddings of coordinates.
Transformers need at least n+2 embedding dimensions to learn distance in R^n.
Data augmentation with random rotations improves SE(3)-invariance and reduces overfitting.
Adding coordinates to a protein Transformer improves masked token prediction and sequence recovery, especially for amino acids with distinct backbone conformations.
Pretraining a protein Transformer with coordinates and then finetuning for function prediction outperforms custom structural models like DeepFRI.
future_direction: Applying the method to other domains like small molecules, 3D objects, vision Transformers, and large language models.
papers.abstract: While conventional Transformers generally operate on sequence data, they can be used in conjunction with structure models, typically SE(3)-invariant or equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs), for 3D applications such as protein structure modelling. These hybrids typically involve either (1) preprocessing/tokenizing structural features as input for Transformers or (2) taking Transformer embeddings and processing them within a structural representation. However, there is evidence that Transformers can learn to process structural information on their own, such as the AlphaFold3 structural diffusion model. In this work we show that Transformers can function independently as structure models when passed linear embeddings of coordinates. We first provide a theoretical explanation for how Transformers can learn to filter attention as a 3D Gaussian with learned variance. We then validate this theory using both simulated 3D points and in the context of masked token prediction for proteins. Finally, we show that pre-training protein Transformer encoders with structure improves performance on a downstream task, yielding better performance than custom structural models. Together, this work provides a basis for using standard Transformers as hybrid structure-language models.

papers.title: The algebra and the geometry aspect of Deep learning
papers.research_question: What are the mathematical foundations of deep learning from the perspectives of geometry, algebra, and differential calculus?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a coordinate-free formulation of backpropagation using the canonical scalar product on matrix spaces and explores the geometric and algebraic foundations of deep learning, including connections to algebraic geometry and category theory.
papers.key_findings:
The canonical scalar product on matrix spaces leads to a coordinate-free formulation of backpropagation.
Neural networks can be viewed as approximating separating algebraic varieties, with the degree of the variety related to generalization.
Graph neural networks can be understood through category theory, with cycles in computational graphs related to memory capacity.
The universal approximation theorem is proven using the Hahn-Banach theorem and Riesz representation.
Backpropagation equations are derived using matrix calculus and the chain rule.
future_direction: Development of a mathematical language model trained on propositions and theorems to solve mathematical problems.
Using algebraic geometry to find low-degree separating manifolds for more efficient classification.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the foundations of deep learning through insight of geometry, algebra and differential calculus. At is core, artificial intelligence relies on assumption that data and its intrinsic structure can be embedded into vector spaces allowing for analysis through geometric and algebraic methods. We thrace the development of neural networks from the perceptron to the transformer architecture, emphasizing on the underlying geometric structures and differential processes that govern their behavior. Our original approach highlights how the canonical scalar product on matrix spaces naturally leads to backpropagation equations yielding to a coordinate free formulation. We explore how classification problems can reinterpreted using tools from differential and algebraic geometry suggesting that manifold structure, degree of variety, homology may inform both convergence and interpretability of learning algorithms We further examine how neural networks can be interpreted via their associated directed graph, drawing connection to a Quillen model defined in [1] and [13] to describe memory as an homotopy theoretic property of the associated network.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Learning words in groups: fusion algebras, tensor ranks and grokking
papers.research_question: How can a simple two-layer neural network learn arbitrary word operations in finite groups, and why does it exhibit grokking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a two-layer neural network can learn group word operations by finding low-rank implementations of the word tensor, and this explains the grokking phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Word operations are learned through low-rank tensor representations that decompose along the basic self-conjugate representations of the group, shedding light on the grokking mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
The network learns word operations by finding low-rank implementations of the word tensor.
The rank of the word tensor is often much lower than the a priori upper bound of |G|^2.
The HD model finds solutions that align with basic self-conjugate representations (bscs) of the group.
For the multiplication word, the network effectively implements efficient matrix multiplication in the sense of Strassen.
Under gradient descent, the weights converge to mono-bsc-aligned configurations, partitioning the rows by bsc.
future_direction: Extending the findings to deeper networks and other architectures.
Studying the dynamics of the training process more closely.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that a simple two-layer neural network with standard activation functions can learn an arbitrary word operation in any finite group, provided sufficient width is available and exhibits grokking while doing so.
