To explain the mechanism by which this is achieved, we reframe the problem as that of learning a particular $3$-tensor, which we show is typically of low rank. A key insight is that low-rank implementations of this tensor can be obtained by decomposing it along triplets of basic self-conjugate representations of the group and leveraging the fusion structure to rule out many components. Focusing on a phenomenologically similar but more tractable surrogate model, we show that the network is able to find such low-rank implementations (or approximations thereof), thereby using limited width to approximate the word-tensor in a generalizable way. In the case of the simple multiplication word, we further elucidate the form of these low-rank implementations, showing that the network effectively implements efficient matrix multiplication in the sense of Strassen. Our work also sheds light on the mechanism by which a network reaches such a solution under gradient descent.

papers.title: LLaVA Steering: Visual Instruction Tuning with 500x Fewer Parameters through Modality Linear Representation-Steering
papers.research_question: How can the number of trainable parameters for visual instruction tuning in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) be significantly reduced by addressing the intrinsic imbalance between text and visual modalities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Modality Linear Representation-Steering (MoReS), a method that rebalances text and visual modalities in MLLMs by steering visual representations through linear transformations, achieving comparable performance to LoRA with 500x fewer trainable parameters.
papers.conclusion: MoReS provides an efficient and effective approach for visual instruction tuning in MLLMs by addressing modality imbalance, significantly reducing parameter count while maintaining performance, and offering a pathway for more accessible and customizable multimodal model development.
papers.key_findings:
MoReS requires 287 to 1,150 times fewer trainable parameters than LoRA while maintaining competitive performance on multiple visual benchmarks.
MoReS effectively rebalances the attention distribution between visual and textual representations, mitigating the intrinsic modality imbalance in MLLMs.
The method reduces hallucination in MLLMs, as shown by improved performance on POPE and HallucinationBench.
MoReS preserves the LLM's pre-trained world knowledge and performs well on text-only tasks, demonstrating its generalizability.
A dynamic steering ratio mechanism allows MoReS to adapt to tasks of varying complexity, with optimal ratios differing per dataset.
papers.abstract: Jinhe Bi, Yujun Wang, Haokun Chen, Xun Xiao, Artur Hecker, Volker Tresp, Yunpu Ma. Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: On Privileged and Convergent Bases in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons in neural networks, and do networks converge to a unique basis across different training runs?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks do not naturally converge to a unique basis, but freezing early layers can enforce basis convergence, and linear mode connectivity improvements with width are not due to increased basis correlation.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks do not have a privileged basis that is unique across runs, but a convergent basis can be achieved by freezing early layers, which is useful for interpretability and modular training.
papers.key_findings:
perm-corr remains nearly constant across width, indicating no convergence to a unique basis.
LMC barrier decreases with width, but this improvement is not due to increased basis correlation.
Networks cannot learn rotationally invariant representations; random rotations degrade performance.
Freezing early layers increases basis correlation and reduces identity stitching penalty.
Basis correlation is higher when early layers are frozen identically.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether the representations learned by neural networks possess a privileged and convergent basis. Specifically, we examine the significance of feature directions represented by individual neurons. First, we establish that arbitrary rotations of neural representations cannot be inverted (unlike linear networks), indicating that they do not exhibit complete rotational invariance. Subsequently, we explore the possibility of multiple bases achieving identical performance. To do this, we compare the bases of networks trained with the same parameters but with varying random initializations. Our study reveals two findings: (1) Even in wide networks such as WideResNets, neural networks do not converge to a unique basis; (2) Basis correlation increases significantly when a few early layers of the network are frozen identically. Furthermore, we analyze Linear Mode Connectivity, which has been studied as a measure of basis correlation. Our findings give evidence that while Linear Mode Connectivity improves with increased network width, this improvement is not due to an increase in basis correlation.

papers.title: In-Context Algebra
papers.research_question: What computational strategies do transformers develop when tokens serve as pure variables, acquiring meaning only through their interactions within each sequence, rather than relying on fixed information encoded in token embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on an in-context variable assignment task develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms (commutative copying, identity element recognition, closure-based cancellation) that differ from the geometric representations learned in fixed-token arithmetic settings, showing that learned reasoning strategies depend on task structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context about variables whose meanings are not fixed, showing that the kinds of learned strategies are dependent on the task structure.
papers.key_findings:
Models learn a commutative copying mechanism where a dedicated attention head copies answers from previously seen commutative facts.
Models develop an identity element recognition mechanism that distinguishes and solves facts containing the group's identity element.
Models implement a closure-based cancellation mechanism that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers by eliminating impossible variables.
The reasoning strategies learned by transformers are dependent on the task structure, with symbolic, context-based strategies emerging when tokens carry no consistent meaning across contexts.
Models achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and generalize to unseen groups.
papers.limitation: The study is conducted on synthetic algebra tasks with small transformer models, which may limit generalizability to larger models or more complex, real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Exploring more complex algebraic structures and reasoning tasks.
Scaling the analysis to larger transformer models.
Investigating whether similar symbolic mechanisms emerge in other in-context learning settings.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanisms that arise when transformers are trained to solve arithmetic on sequences where tokens are variables whose meaning is determined only through their interactions. While prior work has found that transformers develop geometric embeddings that mirror algebraic structure, those previous findings emerge from settings where arithmetic-valued tokens have fixed meanings. We devise a new task in which the assignment of symbols to specific algebraic group elements varies from one sequence to another. Despite this challenging setup, transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on the task and even generalize to unseen algebraic groups. We develop targeted data distributions to create causal tests of a set of hypothesized mechanisms, and we isolate three mechanisms models consistently learn: commutative copying where a dedicated head copies answers, identity element recognition that distinguishes identity-containing facts, and closure-based cancellation that tracks group membership to constrain valid answers. Complementary to the geometric representations found in fixed-symbol settings, our findings show that models develop symbolic reasoning mechanisms when trained to reason in-context with variables whose meanings are not fixed.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: GENNI: Visualising the Geometry of Equivalences for Neural Network Identifiability
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently identify and visualize the subspace of functionally equivalent parameters (symmetries) in neural networks to study identifiability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GENNI, an efficient optimization-based method to identify and visualize the subspace of functionally equivalent parameters (symmetries) in neural networks, aiding the study of identifiability.
papers.conclusion: GENNI is a scalable method for visualizing equivalence classes of neural network parameters, which can be used to study identifiability and inform initialization techniques.
papers.key_findings:
GENNI can efficiently find and visualize equivalence classes in neural network parameter spaces.
For a simple ReLU network, the visualized equivalence class shows shapes consistent with scaling and permutation symmetries.
For LeNet, the equivalence class exhibits a large connected region with low loss, indicating many symmetries.
The method scales to high-dimensional networks like LeNet (60,000 parameters).
Visualizations via UMAP can reveal topological properties like connectedness even in higher dimensions.
papers.limitation:
Visualization becomes computationally infeasible for high-dimensional hyperplanes (m > 7).
UMAP visualizations in higher dimensions are less interpretable.
The method currently visualizes only a single equivalence class, not the entire quotient set.
future_direction: Develop a guide to deduce symmetries from visualizations for specific architectures.
Explore the quotient space of equivalence classes.
Apply GENNI to understand meta-learning and transfer learning.
papers.abstract: We propose an efficient algorithm to visualise symmetries in neural networks. Typically, models are defined with respect to a parameter space, where non-equal parameters can produce the same input-output map. Our proposed method, GENNI, allows us to efficiently identify parameters that are functionally equivalent and then visualise the subspace of the resulting equivalence class. By doing so, we are now able to better explore questions surrounding identifiability, with applications to optimisation and generalizability, for commonly used or newly developed neural network architectures.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: Sequential Group Composition: A Window into the Mechanics of Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How do neural networks trained over sequences acquire the ability to perform structured operations, such as arithmetic, geometric, and algorithmic computation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the sequential group composition task as a tractable setting to study how neural networks learn structured operations from sequences, providing theoretical and empirical analysis of feature learning and architectural efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The sequential group composition task offers a principled lens for developing a mathematical theory of how neural networks learn from sequential data, with broader implications for understanding structured computation.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer networks learn the task one irreducible representation at a time in an order determined by the Fourier statistics of the encoding.
Two-layer networks require a hidden width exponential in the sequence length to perfectly learn the task.
Recurrent neural networks compose elements sequentially in linear steps, while multilayer networks compose adjacent pairs in parallel in logarithmic layers, dramatically improving scaling.
Networks exhibit a bias towards learning lower-dimensional irreducible representations first, especially for longer sequences.
The Alternating Gradient Flow framework explains the stepwise emergence of Fourier features during training.
papers.limitation: The work does not fully characterize how transformers learn the task, leaving open questions about algebraic shortcuts and training biases.
future_direction: Extending the framework from groups to semiautomata to study reversible and irreversible computations.
Extending from semiautomata to formal grammars to study hierarchical rules and recursion.
Characterizing algebraic shortcuts in transformers and understanding when gradient-based training biases toward them.
papers.abstract: How do neural networks trained over sequences acquire the ability to perform structured operations, such as arithmetic, geometric, and algorithmic computation? To gain insight into this question, we introduce the sequential group composition task. In this task, networks receive a sequence of elements from a finite group encoded in a real vector space and must predict their cumulative product. The task can be order-sensitive and requires a nonlinear architecture to be learned. Our analysis isolates the roles of the group structure, encoding statistics, and sequence length in shaping learning. We prove that two-layer networks learn this task one irreducible representation of the group at a time in an order determined by the Fourier statistics of the encoding. These networks can perfectly learn the task, but doing so requires a hidden width exponential in the sequence length $k$. In contrast, we show how deeper models exploit the associativity of the task to dramatically improve this scaling: recurrent neural networks compose elements sequentially in $k$ steps, while multilayer networks compose adjacent pairs in parallel in $\log k$ layers. Overall, the sequential group composition task offers a tractable window into the mechanics of deep learning.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: How does training shape the Riemannian geometry of neural network representations?
papers.research_question: How does training shape the Riemannian geometry induced by neural network feature maps?
papers.core_contribution: Training shapes the Riemannian geometry of neural network feature maps to magnify local areas along decision boundaries, a phenomenon observed in both supervised and self-supervised learning.
papers.conclusion: Training molds the Riemannian geometry of neural network representations to magnify areas along decision boundaries, providing a preliminary picture of how feature learning shapes geometry and opening avenues for understanding geometric inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
At infinite width, neural networks with random parameters induce highly symmetric metrics on input space.
Feature learning breaks this symmetry: networks trained for classification learn to expand the volume element (local area magnification) near decision boundaries.
This area expansion near decision boundaries holds for shallow networks on toy tasks, deep ResNets on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and in self-supervised learning with Barlow Twins.
The volume element is largest near decision boundaries and smallest within class regions.
The contrast in volume element between decision boundaries and class regions increases with network depth.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on toy tasks with two-dimensional input domains or low-dimensional slices through high-dimensional domains, limiting visualization of the full geometry.
Computational constraints, particularly for computing anisotropic measures like the Ricci scalar, and numerical challenges in curvature estimation.
The approach does not apply directly to networks with ReLU activation functions due to non-differentiability, requiring analysis of piecewise-constant magnification factors across activation regions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient and numerically stable algorithms for computing geometric quantities like curvature in state-of-the-art architectures.
Investigating when the flexible, nonlinear form of feature learning that reshapes embedding curvature is necessary for generalization, compared to linear methods.
Applying the geometric analysis to pre-trained networks, including those for which training classes are unknown, and to differentiable approximations of biological neural networks.
papers.abstract: In machine learning, there is a long history of trying to build neural networks that can learn from fewer example data by baking in strong geometric priors. However, it is not always clear a priori what geometric constraints are appropriate for a given task. Here, we explore the possibility that one can uncover useful geometric inductive biases by studying how training molds the Riemannian geometry induced by unconstrained neural network feature maps. We first show that at infinite width, neural networks with random parameters induce highly symmetric metrics on input space. This symmetry is broken by feature learning: networks trained to perform classification tasks learn to magnify local areas along decision boundaries. This holds in deep networks trained on high-dimensional image classification tasks, and even in self-supervised representation learning. These results begin to elucidate how training shapes the geometry induced by unconstrained neural network feature maps, laying the groundwork for an understanding of this richly nonlinear form of feature learning.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Grokking Finite-Dimensional Algebra
papers.research_question: How does the grokking phenomenon extend to learning multiplication in finite-dimensional algebras, and how do algebraic properties (commutativity, associativity, unitality) and structural properties of the structure tensor (sparsity, rank) influence grokking delay and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tensorial framework for studying grokking in finite-dimensional algebras, extending analysis beyond groups, and shows how algebraic and structural properties affect grokking and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The FDA framework provides a unified setting for grokking across algebraic structures and yields new insights into how mathematical structure governs neural network generalization dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning group operations is a special case of learning multiplication in finite-dimensional algebras.
For algebras over real numbers, learning connects to matrix factorization with an implicit low-rank bias; over finite fields, grokking emerges as models learn discrete representations of algebraic elements.
Algebraic properties (commutativity, associativity, unitality) significantly influence grokking delay and generalization patterns.
Structural properties of the structure tensor (sparsity, rank) influence generalization dynamics.
Generalization coincides with the emergence of algebra-consistent representations in model layers.
papers.limitation: Principled empirical study over real numbers is difficult because structured algebras form a measure-zero subset, leading to almost always degenerate algebras when sampling randomly; thus the work focuses on finite fields.
future_direction: Investigating how properties of the algebra affect the rank and local coherences of the structure tensor's unfoldings.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the grokking phenomenon, which refers to the sudden transition from a long memorization to generalization observed during neural networks training, in the context of learning multiplication in finite-dimensional algebras (FDA). While prior work on grokking has focused mainly on group operations, we extend the analysis to more general algebraic structures, including non-associative, non-commutative, and non-unital algebras. We show that learning group operations is a special case of learning FDA, and that learning multiplication in FDA amounts to learning a bilinear product specified by the algebra's structure tensor. For algebras over the reals, we connect the learning problem to matrix factorization with an implicit low-rank bias, and for algebras over finite fields, we show that grokking emerges naturally as models must learn discrete representations of algebraic elements. This leads us to experimentally investigate the following core questions: (i) how do algebraic properties such as commutativity, associativity, and unitality influence both the emergence and timing of grokking, (ii) how structural properties of the structure tensor of the FDA, such as sparsity and rank, influence generalization, and (iii) to what extent generalization correlates with the model learning latent embeddings aligned with the algebra's representation. Our work provides a unified framework for grokking across algebraic structures and new insights into how mathematical structure governs neural network generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we understand the unprecedented performance and robustness of deep neural networks using field theory and spontaneous symmetry breaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a field theory framework for deep neural networks, showing that spontaneous symmetry breaking of weight symmetries explains generalization, robustness, and phenomena like training on random labels and gradient variance explosion.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a field theory understanding of deep neural networks, explaining many experimentally observed phenomena and offering a new perspective for architecture design and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking, which generates long-range correlations in weights and feature maps.
Spontaneous symmetry breaking explains the gradient variance explosion observed during training.
The framework explains why neural networks are robust and can train on random labels.
In residual networks, the decoupling limit leads to spontaneous symmetry breaking more easily due to small residual units.
The theory predicts weight freeze-out and the shattered gradients problem in non-residual networks.
papers.abstract: We propose a framework to understand the unprecedented performance and robustness of deep neural networks using field theory. Correlations between the weights within the same layer can be described by symmetries in that layer, and networks generalize better if such symmetries are broken to reduce the redundancies of the weights. Using a two parameter field theory, we find that the network can break such symmetries itself towards the end of training in a process commonly known in physics as spontaneous symmetry breaking. This corresponds to a network generalizing itself without any user input layers to break the symmetry, but by communication with adjacent layers. In the layer decoupling limit applicable to residual networks (He et al., 2015), we show that the remnant symmetries that survive the non-linear layers are spontaneously broken. The Lagrangian for the non-linear and weight layers together has striking similarities with the one in quantum field theory of a scalar. Using results from quantum field theory we show that our framework is able to explain many experimentally observed phenomena,such as training on random labels with zero error (Zhang et al., 2017), the information bottleneck, the phase transition out of it and gradient variance explosion (Shwartz-Ziv & Tishby, 2017), shattered gradients (Balduzzi et al., 2017), and many more.

papers.title: Geodesics of learned representations
papers.research_question: How can we visualize and assess the invariance properties of learned representations, specifically testing whether they linearize the action of transformations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for synthesizing geodesic sequences to visualize and assess the invariance properties of learned representations, and uses it to show that the VGG network fails to linearize basic geometric transformations, but replacing max pooling with L2 pooling improves linearization.
papers.conclusion: Geodesic sequences provide a powerful diagnostic tool for evaluating the invariance properties of learned representations and can guide improvements in model design.
papers.key_findings:
The VGG network with max pooling fails to linearize basic geometric transformations (translation, rotation, dilation).
Replacing max pooling with L2 pooling in the VGG network enables it to linearize these transformations.
The geodesic method can reveal both excessive and insufficient invariance in a representation.
The method can be applied to natural image sequences and reveals temporal aliasing issues.
The ability to linearize transformations depends on the complexity of the representation, not just the receptive field size.
papers.limitation: The method may suffer from temporal aliasing in natural image sequences, especially when there is periodic structure.
future_direction: Extending the method to hierarchical representations using a coarse-to-fine approach to solve temporal aliasing.
Applying the method to test object identity invariance by generating geodesics between images of the same object category.
papers.abstract: We develop a new method for visualizing and refining the invariances of learned representations. Specifically, we test for a general form of invariance, linearization, in which the action of a transformation is confined to a low-dimensional subspace. Given two reference images (typically, differing by some transformation), we synthesize a sequence of images lying on a path between them that is of minimal length in the space of the representation (a "representational geodesic"). If the transformation relating the two reference images is linearized by the representation, this sequence should follow the gradual evolution of this transformation. We use this method to assess the invariance properties of a state-of-the-art image classification network and find that geodesics generated for image pairs differing by translation, rotation, and dilation do not evolve according to their associated transformations. Our method also suggests a remedy for these failures, and following this prescription, we show that the modified representation is able to linearize a variety of geometric image transformations.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Inductive Bias in Transformers: A View From Infinity
papers.research_question: What is the inductive bias of Transformers in terms of permutation symmetry, and how can it be characterized using representation theory and the Gaussian process limit?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers have an inductive bias towards permutation symmetric functions, and using representation theory of the symmetric group, one can derive quantitative predictions for learnability and scaling laws in the Gaussian process limit.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that transformers have an inductive bias towards permutation symmetric functions, which can be analyzed using representation theory, and provides evidence of such symmetry in natural language data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers tend to be biased towards more permutation symmetric functions in sequence space.
The representation theory of the symmetric group can be used to give quantitative analytical predictions when the dataset is symmetric to permutations.
For a simplified transformer block, the model can be solved at the GP limit, yielding accurate predictions for learning curves and network outputs.
Tight bounds in the form of a scaling law for learnability as a function of context length are derived.
The WikiText dataset exhibits a degree of permutation symmetry, suggesting the theory applies to natural language.
papers.abstract: We study inductive bias in Transformers in the infinitely over-parameterized Gaussian process limit and argue transformers tend to be biased towards more permutation symmetric functions in sequence space. We show that the representation theory of the symmetric group can be used to give quantitative analytical predictions when the dataset is symmetric to permutations between tokens. We present a simplified transformer block and solve the model at the limit, including accurate predictions for the learning curves and network outputs. We show that in common setups, one can derive tight bounds in the form of a scaling law for the learnability as a function of the context length. Finally, we argue WikiText dataset, does indeed possess a degree of permutation symmetry.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: A comparison of explainable artificial intelligence methods in the phase classification of multi-principal element alloys
papers.research_question: How do two model-agnostic local post-hoc interpretability methods (breakDown and SHAP) compare in explaining the predictions of a black-box classification model for multi-principal element alloy phase formation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both breakDown and SHAP interpretability methods can identify composition clusters with similar phase labels, with SHAP agreeing more closely with literature, and reveals that there can be multiple explanations for phase formation rules in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.conclusion: Both breakDown and SHAP are useful for interpretability in materials science, and there is more than one explanation for phase formation rules in multi-principal element alloys.
papers.key_findings:
Both breakDown and SHAP transformed data capture aggregation of chemical compositions with similar phase labels when visualized with t-SNE.
Variable attribution from breakDown and SHAP do not agree on all levels, but SHAP results are more consistent with published literature.
Despite differences in variable attribution, k-means clustering on breakDown and SHAP data yields similar composition clusters (e.g., 87% overlap for FCC clusters).
CP profile plots show similar functional dependencies between feature values and predicted responses for clusters from both methods.
The ensemble SVM model produces large error bars in variable attribution, indicating model-to-model variation due to limited data.
papers.limitation:
Materials science suffers from limited and sparse data, which affects model training and interpretability.
The eSVM method produces large error bars in variable attribution, suggesting large model-to-model variation between ensembles due to limited samples.
The independence assumption of input features may not hold completely, which affects the breakDown method.
future_direction: A more detailed analysis on the basis of disentangled representations to evaluate whether the breakDown and SHAP data sets have entangled representations.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate the capabilities of two model-agnostic local post-hoc model interpretability methods, namely breakDown (BD) and shapley (SHAP), to explain the predictions of a black-box classification learning model that establishes a quantitative relationship between chemical composition and multi-principal element alloys (MPEA) phase formation. We trained an ensemble of support vector machines using a dataset with 1,821 instances, 12 features with low pair-wise correlation, and seven phase labels. Feature contributions to the model prediction are computed by BD and SHAP for each composition. The resulting BD and SHAP transformed data are then used as inputs to identify similar composition groups using k-means clustering. Explanation-of-clusters by features reveal that the results from SHAP agree more closely with the literature. Visualization of compositions within a cluster using Ceteris-Paribus (CP) profile plots show the functional dependencies between the feature values and predicted response. Despite the differences between BD and SHAP in variable attribution, only minor changes were observed in the CP profile plots. Explanation-of-clusters by examples show that the clusters that share a common phase label contain similar compositions, which clarifies the similar-looking CP profile trends. Two plausible reasons are identified to describe this observation: (1) In the limits of a dataset with independent and non-interacting features, BD and SHAP show promise in recognizing MPEA composition clusters with similar phase labels. (2) There is more than one explanation for the MPEA phase formation rules with respect to the set of features considered in this work.

papers.title: Global Geometry Is Not Enough for Vision Representations
papers.research_question: Does global embedding geometry, commonly used to evaluate representation quality, predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders?
papers.core_contribution: Global embedding geometry does not predict compositional binding capability in vision encoders; functional sensitivity, measured by the Jacobian effective rank, is a strong predictor and reveals a gap arising from objective design.
papers.conclusion: Global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence; functional sensitivity is a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.
papers.key_findings:
Standard geometric metrics (e.g., isotropy, participation ratio) show near-zero correlation with compositional binding accuracy across 21 vision encoders.
Jacobian Effective Rank (JER), a measure of local input-output sensitivity, strongly correlates with binding performance.
The disparity between geometry and function arises because existing training objectives explicitly constrain global embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping largely unconstrained.
Variance-decorrelation objectives (e.g., Barlow Twins, VICReg) preserve high functional rank and achieve better binding, while other objectives (e.g., CLIP, MAE) exhibit functional rank collapse.
Alternative geometric readouts (kNN, local PCA) cannot recover binding information from frozen embeddings; linear accessibility is intrinsic to the pretraining objective.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted in a controlled synthetic setting to isolate compositional binding, and is not intended to exhaustively characterize all forms of structure in large-scale or naturalistic representations.
future_direction: Developing training objectives and evaluation benchmarks that target functional structure more directly than geometry-based criteria or linear probing.
papers.abstract: A common assumption in representation learning is that globally well-distributed embeddings support robust and generalizable representations. This focus has shaped both training objectives and evaluation protocols, implicitly treating global geometry as a proxy for representational competence. While global geometry effectively encodes which elements are present, it is often insensitive to how they are composed. We investigate this limitation by testing the ability of geometric metrics to predict compositional binding across 21 vision encoders. We find that standard geometry-based statistics exhibit near-zero correlation with compositional binding. In contrast, functional sensitivity, as measured by the input-output Jacobian, reliably tracks this capability. We further provide an analytic account showing that this disparity arises from objective design, as existing losses explicitly constrain embedding geometry but leave the local input-output mapping unconstrained. These results suggest that global embedding geometry captures only a partial view of representational competence and establish functional sensitivity as a critical complementary axis for modeling composite structure.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Emergence of brain-like mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: Why does mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning emerge in convolutional neural networks and the primate brain?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a learning-driven explanation for the emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in CNNs, showing that it arises from learning to discriminate bilaterally symmetric object categories and spatial pooling, and provides a theory for how this tuning might emerge in the primate brain.
papers.conclusion: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning emerges from learning to discriminate bilaterally symmetric objects and spatial pooling, providing a parsimonious theory for its emergence in both CNNs and the primate brain.
papers.key_findings:
Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning emerges in the fully connected layers of CNNs trained on object recognition tasks, even when the training dataset does not include faces.
This tuning emerges for multiple object categories with bilateral symmetry, not just faces.
The emergence is due to learning reflection-equivariant representations in convolutional layers and spatial pooling in fully connected layers, which yields reflection-invariant representations.
Mirror-symmetric tuning is driven by the presence of local features rather than global configurations.
The reflection-invariant representations in CNNs align with the representations in the macaque AL face patch.
future_direction: Probing non-face-specific visual regions in primate brains with bilaterally symmetric objects to test for mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
papers.abstract: Primates can recognize objects despite 3D geometric variations such as in-depth rotations. The computational mechanisms that give rise to such invariances are yet to be fully understood. A curious case of partial invariance occurs in the macaque face-patch AL and in fully connected layers of deep convolutional networks in which neurons respond similarly to mirror-symmetric views (e.g. left and right profiles). Why does this tuning develop? Here, we propose a simple learning-driven explanation for mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning. We show that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces emerges in the fully connected layers of convolutional deep neural networks trained on object recognition tasks, even when the training dataset does not include faces. First, using 3D objects rendered from multiple views as test stimuli, we demonstrate that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in convolutional neural network models is not unique to faces: it emerges for multiple object categories with bilateral symmetry. Second, we show why this invariance emerges in the models. Learning to discriminate among bilaterally symmetric object categories induces reflection-equivariant intermediate representations. AL-like mirror-symmetric tuning is achieved when such equivariant responses are spatially pooled by downstream units with sufficiently large receptive fields. These results explain how mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can emerge in neural networks, providing a theory of how they might emerge in the primate brain. Our theory predicts that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can emerge as a consequence of exposure to bilaterally symmetric objects beyond the category of faces, and that it can generalize beyond previously experienced object categories.

papers.title: Weight Decay Improves Language Model Plasticity
papers.research_question: How does weight decay during language model pretraining affect model plasticity, i.e., the pretrained model’s ability to learn new knowledge during subsequent training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that weight decay during pretraining improves model plasticity, leading to better downstream performance after fine-tuning, and that optimizing pretraining hyperparameters solely for validation loss may not yield the best downstream model.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Weight decay improves language model plasticity and downstream performance.
The optimal pretraining weight decay for downstream performance is larger than the default of 0.1.
Pretraining validation loss is not perfectly predictive of downstream performance after fine-tuning.
Weight decay encourages linearly separable representations in the model.
Weight decay reduces the rank of attention matrices and reduces overfitting on training data.
papers.limitation:
The benefits of increased plasticity must be weighed against other effects that may depend on model size, training duration, and other parameters of the training setup.
In heavily overtrained scenarios or for very large models, the benefits of lower pretraining validation loss may outweigh those of plasticity.
future_direction: Investigate trade-offs between stability and plasticity and the extent to which results hold in large-model and heavily overtrained scenarios.
Investigate the role of weight decay in model plasticity for foundation models beyond language (e.g., multimodal foundation models).
Investigate the role of weight decay for other downstream desiderata (e.g., safety alignment).
papers.abstract: The prevailing paradigm in large language model (LLM) development is to pretrain a base model, then perform further training to improve performance and model behavior. However, hyperparameter optimization and scaling laws have been studied primarily from the perspective of the base model's validation loss, ignoring downstream adaptability. In this work, we study pretraining from the perspective of model plasticity, that is, the ability of the base model to successfully adapt to downstream tasks through fine-tuning. We focus on the role of weight decay, a key regularization parameter during pretraining. Through systematic experiments, we show that models trained with larger weight decay values are more plastic, meaning they show larger performance gains when fine-tuned on downstream tasks. This phenomenon can lead to counterintuitive trade-offs where base models that perform worse after pretraining can perform better after fine-tuning. Further investigation of weight decay's mechanistic effects on model behavior reveals that it encourages linearly separable representations, regularizes attention matrices, and reduces overfitting on the training data. In conclusion, this work demonstrates the importance of using evaluation metrics beyond cross-entropy loss for hyperparameter optimization and casts light on the multifaceted role of that a single optimization hyperparameter plays in shaping model behavior.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: Efficient, probabilistic analysis of combinatorial neural codes
papers.research_question: How can combinatorial neural codes be efficiently and probabilistically analyzed to infer algebraic, geometric, and topological characteristics, and how do these characteristics relate to learning and experience in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper improves the computational complexity of analyzing combinatorial neural codes from factorial to quadratic time and introduces a probabilistic hypothesis testing framework, enabling efficient analysis of large neural codes from both artificial and biological neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Efficient and probabilistic analysis of combinatorial neural codes is feasible and provides insights into how internal representations change with learning and network depth.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method reduces the time complexity of computing the canonical form's generators from factorial to quadratic, enabling analysis of large neural codes.
Applied to simulated place cell data, the method correctly infers the number of holes in 2D navigation environments.
Applied to an MLP trained on MNIST, the method shows that internal representations become lower-dimensional and more spread out during training.
papers.limitation:
Assumes joint activity of neurons corresponds to common inputs or selectivity thereof.
Binarizes neural signals into 'on' and 'off' states.
future_direction: Performing causal inference tests on neural co-activations.
Considering polynomials over larger finite fields or extending methods to more continuous structures.
papers.abstract: Artificial and biological neural networks (ANNs and BNNs) can encode inputs in the form of combinations of individual neurons' activities. These combinatorial neural codes present a computational challenge for direct and efficient analysis due to their high dimensionality and often large volumes of data. Here we improve the computational complexity -- from factorial to quadratic time -- of direct algebraic methods previously applied to small examples and apply them to large neural codes generated by experiments. These methods provide a novel and efficient way of probing algebraic, geometric, and topological characteristics of combinatorial neural codes and provide insights into how such characteristics are related to learning and experience in neural networks. We introduce a procedure to perform hypothesis testing on the intrinsic features of neural codes using information geometry. We then apply these methods to neural activities from an ANN for image classification and a BNN for 2D navigation to, without observing any inputs or outputs, estimate the structure and dimensionality of the stimulus or task space. Additionally, we demonstrate how an ANN varies its internal representations across network depth and during learning.

papers.title: Phase transition encoded in neural network
papers.research_question: How do temperature-supervised neural networks capture information of phase transition and what physical quantities do they learn?
papers.core_contribution: Temperature-supervised neural networks encode phase transition information in their weights, learning either magnetization or internal energy as features depending on network architecture and prediction accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained to predict temperature encode phase transition information in their weights, and the extracted physical quantity (magnetization or energy) depends on the network architecture and training accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
The fully-connected neural network learns magnetization from input spin configurations, and its weights show a drastic change at the critical temperature, enabling phase transition detection.
The convolutional neural network learns internal energy, achieves higher temperature prediction accuracy, and its weights are proportional to free energy, encoding phase transition information more implicitly.
The phase transition information is captured in the neural network weights even without explicit supervision of phase labels.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is theoretically bounded by the overlap of energy probability distributions at different temperatures.
Convolutional networks perform better because they capture spatial correlations, leading to learning internal energy rather than magnetization.
papers.limitation:
The method may not correctly detect phase transitions driven by different physical mechanisms such as Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transitions or topological phase transitions.
The fully-connected network only distinguishes between ordered and disordered phases and cannot predict fine-grained temperatures within each phase.
The accuracy of temperature prediction is limited by the overlap of energy distributions at different temperatures in finite systems.
papers.abstract: Abstract We discuss an aspect of neural networks for the purpose of phase transition detection. To this end, we first train the neural network by feeding Ising/Potts configurations with labels of temperature so that it can predict the temperature of the input. We do not explicitly supervise whether the configurations are in the ordered/disordered phase. Nevertheless, we can identify the critical temperature from the parameters (weights and biases) of the trained neural network. We attempt to understand how temperature-supervised neural networks capture information on the phase transition by paying attention to what quantities they learn. Our detailed analyses reveal that they learn different physical quantities depending on how well they are trained. The main observation in this study is how the weights in the trained neural network can have information on the phase transition in addition to temperature.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark.
