Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems. This work has implications for both foundational understanding and practical deployment; with the potential to accelerate computational chemistry research.

papers.title: Interpreting Equivariant Representations
papers.research_question: How can we properly interpret equivariant latent representations, and how can we obtain invariant representations from equivariant models to avoid misleading conclusions and improve downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the importance of considering the inductive bias of equivariant models when interpreting latent representations and provides principles for choosing invariant projections to obtain unambiguous and informative invariant representations, which improve downstream analysis.
papers.conclusion: Invariant projections are essential for the proper interpretation and utilization of equivariant latent representations, and the proposed tools—isometric cross sections and random invariant projections—effectively address the inherent ambiguity, leading to more reliable downstream analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Equivariant latent representations are ambiguous because each input maps to a set of latent vectors (an orbit) under the group action, leading to ill-defined distances and potentially misleading visualizations and analyses.
Invariant projections, such as sorting for permutation-equivariant representations or random invariant linear projections for rotation-equivariant representations, can extract invariant features that preserve information and improve downstream task performance.
For permutation-equivariant VAEs, an isometric invariant representation obtained by sorting the latent coordinates forms a convex cone, enabling meaningful linear interpolation between molecules.
For rotation-equivariant classifiers, random invariant projections retain a high degree of information and yield latent spaces with clear structure, improving visualization and kNN classification accuracy.
The ambiguity observed in strictly equivariant models also appears in standard deep learning models where invariance is encouraged via data augmentation, highlighting the broader relevance of the issue.
papers.limitation: Choosing a suitable invariant mapping may not always be clear and can depend greatly on the model architecture.
future_direction: Suggesting suitable high-quality invariant mappings relevant for widely applied equivariant architectures.
papers.abstract: Latent representations are used extensively for downstream tasks, such as visualization, interpolation or feature extraction of deep learning models. Invariant and equivariant neural networks are powerful and well-established models for enforcing inductive biases. In this paper, we demonstrate that the inductive bias imposed on the by an equivariant model must also be taken into account when using latent representations. We show how not accounting for the inductive biases leads to decreased performance on downstream tasks, and vice versa, how accounting for inductive biases can be done effectively by using an invariant projection of the latent representations. We propose principles for how to choose such a projection, and show the impact of using these principles in two common examples: First, we study a permutation equivariant variational auto-encoder trained for molecule graph generation; here we show that invariant projections can be designed that incur no loss of information in the resulting invariant representation. Next, we study a rotation-equivariant representation used for image classification. Here, we illustrate how random invariant projections can be used to obtain an invariant representation with a high degree of retained information. In both cases, the analysis of invariant latent representations proves superior to their equivariant counterparts. Finally, we illustrate that the phenomena documented here for equivariant neural networks have counterparts in standard neural networks where invariance is encouraged via augmentation. Thus, while these ambiguities may be known by experienced developers of equivariant models, we make both the knowledge as well as effective tools to handle the ambiguities available to the broader community.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: Neural network interpretation using descrambler groups
papers.research_question: How can inner layer signalling of fully connected neural networks be brought into a human-readable form to improve interpretability, particularly in digital signal processing and scientific computing?
papers.core_contribution: A group-theoretical method (descrambler groups) for interpreting fully connected neural networks by finding orthogonal transformations that make intermediate signals human-readable, successfully revealing sophisticated signal processing operations in a DSP network.
papers.conclusion: The descrambler group method enables interpretation of fully connected neural networks, revealing that even small networks can invent complex mathematical operations, and that reductionist understanding is possible.
papers.key_findings:
The descrambler group method can successfully interpret the inner workings of fully connected neural networks.
DEERNet spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rectifier, frequency division multiplexing, spectral filtering regularization, and a Fourier-like transform mapping harmonics to Chebyshev polynomials.
The method reveals that even small networks can develop complex, interpretable mathematical operations during training.
The descrambling process requires defining a problem-specific interpretability metric, such as signal smoothness or diagonal dominance.
The method is applicable to fully connected layers, which are harder to interpret than convolutional layers.
papers.limitation: The method requires domain-specific expertise to recognize the functionality of descrambled weight matrices, and the descrambled matrix may still be uninterpretable to non-specialists.
future_direction: Neural networks can be mined for new knowledge, possibly discovering previously unknown mathematics.
A staged approach is recommended: first establish the role of each layer empirically, then descramble for implementation details.
papers.abstract: The lack of interpretability and trust is a much-criticized feature of deep neural networks. In fully connected nets, the signaling between inner layers is scrambled because backpropagation training does not require perceptrons to be arranged in any particular order. The result is a black box; this problem is particularly severe in scientific computing and digital signal processing (DSP), where neural nets perform abstract mathematical transformations that do not reduce to features or concepts. We present here a group-theoretical procedure that attempts to bring inner-layer signaling into a human-readable form, the assumption being that this form exists and has identifiable and quantifiable features-for example, smoothness or locality. We applied the proposed method to DEERNet (a DSP network used in electron spin resonance) and managed to descramble it. We found considerable internal sophistication: the network spontaneously invents a bandpass filter, a notch filter, a frequency axis rescaling transformation, frequency-division multiplexing, group embedding, spectral filtering regularization, and a map from harmonic functions into Chebyshev polynomials-in 10 min of unattended training from a random initial guess.

papers.title: Vision-language models learn the geometry of human perceptual space
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether vision-language models learn representations that align with human perceptual space, and whether the axes of their psychological spaces correspond to human perceptual dimensions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that vision-language models learn a representational geometry that aligns with human perceptual axes, and that this AI-derived geometry can better predict human categorization behavior than human-derived similarity spaces, acting as a denoised surrogate for human perception.
papers.conclusion: VLMs capture an idealized or denoised form of human perceptual structure, providing a scalable method for cognitive science and evidence for shared constraints on perceptual organization across different learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs produce similarity judgments that correlate well with human similarity judgments at the category level.
The psychological spaces derived from VLMs via MDS show strong alignment with human perceptual dimensions (e.g., lightness, grain size, shininess) as measured by Procrustes analysis.
VLM-derived spaces, when used as input to the Generalized Context Model (GCM), predict human classification behavior better than spaces derived from human similarity judgments.
Larger VLMs tend to yield higher correlations with human similarity judgments.
The alignment improves when using an overcomplete (10D) MDS solution for GPT-4o, suggesting that human-relevant information is distributed across additional dimensions.
papers.limitation:
Alignment of geometry is not a mechanistic explanation; LLMs/VLMs are not faithful simulators of human cognition, can be prompt- or wording-sensitive, and reflect training-distribution biases.
High geometric correspondence does not guarantee equivalence of features or computations, and shortcut solutions remain a pervasive risk.
The study is focused on a single naturalistic domain, limiting generalizability to other domains and tasks.
future_direction: Establish generalizability of findings to other domains and tasks.
Apply Explainable AI (XAI) techniques to visualize which image regions contribute to the VLM's similarity judgments to test if VLM and humans use the same evidence.
Integrate axis-level alignment with neural measurements (e.g., RSA/CKA) and active pairwise sampling to understand when and why convergence arises.
papers.abstract: In cognitive science and AI, a longstanding question is whether machines learn representations that align with those of the human mind. While current models show promise, it remains an open question whether this alignment is superficial or reflects a deeper correspondence in the underlying dimensions of representation. Here we introduce a methodology to probe the internal geometry of vision-language models (VLMs) by having them generate pairwise similarity judgments for a complex set of natural objects. Using multidimensional scaling, we recover low-dimensional psychological spaces and find that their axes show a strong correspondence with the principal axes of human perceptual space. Critically, when this AI-derived representational geometry is used as the input to a classic exemplar model of categorization, it predicts human classification behavior more accurately than a space constructed from human judgments themselves. This suggests that VLMs can capture an idealized or `denoised' form of human perceptual structure. Our work provides a scalable method to overcome a measurement bottleneck in cognitive science and demonstrates that foundation models can learn a representational geometry that is functionally relevant for modeling key aspects of human cognition, such as categorization.

papers.title: Towards quantifying information flows: relative entropy in deep neural networks and the renormalization group
papers.research_question: How does relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler divergence) behave in renormalization group flows and in deep neural networks as a function of depth, and what are the similarities between the two?
papers.core_contribution: The relative entropy (KL divergence) increases monotonically to a parameter-dependent asymptotic value in both the renormalization group flow of Ising models and in feedforward neural networks as a function of depth, and it is insensitive to the phase structure of either system.
papers.conclusion: Relative entropy provides a useful measure of information flow in both renormalization group and deep neural networks, but it is not sensitive to critical behavior, indicating that more refined probes are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Relative entropy increases monotonically under decimation RG in the 1d and 2d Ising models.
In feedforward neural networks, relative entropy also increases monotonically with depth to an asymptotic value.
The asymptotic value depends on the coupling constant in Ising models and on weight and bias parameters in neural networks.
Relative entropy does not exhibit any change at the critical point of the 2d Ising model or at the phase transition in neural networks.
The monotonic increase in relative entropy confirms the connection with the c-theorem in QFT and may have implications for information maximization methods in machine learning.
papers.limitation: The relative entropy is insensitive to the phase structure of the systems studied, so it cannot capture critical points.
future_direction: Develop more refined probes to fully elucidate the flow of information in these models.
Investigate the implications of the asymptotic behavior for information maximization methods in machine learning and for disentangling compactness and generalizability.
papers.abstract: We investigate the analogy between the renormalization group (RG) and deep neural networks, wherein subsequent layers of neurons are analogous to successive steps along the RG. In particular, we quantify the flow of information by explicitly computing the relative entropy or Kullback-Leibler divergence in both the one- and two-dimensional Ising models under decimation RG, as well as in a feedforward neural network as a function of depth. We observe qualitatively identical behavior characterized by the monotonic increase to a parameter-dependent asymptotic value. On the quantum field theory side, the monotonic increase confirms the connection between the relative entropy and the c-theorem. For the neural networks, the asymptotic behavior may have implications for various information maximization methods in machine learning, as well as for disentangling compactness and generalizability. Furthermore, while both the two-dimensional Ising model and the random neural networks we consider exhibit non-trivial critical points, the relative entropy appears insensitive to the phase structure of either system. In this sense, more refined probes are required in order to fully elucidate the flow of information in these models.

papers.title: Layer of Truth: Probing Belief Shifts under Continual Pre-Training Poisoning
papers.research_question: How does repeated exposure to plausible falsehoods during continual pre-training alter the internal factual representations (beliefs) in large language models? Specifically, does poisoning cause systematic belief replacement, where in the network is corruption localized and recoverable, and how do these shifts generalize across prompts, tasks, and languages?
papers.core_contribution: Continual pre-training on plausible misinformation can systematically overwrite specific factual knowledge in LLMs without degrading overall performance, with belief shifts concentrated in late transformer layers and generalizing across prompts and tasks.
papers.conclusion: Continual pre-training poisoning can overwrite internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating the need for representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.
papers.key_findings:
Poisoning shifts probability mass from correct to counterfactual answers without increasing ambiguity, indicating systematic belief replacement rather than diffuse uncertainty.
Belief flips occur abruptly across checkpoints and are concentrated in late transformer layers (e.g., Layers 29–36 in 3B models).
Activation patching in late layers can partially reverse the corruption, rescuing up to 56.8% of poisoned beliefs.
Poisoned beliefs generalize beyond training prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning (HellaSwag) while leaving alignment benchmarks (TruthfulQA, HH-RLHF) largely stable.
Cross-lingual transfer of poisoned beliefs is imperfect, with weaker expression and higher ambiguity in languages not used during poisoning (e.g., Russian vs. English).
papers.abstract: We show that continual pretraining on plausible misinformation can overwrite specific factual knowledge in large language models without degrading overall performance. Unlike prior poisoning work under static pretraining, we study repeated exposure to counterfactual claims during continual updates. Using paired fact-counterfact items with graded poisoning ratios, we track how internal preferences between competing facts evolve across checkpoints, layers, and model scales. Even moderate poisoning (50-100%) flips over 55% of responses from correct to counterfactual while leaving ambiguity nearly unchanged. These belief flips emerge abruptly, concentrate in late layers (e.g., Layers 29-36 in 3B models), and are partially reversible via patching (up to 56.8%). The corrupted beliefs generalize beyond poisoned prompts, selectively degrading commonsense reasoning while leaving alignment benchmarks largely intact and transferring imperfectly across languages. These results expose a failure mode of continual pre-training in which targeted misinformation replaces internal factual representations without triggering broad performance collapse, motivating representation-level monitoring of factual integrity during model updates.

papers.title: SEIS: Subspace-based Equivariance and Invariance Scores for Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify and disentangle equivariance and invariance in neural representations under geometric transformations without requiring labels or explicit transformation knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SEIS, a subspace-based metric that disentangles equivariance from invariance in neural representations under geometric transformations, enabling label-free analysis without explicit transformation priors.
papers.conclusion: SEIS provides a necessary lens for ensuring that models intended for geometric tasks respect the symmetries they are assumed to learn and beyond.
papers.key_findings:
SEIS correctly recovers known transformations in synthetic validation.
In trained classification networks, SEIS reveals a transition from equivariance in early layers to invariance in deeper layers.
Data augmentation increases invariance while preserving equivariance.
Multi-task learning induces synergistic gains in both equivariance and invariance at the shared encoder.
Skip connections restore equivariance lost during decoding.
papers.abstract: Understanding how neural representations respond to geometric transformations is essential for evaluating whether learned features preserve meaningful spatial structure. Existing approaches primarily assess robustness by comparing model outputs under transformed inputs, offering limited insight into how geometric information is organized within internal representations and failing to distinguish between information loss and re-encoding. In this work, we introduce SEIS (Subspace-based Equivariance and Invariance Scores), a subspace metric for analyzing layer-wise feature representations under geometric transformations, disentangling equivariance from invariance without requiring labels or explicit knowledge of the transformation. Synthetic validation confirms that SEIS correctly recovers known transformations. Applied to trained classification networks, SEIS reveals a transition from equivariance in early layers to invariance in deeper layers, and that data augmentation increases invariance while preserving equivariance. We further show that multi-task learning induces synergistic gains in both properties at the shared encoder, and skip connections restore equivariance lost during decoding.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: Hierarchical Associative Memory, Parallelized MLP-Mixer, and Symmetry Breaking
papers.research_question: How can hierarchical associative memory be integrated with MetaFormers to represent Transformer blocks as Hopfield networks, and what is the impact of symmetry in weight matrices on performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper integrates hierarchical associative memory with MetaFormers to derive a parallelized MLP-Mixer from a three-layer Hopfield network, and shows that symmetry-breaking in weight matrices is crucial for performance in image recognition tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a correspondence between Hopfield networks and MLP-Mixer models, demonstrating that symmetry breaking in weight matrices is essential for effective performance in image recognition.
papers.key_findings:
Symmetric weight matrices in Mixer models hinder performance on image recognition tasks.
Introducing symmetry-breaking effects improves performance to match vanilla MLP-Mixer.
Parallelized MLP-Mixer (ParaMixer) performs competitively with vanilla MLP-Mixer.
Iterative application of mixing layers shows that SymMixer maintains performance over iterations, while ParaMixer degrades.
The degeneracy of attractors in Hopfield networks is resolved by symmetry breaking.
papers.limitation:
narrow focus on the Lagrangians in the formulation
lack of examination of applications to practical problems
future_direction: Reconsideration of Lagrangians for hidden neurons
Exploration of task domains suitable for SymMixer such as denoising or image retrieval
Quantitative analysis of memorization capacity
papers.abstract: Transformers have established themselves as the leading neural network model in natural language processing and are increasingly foundational in various domains. In vision, the MLP-Mixer model has demonstrated competitive performance, suggesting that attention mechanisms might not be indispensable. Inspired by this, recent research has explored replacing attention modules with other mechanisms, including those described by MetaFormers. However, the theoretical framework for these models remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a novel perspective by integrating Krotov's hierarchical associative memory with MetaFormers, enabling a comprehensive representation of the entire Transformer block, encompassing token-/channel-mixing modules, layer normalization, and skip connections, as a single Hopfield network. This approach yields a parallelized MLP-Mixer derived from a three-layer Hopfield network, which naturally incorporates symmetric token-/channel-mixing modules and layer normalization. Empirical studies reveal that symmetric interaction matrices in the model hinder performance in image recognition tasks. Introducing symmetry-breaking effects transitions the performance of the symmetric parallelized MLP-Mixer to that of the vanilla MLP-Mixer. This indicates that during standard training, weight matrices of the vanilla MLP-Mixer spontaneously acquire a symmetry-breaking configuration, enhancing their effectiveness. These findings offer insights into the intrinsic properties of Transformers and MLP-Mixers and their theoretical underpinnings, providing a robust framework for future model design and optimization.

papers.title: The Representational Alignment Hypothesis: Evidence for and Consequences of Invariant Semantic Structure Across Embedding Modalities
papers.research_question: Is there an underlying invariant semantic structure common to independently trained representation spaces (e.g., neural, textual, visual, auditory)? If so, is it an inherent property of meaning, or does it reflect shared biological, environmental, and cultural conditions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper surveys evidence for the Representational Alignment Hypothesis (RAH), which posits an invariant semantic structure across embedding modalities, and argues against the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, offering alternative explanations rooted in metasemantics.
papers.conclusion: The paper reviews evidence for the Representational Alignment Hypothesis and argues against the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, suggesting the invariant structure may reflect human-specific conditions rather than fundamental reality.
papers.key_findings:
Two complementary research strands (transformation-based approaches and internal structure comparison methods) provide converging evidence that independently trained embeddings from text, vision, audio, and neural signals can exhibit a shared semantic organization.
Simple linear transformations can align embeddings with minimal supervision, suggesting the underlying geometries are 'near-isomorphic.'
Purely geometric or relational analyses (e.g., RSA, topological data analysis) reveal strong cross-modal parallels in how items cluster or correlate.
The observed alignment might stem from shared data-generating conditions (human biology, culture, environment) rather than a fundamental, Platonic reality.
papers.limitation:
The invariant structure might arise from the embedding algorithms themselves, not from an inherent property of meaning.
The alignment might reflect how the human brain processes information, imposing its own constraints and biases on any data.
The semantic structure identified might be specific to Earth's unique biological and environmental context, not universally invariant.
future_direction: Constructing simulated environments where underlying 'semantic' factors are controlled to test the emergence of invariant representations.
Cross-cultural and cross-species comparisons to test the depth and universality of the alignments.
Developing new interpretability methods to reveal which semantic attributes drive alignment across modalities.
papers.abstract: There is growing evidence that independently trained AI systems come to represent the world in the same way. In other words, independently trained embeddings from text, vision, audio, and neural signals share an underlying geometry. We call this the Representational Alignment Hypothesis (RAH) and investigate evidence for and consequences of this claim. The evidence is of two kinds: (i) internal structure comparison techniques, such as representational similarity analysis and topological data analysis, reveal matching relational patterns across modalities without explicit mapping; and (ii) methods based on cross-modal embedding alignment, which learn mappings between representation spaces, show that simple linear transformations can bring different embedding spaces into close correspondence, suggesting near-isomorphism. Taken together, the evidence suggests that, even after controlling for trivial commonalities inherent in standard data preprocessing and embedding procedures, a robust structural correspondence persists, hinting at an underlying organizational principle. Some have argued that this result shows that the shared structure is getting at a fundamental, Platonic level of reality. We argue that this conclusion is unjustified. Moreover, we aim to give the idea an alternative philosophical home, rooted in contemporary metasemantics (i.e., theories of what makes a representation and what makes something meaningful) and responses to the symbol grounding problem. We conclude by considering the scope of the RAH and proposing new ways of distinguishing semantic structures that are genuinely invariant from those that inevitably arise due to the fact that all our data is generated under human-specific conditions on Earth.

papers.title: Algorithmic Determination of the Combinatorial Structure of the Linear Regions of ReLU Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we algorithmically determine the full combinatorial structure of the canonical polyhedral complex of a ReLU neural network, and what topological properties do the decision boundaries of such networks have at initialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an algorithm to compute the sign sequence complex, which fully encodes the combinatorial structure of the canonical polyhedral complex of a ReLU network, and uses it to study the topological properties of decision boundaries at initialization.
papers.conclusion: The sign sequence complex provides a new combinatorial characterization of ReLU networks and is useful for obtaining topological information about networks, though the algorithm is limited to low-dimensional inputs.
papers.key_findings:
The sign sequences of the vertices of the canonical polyhedral complex determine the full facet structure across all dimensions.
The algorithm is numerically stable and polynomial time in the number of intermediate neurons.
The dual complex to the canonical polyhedral complex is cubical and possesses a multiplication compatible with its facet structure.
At initialization, width alone does not increase observed topology, but width in the presence of depth does.
Bounded connected components of the decision boundary at initialization are rare, and deeper networks show greater variability in topology.
papers.limitation: The algorithm is exponential in the input dimension, so only low-dimensional slices of the true decision boundary can be investigated empirically.
future_direction: Studying the evolution of a network's decision boundary through a training path.
Obtaining distributional properties of local curvature using the local characterization of vertices.
Using the true topology of the decision boundary as a metric for comparison with approximation methods.
papers.abstract: We algorithmically determine the regions and facets of all dimensions of the canonical polyhedral complex, the universal object into which a ReLU network decomposes its input space. We show that the locations of the vertices of the canonical polyhedral complex along with their signs with respect to layer maps determine the full facet structure across all dimensions. We present an algorithm which calculates this full combinatorial structure, making use of our theorems that the dual complex to the canonical polyhedral complex is cubical and it possesses a multiplication compatible with its facet structure. The resulting algorithm is numerically stable, polynomial time in the number of intermediate neurons, and obtains accurate information across all dimensions. This permits us to obtain, for example, the true topology of the decision boundaries of networks with low-dimensional inputs. We run empirics on such networks at initialization, finding that width alone does not increase observed topology, but width in the presence of depth does. Source code for our algorithms is accessible online at https://github.com/mmasden/canonicalpoly.

papers.title: From Neurons to Neutrons: A Case Study in Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can mechanistic interpretability extract scientific knowledge from neural networks trained on physics data, and can such insights align with human-derived domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability can extract scientifically meaningful representations from neural networks trained on nuclear physics data, aligning with human-derived concepts like the semi-empirical mass formula and shell model.
papers.conclusion: These findings provide a proof-of-concept that neural networks, when trained on scientific data, can learn useful representations that align with human knowledge, opening exciting possibilities for future research on richer data and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings of proton and neutron numbers exhibit a helix structure that encodes nuclear physics concepts like the volume and asymmetry terms.
The orderedness of embeddings along the first principal component correlates with generalization performance.
Penultimate layer features correspond to terms in the semi-empirical mass formula and nuclear shell model.
Latent space topography reveals the algorithm used by the model for binding energy prediction, geometrically representing the SEMF.
Models trained on nuclear data learn representations similar to those trained on pseudo data from human-derived theory.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability of extracted knowledge is not guaranteed; representations may be complex and not easily distilled into interpretable theories.
Lack of quantitative metrics to assess interpretability.
Symbolic regression from neural features did not yield fully interpretable improvements over human-derived models.
Requires interdisciplinary collaborations and close partnerships between machine learning researchers and domain experts.
future_direction: Applying interpretability to richer data and more complex tasks.
Developing quantitative metrics for interpretability.
Exploring other scientific domains for knowledge extraction.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) promises a path toward fully understanding how neural networks make their predictions. Prior work demonstrates that even when trained to perform simple arithmetic, models can implement a variety of algorithms (sometimes concurrently) depending on initialization and hyperparameters. Does this mean neuron-level interpretability techniques have limited applicability? We argue that high-dimensional neural networks can learn low-dimensional representations of their training data that are useful beyond simply making good predictions. Such representations can be understood through the mechanistic interpretability lens and provide insights that are surprisingly faithful to human-derived domain knowledge. This indicates that such approaches to interpretability can be useful for deriving a new understanding of a problem from models trained to solve it. As a case study, we extract nuclear physics concepts by studying models trained to reproduce nuclear data.

papers.title: CoT Vectors: Transferring and Probing the Reasoning Mechanisms of LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we transfer the essence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning into LLMs in a compact, reusable, and efficient way? Also, how can CoT Vectors be used to probe the underlying mechanisms of reasoning in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge, and proposes Learnable CoT Vectors optimized via a teacher-student framework for more stable and robust guidance.
papers.conclusion: CoT Vectors extend the task vector paradigm to multi-step reasoning, and Learnable CoT Vectors provide stronger and more stable gains, while also serving as a valuable probe into the mechanisms and organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Extracted CoT Vectors show a U-shaped performance curve across layers, revealing a three-stage reasoning process (perception, reasoning, expression) in LLMs.
Learnable CoT Vectors outperform extracted vectors and are more stable across layers.
CoT Vectors achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA while requiring orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
The effectiveness of CoT Vectors varies with latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences.
CoT Vectors can be used as a probe to analyze the functional organization of reasoning in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Performance variability in intermediate layers highlights structural limitations, suggesting that task-level vectors may not fully capture intra-task diversity.
CoT Vectors can sometimes interfere with correct reasoning paths and lead to incorrect answers, as shown in case studies.
future_direction: Explore finer-grained or adaptive vectorization strategies to improve robustness and generalization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful approach to enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing implementations, such as in-context learning and fine-tuning, remain costly and inefficient. To improve CoT reasoning at a lower cost, and inspired by the task vector paradigm, we introduce CoT Vectors, compact representations that encode task-general, multi-step reasoning knowledge. Through experiments with Extracted CoT Vectors, we observe pronounced layer-wise instability, manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve that reflects a systematic three-stage reasoning process in LLMs. To address this limitation, we propose Learnable CoT Vectors, optimized under a teacher-student framework to provide more stable and robust guidance. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks and models demonstrate that CoT Vectors not only outperform existing baselines but also achieve performance comparable to parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, while requiring fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, by treating CoT Vectors as a probe, we uncover how their effectiveness varies due to latent space structure, information density, acquisition mechanisms, and pre-training differences, offering new insights into the functional organization of multi-step reasoning in LLMs. The source code will be released.

papers.title: The Geometry of Concepts: Sparse Autoencoder Feature Structure
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of sparse autoencoder features at atomic, intermediate, and large scales?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features exhibit geometric structure at three scales: atomic crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids), intermediate functional lobes (e.g., for math and code), and large-scale anisotropic point clouds with power-law eigenvalue spectra.
papers.conclusion: SAE features have geometric structure at multiple scales, which may help understand how networks represent features and improve AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Atomic-scale crystal structures (parallelograms/trapezoids) are revealed after projecting out distractor features using linear discriminant analysis (LDA).
Intermediate-scale functional lobes exist where co-occurring features (e.g., math and code features) cluster together spatially, quantified by mutual information and classification accuracy.
Large-scale point cloud structure is anisotropic with a power-law eigenvalue spectrum, steepest in middle layers.
Clustering entropy (negentropy) is lower in middle layers, indicating more structured representations.
The eigenvalue spectrum of SAE features decays as a power law, more steeply than for raw activations.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explain why the observed geometric structure forms.
future_direction: Further work to explain the origin of the geometric structure in SAE features.
Investigate whether variations in structure across layers depend on the prominence of crystals or lobes or have a different origin.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders have recently produced dictionaries of high-dimensional vectors corresponding to the universe of concepts represented by large language models. We find that this concept universe has interesting structure at three levels: 1) The "atomic" small-scale structure contains "crystals" whose faces are parallelograms or trapezoids, generalizing well-known examples such as (man-woman-king-queen). We find that the quality of such parallelograms and associated function vectors improves greatly when projecting out global distractor directions such as word length, which is efficiently done with linear discriminant analysis. 2) The "brain" intermediate-scale structure has significant spatial modularity; for example, math and code features form a "lobe" akin to functional lobes seen in neural fMRI images. We quantify the spatial locality of these lobes with multiple metrics and find that clusters of co-occurring features, at coarse enough scale, also cluster together spatially far more than one would expect if feature geometry were random. 3) The "galaxy" scale large-scale structure of the feature point cloud is not isotropic, but instead has a power law of eigenvalues with steepest slope in middle layers. We also quantify how the clustering entropy depends on the layer.

papers.title: TabPFN Through The Looking Glass: An interpretability study of TabPFN and its internal representations
papers.research_question: How does TabPFN, a tabular foundational model, process and transform input features? What information is encoded in its hidden representations and how do these representations evolve across layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that TabPFN encodes intermediate and final quantities of simple arithmetic tasks in its hidden representations in a linearly decodable manner, suggesting the model performs structured, hierarchical computation internally.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN implements systematic, hierarchical computation, with intermediate results linearly represented in the residual stream, moving towards more interpretable and trustworthy tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear regression coefficients can be linearly decoded from the model's hidden states within a single model fit, but not across different fits.
Intermediate arithmetic terms (e.g., a*b) are linearly decodable from middle-layer activations, indicating the model respects the order of operations.
The final answer can be decoded from hidden states earlier in the network (layer 5) than it is correctly projected to the output space via the logit lens (layer 8).
Input values and their linear combinations can be decoded from the activations of the answer token early in the model, suggesting a copying mechanism.
The model does not maintain a fixed, universal encoding of coefficients across different fits; representations are fit-specific.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to simple arithmetic (additive/multiplicative) toy expressions, unlike the highly complex, noisy functions found in real-world datasets.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex, real-world functions.
Using mechanistic interpretability methods like activation patching to find the mechanisms through which the answer is computed.
Manipulating the function through steering vectors or vector ablation.
papers.abstract: Tabular foundational models are pre-trained models designed for a wide range of tabular data tasks. They have shown strong performance across domains, yet their internal representations and learned concepts remain poorly understood. This lack of interpretability makes it important to study how these models process and transform input features. In this work, we analyze the information encoded inside the model's hidden representations and examine how these representations evolve across layers. We run a set of probing experiments that test for the presence of linear regression coefficients, intermediate values from complex expressions, and the final answer in early layers. These experiments allow us to reason about the computations the model performs internally. Our results provide evidence that meaningful and structured information is stored inside the representations of tabular foundational models. We observe clear signals that correspond to both intermediate and final quantities involved in the model's prediction process. This gives insight into how the model refines its inputs and how the final output emerges. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal mechanics of tabular foundational models. They show that these models encode concrete and interpretable information, which moves us closer to making their decision processes more transparent and trustworthy.

papers.title: Task Schema and Binding: A Double Dissociation Study of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning decompose into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning decomposes into two separable mechanisms—Task Schema (encoded in late MLP layers) and Binding (encoded in the residual stream)—and demonstrates a Prior-Schema trade-off where schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning operates through a compositional mechanism with two separable components (Task Schema and Binding), and the bottleneck for binding failures is attentional (recency bias) rather than output-level prior competition.
papers.key_findings:
Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching, proving separable mechanisms.
Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman ρ=-0.596, p<0.001).
Architecture generality: The Task Schema mechanism operates across all tested Transformer families and the non-Transformer Mamba model.
Binding failures are primarily due to recency-biased mis-attention (72.7%) and not prior competition (0%).
Task Schema is encoded in late MLP layers (75-95% network depth) and is robust to demonstration ordering.
papers.limitation:
Model scale: only tested up to 13B parameters; 70B+ and proprietary models remain untested.
Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning are not tested.
Binding control is incomplete (62% success rate).
Prior measurement (zero-shot probability) is an imperfect proxy that may miss latent associations.
Ecological validity: controlled tasks may not fully represent real-world ICL with noisy demonstrations and ambiguous specifications.
future_direction: Testing larger models (70B+).
Investigating Chain-of-thought (CoT) and multi-step reasoning.
Improving binding control (e.g., via attention weight patching or activation steering).
papers.abstract: We provide causal mechanistic validation that in-context learning (ICL) decomposes into two separable mechanisms: Task Schema (abstract task type recognition) and Binding (specific input-output associations). Through activation patching experiments across 9 models from 7 Transformer families plus Mamba (370M-13B parameters), we establish three key findings: 1. Double dissociation: Task Schema transfers at 100% via late MLP patching; Binding transfers at 62% via residual stream patching -- proving separable mechanisms 2. Prior-Schema trade-off: Schema reliance inversely correlates with prior knowledge (Spearman rho = -0.596, p < 0.001, N=28 task-model pairs) 3. Architecture generality: The mechanism operates across all tested architectures including the non-Transformer Mamba These findings offer a mechanistic account of the ICL puzzle that contrasts with prior views treating ICL as a monolithic mechanism (whether retrieval-based, gradient descent-like, or purely Bayesian). By establishing that Schema and Binding are neurally dissociable -- not merely behavioral modes -- we provide causal evidence for dual-process theories of ICL. Models rely on Task Schema when prior knowledge is absent, but prior knowledge interferes through attentional mis-routing (72.7% recency bias) rather than direct output competition (0%). This explains why arbitrary mappings succeed (zero prior leads to full Schema reliance) while factual overrides fail -- and reveals that the true bottleneck is attentional, not output-level. Practical implications: Understanding these dual mechanisms enables more efficient prompt engineering -- reliable schema transfer reduces required demonstrations for novel tasks, while prior-aware design can mitigate the 38% binding failure rate in high-prior scenarios, improving ICL system reliability in production deployments.

papers.title: Hidden symmetries of ReLU networks
papers.research_question: What conditions determine when feedforward ReLU neural networks have hidden symmetries beyond permutation and scaling?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that for feedforward ReLU networks with layers at least as wide as the input, a positive-measure subset of parameters has no hidden symmetries, and describes mechanisms through which hidden symmetries arise.
papers.conclusion: The probability that a network has no hidden symmetries decreases towards 0 as depth increases, while increasing towards 1 as width and input dimension increase.
papers.key_findings:
Theorem 4.1 establishes that for architectures where no layer is narrower than the input, there exist parameter settings with no hidden symmetries.
Four mechanisms are described through which hidden symmetries can arise, such as stably unactivated neurons or pairs of never co-active neurons.
Empirical approximations show that the probability of no hidden symmetries decreases with depth and increases with width and input dimension.
papers.abstract: The parameter space for any fixed architecture of feedforward ReLU neural networks serves as a proxy during training for the associated class of functions - but how faithful is this representation? It is known that many different parameter settings can determine the same function. Moreover, the degree of this redundancy is inhomogeneous: for some networks, the only symmetries are permutation of neurons in a layer and positive scaling of parameters at a neuron, while other networks admit additional hidden symmetries. In this work, we prove that, for any network architecture where no layer is narrower than the input, there exist parameter settings with no hidden symmetries. We also describe a number of mechanisms through which hidden symmetries can arise, and empirically approximate the functional dimension of different network architectures at initialization. These experiments indicate that the probability that a network has no hidden symmetries decreases towards 0 as depth increases, while increasing towards 1 as width and input dimension increase.

papers.title: Unification of Symmetries Inside Neural Networks: Transformer, Feedforward and Neural ODE
papers.research_question: How can gauge symmetries from physics be applied to understand parametric redundancies in neural networks, and can the inner workings of neural networks be interpreted through spacetime diffeomorphisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies symmetries in neural networks by interpreting parametric redundancies as gauge symmetries, showing that gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are spacetime diffeomorphisms, and that rescaling symmetries in feedforward networks and transformers correspond to these diffeomorphisms.
papers.conclusion: Gauge symmetries provide a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures, bridging machine learning and physics.
papers.key_findings:
Parametric redundancies in neural networks can be interpreted as gauge symmetries in physics.
Gauge symmetries in neural ODEs are mathematically characterized by spacetime diffeomorphisms.
The rescaling symmetry of feedforward neural networks is lifted to spacetime diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs.
Transformers can be viewed as integrated nonlinear neural ODEs, and their gauge symmetries correspond to diffeomorphisms.
Regularizations in neural networks can be understood as gauge fixing conditions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of neural networks, including transformers, remains one of the most challenging puzzles in machine learning. This study introduces a novel approach by applying the principles of gauge symmetries, a key concept in physics, to neural network architectures. By regarding model functions as physical observables, we find that parametric redundancies of various machine learning models can be interpreted as gauge symmetries. We mathematically formulate the parametric redundancies in neural ODEs, and find that their gauge symmetries are given by spacetime diffeomorphisms, which play a fundamental role in Einstein's theory of gravity. Viewing neural ODEs as a continuum version of feedforward neural networks, we show that the parametric redundancies in feedforward neural networks are indeed lifted to diffeomorphisms in neural ODEs. We further extend our analysis to transformer models, finding natural correspondences with neural ODEs and their gauge symmetries. The concept of gauge symmetries sheds light on the complex behavior of deep learning models through physics and provides us with a unifying perspective for analyzing various machine learning architectures.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-as-a-Judge: Representation-as-a-Judge with Small Language Models via Semantic Capacity Asymmetry
papers.research_question: Can small language models serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations, even when their generation is poor?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis and introduces INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that extracts evaluation signals from small model representations, enabling efficient and accurate reference-free evaluation.
papers.conclusion: Small LMs retain strong evaluative signals in their internal representations, and the Representation-as-a-Judge paradigm via INSPECTOR offers a scalable and interpretable solution for evaluation and data curation.
papers.key_findings:
Small LMs encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states despite weak generation.
Probing internal representations with INSPECTOR outperforms prompt-based evaluation with small LMs and closely approximates large LLM judges.
The Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis is supported: evaluation requires less semantic capacity than generation.
Probing classifiers can serve as reliable data filters for supervised fine-tuning, leading to performance gains.
Larger LLMs do not necessarily provide stronger evaluation signals than smaller ones.
papers.limitation:
Multiclass prediction performance of probing classifiers is modest (50-60%) compared to binary classification.
Out-of-distribution generalization for multiclass probing is limited, with F1 scores dropping significantly.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as reference-free evaluators via prompting, but this "LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm is costly, opaque, and sensitive to prompt design. In this work, we investigate whether smaller models can serve as efficient evaluators by leveraging internal representations instead of surface generation. We uncover a consistent empirical pattern: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states. This motivates us to propose the Semantic Capacity Asymmetry Hypothesis: evaluation requires significantly less semantic capacity than generation and can be grounded in intermediate representations, suggesting that evaluation does not necessarily need to rely on large-scale generative models but can instead leverage latent features from smaller ones. Our findings motivate a paradigm shift from LLM-as-a-Judge to Representation-as-a-Judge, a decoding-free evaluation strategy that probes internal model structure rather than relying on prompted output. We instantiate this paradigm through INSPECTOR, a probing-based framework that predicts aspect-level evaluation scores from small model representations. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, GPQA) show that INSPECTOR substantially outperforms prompting-based small LMs and closely approximates full LLM judges, while offering a more efficient, reliable, and interpretable alternative for scalable evaluation.

papers.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Interpretability Methods through Explanation Invariance and Equivariance
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the robustness of interpretability methods when the model is invariant under a symmetry group? Specifically, do explanations remain invariant or equivariant under the same symmetries?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to evaluate the robustness of interpretability methods through explanation invariance and equivariance, provides theoretical guarantees for some methods, and empirical evaluation across multiple modalities and symmetry groups.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the proposed framework allows for evaluating and improving the robustness of interpretability methods, and provides practical guidelines for users.
papers.key_findings:
Not all interpretability methods are robust; some lack invariance/equivariance when the model is invariant.
Theoretical guarantees exist for some methods under certain conditions (e.g., invariant baselines).
Robustness can be improved by aggregating explanations over symmetries (Proposition 2.3).
Empirical evaluation shows that methods like Integrated Gradients and DeepLift are more robust than Gradient Shap and perturbation-based methods.
The framework provides guidelines for users to obtain robust explanations.
papers.limitation:
The framework does not apply to tabular data, as it requires structure in the data.
The metrics can be expensive to compute for large symmetry groups, requiring Monte Carlo estimation.
The framework assumes the model is invariant, which may not hold in practice.
future_direction: Extend the framework to infinite symmetry groups.
Apply the framework to other invariant architectures beyond those studied.
Investigate the effect of distribution shift on robustness metrics.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods are valuable only if their explanations faithfully describe the explained model. In this work, we consider neural networks whose predictions are invariant under a specific symmetry group. This includes popular architectures, ranging from convolutional to graph neural networks. Any explanation that faithfully explains this type of model needs to be in agreement with this invariance property. We formalize this intuition through the notion of explanation invariance and equivariance by leveraging the formalism from geometric deep learning. Through this rigorous formalism, we derive (1) two metrics to measure the robustness of any interpretability method with respect to the model symmetry group; (2) theoretical robustness guarantees for some popular interpretability methods and (3) a systematic approach to increase the invariance of any interpretability method with respect to a symmetry group. By empirically measuring our metrics for explanations of models associated with various modalities and symmetry groups, we derive a set of 5 guidelines to allow users and developers of interpretability methods to produce robust explanations.

papers.title: Emergent Extreme-View Geometry in 3D Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do 3D foundation models have an emergent understanding of extreme-view geometry, and how can we enhance it through lightweight alignment?
papers.core_contribution: We find that 3D foundation models have an emergent understanding of extreme-view geometry and propose a lightweight alignment scheme that fine-tunes only backbone biases to improve extreme-view pose estimation while preserving multi-task performance, and introduce the MegaUnScene benchmark for evaluation.
papers.conclusion: 3D foundation models possess an internal 3D language that enables emergent extreme-view geometry understanding; this can be enhanced via lightweight bias-only fine-tuning, and the MegaUnScene benchmark facilitates evaluation in unconstrained settings.
papers.key_findings:
3DFMs exhibit emergent understanding of extreme-view geometry, as shown by cross-view attention maps.
A lightweight alignment scheme that tunes only backbone biases significantly improves relative pose estimation under extreme views without degrading other tasks.
The proposed method sets new state-of-the-art on extreme rotation estimation benchmarks.
The introduced MegaUnScene benchmark provides a challenging testbed for 3DFMs on unseen Internet scenes.
papers.limitation: Large translational displacements remain intrinsically challenging and are not improved by the proposed alignment.
future_direction: Improving translation estimation for extreme-view pairs
Extending the alignment scheme to other 3D tasks
Exploring the internal 3D language in other 3D foundation models
papers.abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) have recently transformed 3D vision, enabling joint prediction of depths, poses, and point maps directly from images. Yet their ability to reason under extreme, non-overlapping views remains largely unexplored. In this work, we study their internal representations and find that 3DFMs exhibit an emergent understanding of extreme-view geometry, despite never being trained for such conditions.
